name: Masahiro
explanation: Masahiro can be written with two different kanji. One means "righteous breadth", and the other means "elegant breadth". The choice of kanji could reflect what a family hopes to see in a son, such as an upright administrator whose fairness reaches every corner of the domain or a courtier of wide and graceful accomplishment.
notes: Masahiro is a very common real Japanese male given name. Common kanji include 正広 (correct/righteous + wide/prosperous) or 雅広 (elegant + wide). The explanation's 'righteous breadth' and 'elegant breadth' are reasonable glosses of 正広 and 雅広. The rest of the explanation is Rokugan-flavored but the name itself is authentic.

name: Kenshiro
explanation: Kenshiro - Stemming from the word "ken", which denotes health and sturdiness of body, this name embodies the spirit of a son expected to grow strong enough to carry his house's burdens. It resonates with those who are hardy, plain-spoken, and slow to complain.
notes: Kenshiro is a real but uncommon Japanese male name, most famous from the manga 'Fist of the North Star' (Hokuto no Ken). Common kanji would be 健史郎 (healthy + history + son) or 謙四郎.

name: Noboru
explanation: Noboru means "to ascend" or "to climb", which can suggest ambition tempered by patience or a steady rise through the ranks of the Imperial bureaucracy. People with this name may be persistent and quietly determined.
notes: Noboru is a very common real Japanese male given name, written 昇 or 登. It genuinely means 'to ascend/climb.' The explanation is accurate for the name's real meaning. The 'Imperial bureaucracy' reference is Rokugan-flavored but the core meaning is correct.

name: Yasunori
explanation: Yasunori - A name that means "peaceful law", evoking the magistrate who keeps order in a province without ever needing to raise their voice.
notes: Yasunori is a real Japanese male given name. Common kanji include 安典 (peaceful + law/ceremony) and 泰典 (tranquil + law). The explanation's meaning is a reasonable gloss of 安典. 安徳 (peaceful + virtue) is another real writing.

name: Touma
explanation: Touma - This name is inspired by the natural element of the winter horse, symbolizing endurance that carries its rider through the hardest season. It is often chosen for its connection to the snowbound roads of the northern provinces and its representation of resilience valued above comfort.
notes: Touma is a real Japanese male given name, sometimes written 当麻, 斗真, or 冬馬. The reading 冬馬 (winter + horse) exists but is uncommon; more common kanji don't mean 'winter horse.' The explanation picks a poetic but less common interpretation. The name itself is authentic.

name: Isao
explanation: Isao can be written with two different kanji. One means "merit", and the other means "distinguished service". The choice of kanji could reflect the deed a family most hopes to see, such as steady accomplishment in office or a single act of valor recorded in the clan annals.
notes: Isao is a very common real Japanese male given name, written 功 or 勲, genuinely meaning 'merit/accomplishment/achievement.' The explanation is accurate.

name: Tadashi
explanation: Tadashi chose their name in honor of the famous Akodo Tadashi, who held the line at Beiden Pass with only forty ashigaru against a bandit army of hundreds.
notes: Tadashi is a very common real Japanese male given name, written 正 or 忠, meaning 'correct/righteous' or 'loyal.' Akodo is a fictional L5R Lion clan family name, and Beiden Pass is a fictional L5R location. The story is entirely Rokugan-specific fiction.

name: Shunichi
explanation: Shunichi can be written with two different kanji. One means "talented first son", and the other means "first of spring". The choice of kanji could reflect what the family chose to record, such as high hopes for an eldest boy's gifts or a birth in the first month of the year.
notes: Shunichi is a common real Japanese male given name, often written 俊一 (talented + one) or 春一 (spring + one). The explanation's two glosses follow 俊一 and 春一. The name is authentic.

name: Takehiko
explanation: Takehiko - This name is inspired by the natural element of bamboo, symbolizing strength that bends without breaking. It is often chosen for its connection to the groves that shelter a village from the wind and its representation of a noble bearing that yields to the storm and stands again.
notes: Takehiko is a real Japanese male given name, commonly written 竹彦 (bamboo + prince/boy) or 武彦 (martial + prince). The explanation accurately describes the 竹彦 reading. 彦 (hiko) is a classical element meaning 'prince' or 'lad' used in many traditional male names. The bamboo symbolism is genuinely part of Japanese culture.

name: Moriyasu
explanation: Moriyasu - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Forest Guardian, in which a woodcutter spared a sacred grove and was blessed by the Fortune of Rice. It reflects qualities such as reverence for nature and selfless restraint.
notes: Moriyasu is a real Japanese male given name, written 守安 (protect + peace) or 盛安. The tale of the 'Forest Guardian' and the 'Fortune of Rice' are fictional Rokugan elements (Fortunes are the L5R setting's divine beings). The name itself is authentic but the backstory is setting-specific.

name: Noriyoshi
explanation: Noriyoshi means "law and righteousness" or "ceremony rightly kept", which can suggest a magistrate's exactness or a courtier's care for the proper form of things. People with this name may be sticklers who believe that doing a thing correctly is the same as doing it well.
notes: Noriyoshi is a real Japanese male given name, written 典義 (law/ceremony + righteousness) or 法義.

name: Tetsuro
explanation: Tetsuro can be written with two different kanji. One means "clear-minded philosophy", and the other means "bright iron". The choice of kanji could reflect the path a family foresees, such as a scholar of the courts or a bushi tempered like a blade.
notes: Tetsuro (or Tetsurou) is a real Japanese male given name, commonly written 哲朗 (philosophy + clear) or 鉄朗 (iron + clear). The explanation's two glosses follow 哲朗 and 鉄朗. The name is well-attested in real Japan.

name: Hayato
explanation: Hayato can be written with two different kanji. One means "falcon person", and the other means "swift person". The choice of kanji could reflect what a family prizes, such as the keen eye of a hunter or the speed of a courier who never fails to deliver.
notes: Hayato is a very common real Japanese male given name, written 隼人 (falcon + person) or 速人 (speed + person). The falcon interpretation (隼人) is accurate. Historically, Hayato also refers to the Hayato people of ancient southern Kyushu.

name: Yoshikuni
explanation: Yoshikuni can be written with two different kanji. One means "righteous province", and the other means "virtuous province". The choice of kanji could reflect the kind of rule a family hopes its son will bring, such as strict justice in the magistrate's court or gentle benevolence toward the farmers who feed the domain.
notes: Yoshikuni is a real Japanese male given name, written 義都 (righteousness + country) or 善都. The kanji breakdown is accurate: 義 (yoshi, righteousness) + 都 (kuni, country/province). Minamoto no Yoshikuni was a notable historical figure (Heian period). The name analysis is correct.

name: Fumihiko
explanation: Fumihiko - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of calligraphy, this name represents the belief that a brush can shape the world as surely as a blade. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the discipline of the written word and have a deep respect for the scholars who preserve the Empire's history.
notes: Fumihiko is a real Japanese male given name, written 文彦 (writing/literature + prince) or 史彦. The calligraphy connection is appropriate since 文 (fumi) relates to writing and literature. Calligraphy (shodo) is a genuine traditional Japanese art form. The 'Empire' reference is Rokugan-specific.

name: Muneharu
explanation: The name Muneharu is associated with the famous Siege of Takamatsu Castle, in which a loyal commander chose to take his own life by ritual suicide performed in a boat upon the flooded waters surrounding his castle, so that his garrison might be spared. Those who choose this name try to embody values of selfless loyalty and the willingness to sacrifice oneself for those in one's care.
notes: Muneharu is a real Japanese name, famously borne by Shimizu Muneharu, a Sengoku-period castle lord. During Toyotomi Hideyoshi's siege of Takamatsu Castle, the castle was flooded by damming a river. Muneharu agreed to commit seppuku in a boat on the floodwaters in exchange for his garrison's lives - an act of loyalty celebrated in Japanese history.

name: Tesshin
explanation: The name Tesshin is inspired by the great training halls of the capital, known for producing swordsmen who were equally devoted to the way of the brush and the way of the blade. The name reflects the discipline of the place and is often chosen by those who value the pursuit of mastery in both martial arts and the contemplative traditions.
notes: Tesshin is a real Japanese name, most famously borne by Yamaoka Tesshu (also read Tesshin), the renowned Meiji-era swordsman, calligrapher, and Zen practitioner who founded the Shumpukan dojo. Written 鉄舟 (iron + rudder) or 哲心 (philosophy + heart).

name: Harumichi
explanation: Harumichi - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the First Blossom, an event that emphasizes renewal and the beauty of impermanence. People choose this name to reflect their values for appreciating each season of life as it comes.
notes: Harumichi is a real but uncommon Japanese male given name, written 春道 (spring + path) or 春通. The 'Festival of the First Blossom' is likely a Rokugan-specific event, though Japan does have many real hanami (cherry blossom viewing) festivals. The theme of impermanence (mono no aware) is a genuine Japanese aesthetic concept.

name: Sadakazu
explanation: Sadakazu can be written with two different kanji. One means "loyal and single-minded", and the other means "settled harmony". The choice of kanji could reflect the temperament a family hopes for, such as an unwavering retainer or a mediator who keeps the peace in a divided household.
notes: Sadakazu is a real Japanese male given name, written 貞一 (loyal/chaste + one) or 定和 (fixed/determined + harmony). The explanation's glosses follow 貞一 and 定和. The name is authentic and the meaning is reasonable.

name: Jinsaku
explanation: Jinsaku - This name means "benevolent design". It represents the careful forethought of a leader who plans for the wellbeing of those under his care.
notes: Jinsaku is a plausible but uncommon Japanese male name. It could be written 仁作 (benevolence + make/create) or 仁策 (benevolence + plan). The meaning 'benevolent design' is a reasonable interpretation. The name follows Japanese naming conventions but is not commonly attested.

name: Makoto
explanation: Makoto can be written with two different kanji. One means "sincerity", and the other means "truth". The choice of kanji could reflect which virtue a family holds highest, such as the sincerity of a retainer's service or a devotion to plain truth that no courtier can bend.
notes: Makoto is a very common real Japanese given name (used for both genders, but traditionally male), written 誠 (sincerity) or 真 (truth). The meaning is completely accurate. Makoto/sincerity (gi or makoto) is indeed considered a bushido virtue in various formulations, though 'bushido' as a codified system is somewhat romanticized.

name: Shigemori
explanation: Shigemori can be written with two different kanji. One means "luxuriant prosperity", and the other means "layered abundance". The choice of kanji could reflect one's temperament, such as the quiet flourishing of a well-managed estate or the accumulated weight of generations of service.
notes: Shigemori is a real Japanese male given name, most famously borne by Taira no Shigemori, the eldest son of Taira no Kiyomori in the Heian period. Commonly written 重盛 (heavy/layered + prosperous) or 茂盛 (luxuriant + prosperous). The historical Shigemori was known for his moderate temperament in contrast to his father's ambition.

name: Tomokazu
explanation: Tomokazu can be written with two different kanji. One means "friendly harmony", and the other means "wisdom foremost". The choice of kanji could reflect the gift a family most wishes on a child, such as easy companionship among fellow ashigaru or the sharp mind that rises to village headman.
notes: Tomokazu is a common real Japanese male given name, written 友和 (friend + harmony) or 智一 (wisdom + one). The meaning 'friendly harmony' accurately reflects the 友和 writing. The name is well-attested in modern Japan.

name: Akimoto
explanation: Akimoto - This name is inspired by the natural element of autumn, symbolizing the stillness that settles over the fields once the harvest is in. It is often chosen for its connection to the season when the year's labor is counted and its representation of quiet, well-founded contentment.
notes: Akimoto is primarily known as a Japanese surname (秋元, autumn + origin/foundation), not a given name. It is very common as a family name (e.g., Akimoto Yasushi of AKB48 fame). Using it as a given name would be unusual and might read strangely to a Japanese audience. The meaning 'autumn's foundation' accurately reflects the kanji.

name: Hidetsugu
explanation: Hidetsugu chose their name in honor of the famous Toyotomi Hidetsugu, who rose to become regent and ruled in his uncle's name, only to be undone by the politics of succession and forced to end his own life at Mount Koya.
notes: Hidetsugu is a real Japanese male given name, most infamously borne by Toyotomi Hidetsugu, nephew and adopted heir of Toyotomi Hideyoshi. After Hideyoshi's biological son was born, Hidetsugu fell from favor and was ordered to commit seppuku at Mount Koya in 1595. Written 秀次 (excellent + next).

name: Kuniaki
explanation: Kuniaki can be written with two different kanji. One means "bright capital", and the other means "bright country". The choice of kanji could reflect where the family expects its son to serve, such as a post at the Imperial court or the governance of a rural province.
notes: Kuniaki is a real Japanese male given name, written 都明 (country + bright) or 国明. The explanation's glosses follow 都明 and 国明. Notable bearers include Koiso Kuniaki, a WWII-era Prime Minister of Japan. The name is well-attested historically.

name: Nobuhiko
explanation: Nobuhiko - Composed of the elements "nobu" meaning "trust" and "hiko" meaning "prince", this name symbolizes a leader worthy of faith. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of reliable authority.
notes: Nobuhiko is a real Japanese male given name, written 信彦 (trust/faith + prince). The kanji breakdown is accurate: 信 (nobu, trust) + 彦 (hiko, prince/boy). The name is well-attested, borne by various public figures. The explanation is linguistically sound.

name: Yorimoto
explanation: Yorimoto - With origins in the legend of a general who rallied scattered warrior clans under a single banner and established a new seat of power far from the Imperial capital, this name evokes a sense of bold vision and the will to reshape the world. It appeals to those who admire leaders who forge new orders from the chaos of civil war.
notes: Yorimoto is a plausible Japanese male name, very close to the historical Minamoto no Yoritomo (源頼朝), founder of the Kamakura shogunate - the first military government of Japan, established far from the Imperial court in Kyoto. The explanation now echoes Yoritomo's real accomplishment of uniting the warrior class and founding a new center of power, rather than referencing the fictional Tao of Shinsei.

name: Nagamasa
explanation: Nagamasa - Stemming from the word "naga", which denotes longevity or endurance, this name embodies the spirit of permanence through generations. It resonates with those who are deeply devoted to preserving their family's legacy.
notes: Nagamasa is a real Japanese male given name, most famously borne by Azai Nagamasa, the Sengoku-period daimyo who was brother-in-law to Oda Nobunaga. Written 長政 (long + governance). The element 長 (naga) means 'long' rather than strictly 'longevity,' but the connotation of endurance is appropriate. The name is historically well-attested.

name: Sojuro
explanation: Sojuro - A name derived from the fusion of "lineage" and "tenth son", reflecting a balance between the weight of an inherited tradition and the humility of a last-born who must earn his place in it. It is often embraced by those who strive for mastery of an art handed down through generations.
notes: Sojuro (Soujuurou) is a real but archaic Japanese male name, most famously associated with the kabuki lineage name Sakata Sojuro, a prestigious stage name passed down through generations of kabuki actors since the Edo period. Written 宗十郎 or similar.

name: Narikazu
explanation: Narikazu can be written with two different kanji. One means "becoming harmony", and the other means "becoming one". The choice of kanji could reflect what the family hopes a child will grow into, such as a peacemaker in a quarrelsome village or a man of single, undivided purpose.
notes: Narikazu is a plausible but uncommon Japanese male name. It could be written 成和 (become + harmony) or 成一 (become + one). The kanji breakdown is reasonable: 成 (nari, to become) + 和 (kazu, harmony). However, 和 is more commonly read 'wa' or 'kazu' meaning 'harmony' or 'peace.' The name follows valid Japanese naming conventions.

name: Shinsaku
explanation: Shinsaku - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of sword-polishing, this name represents the patience required to reveal the true beauty hidden within rough steel. It is often chosen by those who appreciate meticulous craftsmanship and have a deep respect for the togishi who spend lifetimes perfecting a single blade.
notes: Shinsaku is a real Japanese male given name, most famously borne by Takasugi Shinsaku, the Bakumatsu-era revolutionary. Written 晋作 (advance + create) or 新作 (new + creation). Togishi (sword polishers) are real traditional Japanese craftspeople. However, the name Shinsaku itself does not etymologically connect to sword-polishing. The togishi reference is culturally authentic even if the name connection is invented.

name: Kanehiro
explanation: The name Kanehiro is associated with the famous Restoration of the Kaiu Wall, in which engineers and warriors labored together for a decade to rebuild what the Shadowlands had shattered. Those who choose this name try to embody values of perseverance and the unity of purpose between sword and craft.
notes: Kanehiro is a real Japanese male given name, written 兼広 (combine + wide) or 金広 (gold + wide). The Kaiu Wall and Shadowlands are fictional L5R elements (the Kaiu are a Crab clan family who maintain a great wall against the Shadowlands). The story is entirely Rokugan-specific. The name itself is authentic.

name: Gennosuke
explanation: The name Gennosuke is inspired by the Seikitsu Mountains, known for their treacherous passes and hidden monasteries. The name reflects the quiet solitude of the place and is often chosen by those who value introspection and the pursuit of deeper truths.
notes: Gennosuke is a real traditional Japanese male given name, written 源之助 (source + possessive particle + help) or similar. It follows the classical -nosuke pattern common in samurai-era names. The Seikitsu Mountains are a fictional L5R location. The name is authentic but the geographical backstory is setting-specific.

name: Natsuhiko
explanation: Natsuhiko - This name pays tribute to the Bon Festival, an event that emphasizes honoring the spirits of ancestors and remembering the debt the living owe to the dead. People choose this name to reflect their values for filial piety and reverence for those who came before.
notes: Natsuhiko is a real but uncommon Japanese male given name, written 夏彦 (summer + prince). The Bon Festival (Obon) is a real and major Japanese Buddhist event held in mid-August to honor deceased ancestors. The description of Obon is accurate. The connection between a 'summer' name and a summer festival is logical, making this explanation culturally grounded.

name: Daigo
explanation: Daigo - This name represents "great enlightenment" and is often chosen by those who are devoted students of the Tao or who are expected to seek wisdom beyond the material world.
notes: Daigo is a real Japanese male given name and also a historically significant name. Emperor Daigo was the 60th emperor of Japan. Written 醜醛 (the finest flavor, a Buddhist term for ultimate truth) or 大悟 (great enlightenment). The meaning 'great enlightenment' is accurate for the 大悟 writing. The 'Tao' reference is L5R-specific (Tao of Shinsei), though 醜醛 has genuine Buddhist connotations.

name: Ujiyasu
explanation: Ujiyasu - This name means "clan protector". It represents steadfast devotion to one's family and the willingness to sacrifice personal glory for the safety of one's kin.
notes: Ujiyasu is a real Japanese male given name, most famously borne by Hojo Ujiyasu (北条氏康), one of the greatest Sengoku-period daimyo known as the 'Lion of Sagami.' Written 氏康 (clan + peace/health). The meaning 'clan protector' is a reasonable interpretation of 氏康, though 康 more precisely means 'peace/ease.' The name is historically significant and authentic.

name: Munetoshi
explanation: Munetoshi can be written with two different kanji. One means "benefit of the lineage", and the other means "virtue of the lineage". The choice of kanji could reflect what a family asks of its heir, such as the practical prosperity of the house or the moral standing that keeps its name honored.
notes: Munetoshi is a real but uncommon Japanese male name, written 宗利 (clan/core + benefit) or 宗徳. The explanation's glosses follow 宗利 and 宗徳. Notable bearer: Kamiizumi Nobutsuna's original name was Kamiizumi Munetoshi, a famous swordsman. The name is authentic and the explanation is reasonable.

name: Hiroki
explanation: Hiroki - This name is inspired by the natural element of the great tree, symbolizing growth that spreads wide and stands for generations. It is often chosen for its connection to the camphor trees that shade a village shrine and its representation of shelter given freely to all beneath its branches.
notes: Hiroki is a very common real Japanese male given name. Common writings include 広樹 (vast + trees), 大樹 (big + trees), and 博喜 (abundant + joy). The explanation follows the 広樹 and 大樹 writings. The camphor tree (kusunoki) reference is a nice cultural detail, as camphor trees are significant in Japanese culture.

name: Mitsunaga
explanation: Mitsunaga can be written with two different kanji. One means "eternal light", and the other means "long light". The choice of kanji could reflect the shade of hope behind it, such as a light that never goes out or one that reaches far across the domain.
notes: Mitsunaga is a real Japanese male given name, written 光永 (light + eternal) or 光長 (light + long). The explanation's glosses follow 光永 and 光長. Historical bearer: Tosa Mitsunaga, a Heian-period painter. The name is authentic and the explanation is accurate.

name: Soushi
explanation: Soushi can be written with two different kanji. One means "creative aspiration", and the other means "history of the lineage". The choice of kanji could reflect the path a family sees for a child, such as an artisan who makes new things or a scholar who records the old ones.
notes: Soushi (Soushi/Soshi) is a plausible Japanese male name with multiple possible writings: 創志 (creative + aspiration), 宗史 (clan + history), or 草紙 (draft paper). The meaning 'creative aspiration' works for 創志. Note that 'Soshi' is also the name of a Scorpion clan family in L5R. As a standalone given name it is somewhat uncommon but valid.

name: Kiyomori
explanation: Kiyomori - Derived from the phrase "clear prosperity", this name embodies the idea of brilliance that rises from humble origins to command the highest circles of power. It is often associated with those whose ambition reshapes the world around them.
notes: Kiyomori is a real and historically famous Japanese male name, most notably borne by Taira no Kiyomori (平清盛), the powerful Heian-period military leader who rose from provincial warrior stock to dominate the Imperial court. Written 清盛 (pure/clear + prosperous/thriving).

name: Nobutada
explanation: Nobutada - Composed of the elements "nobu" meaning "faith" and "tada" meaning "loyal", this name symbolizes unwavering fidelity to one's oaths. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of a samurai who would sooner die than break a vow.
notes: Nobutada is a real Japanese male given name, most famously borne by Oda Nobutada, eldest son of Oda Nobunaga. Written 信忠 (faith + loyal). The kanji breakdown is accurate: 信 (nobu, faith/trust) + 忠 (tada, loyal). The historical Nobutada died fighting at Nijo Castle during the Honno-ji Incident, which poignantly echoes the explanation's theme of dying rather than breaking faith.

name: Arinaga
explanation: Arinaga can be written with two different kanji. One means "eternal existence", and the other means "long existence". The choice of kanji could reflect the scale of a family's hope, such as a line that endures for all time or a son who simply lives long.
notes: Arinaga is a plausible but uncommon Japanese male name. It could be written 有永 (exist + eternal) or 有長 (exist + long). The explanation's glosses follow 有永 and 有長. The name follows standard Japanese naming conventions but is not commonly attested as a given name; it is more recognizable as a surname.

name: Asahito
explanation: Asahito - Composed of the elements "asa" meaning "morning" and "hito" meaning "person", this name symbolizes one who brings the clarity of dawn to all matters. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of fresh resolve and unclouded judgment.
notes: Asahito is a plausible but uncommon Japanese male name. It could be written 朝人 (morning + person). Names ending in -hito are associated with the Imperial family (e.g., Naruhito, Akihito), so this name has a regal connotation. The kanji analysis is accurate. The name follows valid conventions but is not commonly used outside imperial naming traditions.

name: Bunzaemon
explanation: Bunzaemon - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Literate Gatekeeper, in which a humble ashigaru taught himself to read the classics and was elevated to serve as a magistrate's scribe. It reflects qualities such as self-improvement and the belief that learning transcends caste.
notes: Bunzaemon is a real traditional Japanese male name following the classical -zaemon (左衛門) pattern, originally a court guard title that became a common name suffix in the Edo period. Written 文左衛門 (literature + left guard gate). The tale of the 'Literate Gatekeeper' appears to be invented for the setting, and ashigaru is a real term for foot soldiers. The name pattern is historically authentic.

name: Bokuden
explanation: Bokuden - With origins in the legend of a wandering swordsman who defeated a hundred challengers without drawing his blade, this name evokes a sense of mastery achieved through restraint. It appeals to those who admire the principle that the greatest victory requires no violence.
notes: Bokuden is a real historical Japanese name, most famously borne by Tsukahara Bokuden (塚原卜伝), a legendary swordsman of the Muromachi/Sengoku period. The explanation closely mirrors real legends about Bokuden, who was indeed famous for stories about winning without fighting - most famously, he allegedly defeated a braggart on a boat by stranding him on an island without drawing his sword. This is one of the most historically grounded entries in the pool.

name: Busho
explanation: Busho - Stemming from the word "bu", which denotes martial valor, this name embodies the spirit of the warrior who leads from the front. It resonates with those who are bold in battle and unflinching before danger.
notes: Busho is not a common Japanese given name. The word busho (武将) means 'military commander/general' and is a common noun rather than a personal name. Using it as a given name would be unusual, somewhat like naming someone 'General' in English. 武 (bu, martial) is accurately described. The name is plausible in a fantasy setting but would be atypical in real Japan.

name: Chikara
explanation: Chikara - This name means "strength" or "power". It represents the inner fortitude of one who bears heavy burdens without complaint, as much as it does physical might.
notes: Chikara (力) is a real Japanese given name meaning 'strength' or 'power.' The explanation is accurate regarding the kanji meaning. It is used as a male given name in Japan, though not extremely common.

name: Chusei
explanation: Chusei - This name signifies "loyalty" or "fidelity", and may suggest that the one who chooses it values the bond between lord and vassal above all earthly concerns.
notes: Chusei (忠誠) means 'loyalty' or 'fidelity' in Japanese, and the explanation is accurate. As a given name it is uncommon but plausible; it follows Japanese naming conventions. The 'lord and vassal' framing is setting-flavored but consistent with historical samurai culture.

name: Chikahito
explanation: Chikahito - A name derived from the fusion of "chika" meaning "near" or "familiar" and "hito" meaning "person", reflecting a balance between intimacy and duty. It is often embraced by those who strive for closeness to the people they serve and protect.
notes: Chikahito is a plausible Japanese given name. 'Chika' (近/親) can mean 'near' or 'intimate' and 'hito' (人) means 'person,' so the etymology is accurate. It has been used historically as a Japanese male name, including by imperial princes (e.g., Prince Chikahito).

name: Doshin
explanation: Doshin - Derived from the phrase "heart of the way", this name embodies the idea of a seeker who walks a spiritual path with unwavering purpose. It is also a historical term for low-ranking law enforcement officers in Edo-period Japan, and is often associated with those who serve as ward constables or devoted students of philosophy.
notes: Doshin (道心) meaning 'heart of the way' is a real Buddhist term. Additionally, 'doshin' (同心) was a real Edo-period title for low-ranking police officers/constables. Updated to remove the fictional reference and note the historical police role, which the explanation already alluded to with 'ward constables.'

name: Daishin
explanation: Daishin - Stemming from the word "dai", which denotes greatness, this name embodies the spirit of a heart large enough to hold everyone who depends on it. It resonates with those who are generous, open-handed and slow to take offense.
notes: Daishin is a plausible Japanese name. 大心 ('great heart') and 大神 ('great spirit/deity') are valid kanji combinations. The name is more commonly encountered in Buddhist contexts (e.g., monk names) than as a secular given name. The explanation is reasonable.

name: Eiichi

name: Jubei
explanation: Jubei chose their name in honor of the famous Yagyu Jubei, the one-eyed swordsman who vanished from public life for over a decade and returned as one of the greatest duelists his clan had ever produced, his missing years the subject of endless legend.

name: Okimasa

name: Rensho

name: Umehiko

name: Wataru

name: Watarai

name: Zentaro

explanation: Ryunoshin means "advance of the dragon" or "the dragon's progress", which can suggest a boy expected to rise as the dragon does through storm clouds or a family's hope that its fortunes are climbing. name: Ukyo

name: Wakizaka

notes: Wakizaka (脇坂) is a real Japanese surname. Wakizaka Yasuharu (1554-1626) was a daimyo who famously switched sides from the Western Army to the Eastern Army during the Battle of Sekigahara (1600), contributing to Tokugawa Ieyasu's decisive victory.

name: Yasumichi

name: Zoroku

name: Nariakira

name: Naomasa
explanation: Naomasa - A name derived from the fusion of "honesty" and "governance", reflecting a balance between plain-spoken truth and the careful exercise of authority. It is often embraced by those who strive for upright rule and straight dealing.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 直政: 直 'straight, honest' (nao) and 政 'governance, administration' (masa). Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Ii Naomasa, one of Tokugawa Ieyasu's Four Guardian Generals.

name: Akikiyo
explanation: Akikiyo - Derived from the phrase "a light that stays clear", this name embodies the idea of brightness that does not dim or cloud. It is often associated with those who keep their judgment clear when others are dazzled.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 光清: 光 'light, shine' (aki is a nanori reading; the everyday reading is hikari or mitsu) and 清 'pure, clear' (kiyo). Samurai formal-name style; the 光 = aki reading is a nanori convention worth flagging.

name: Jinshiro
explanation: Jinshiro - A name derived from the fusion of "greatly" and "fourth son", reflecting a balance between the modest place of a late-born child and the outsized welcome that greeted him. It is often embraced by those who strive for more than their birth order promised.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and among Sengoku and late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 甚四郎: 甚 'very, greatly' (jin) plus 四郎 'fourth son' (shiro), a birth-order name of the everyday commoner type. Commoner/everyday style, not a samurai formal name.

name: Fuyufusa
explanation: Fuyufusa - This name is inspired by the natural element of winter, symbolizing the season that gathers a household into one warm chamber. It is often chosen for its connection to the cold months when a warrior's family draws close and its representation of fellowship that outlasts the snow.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 冬房: 冬 'winter' (fuyu) and 房 'chamber, cluster, tassel' (fusa). Samurai formal-name style; 房 as a nanori element is typical of Kamakura-period warrior names.

name: Bunkichi
explanation: Bunkichi - This name signifies good fortune found in letters and learning, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values literacy, careful accounts, and the luck that follows a well-kept ledger.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 文吉: 文 'letters, writing' (bun) and 吉 'good luck' (kichi). Commoner/everyday style, of the -kichi type common among late-Edo townsmen and villagers.

name: Chikakiyo
explanation: Chikakiyo chose their name in honor of the famous Doji Chikakiyo, who cleared a governor's household of a decade of embezzlement without once raising their voice or shaming a single clerk in public.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian, Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 親清: 親 'parent, intimate' (chika is a nanori reading) and 清 'pure, clear' (kiyo). Samurai formal-name style; the 親 = chika reading is a standard nanori convention.

name: Juemon
explanation: Juemon - This name signifies the weight of duty carried at a household's gate, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values responsibility, reliability, and the steady bearing of burdens others set down.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers, Edo village registers (Kiyose) and among early and late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 重右衛門: 重 'heavy, weighty, layered' (ju) plus 右衛門 'guard of the right gate' (emon), the hereditary-office suffix that Edo commoners wore as a name ending. Commoner/everyday style of the -emon type.

name: Chikatane
explanation: Chikatane - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The parent is known by the seed", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value the raising of a worthy heir above any deed of their own.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 親胤: 親 'parent, intimate' (chika, nanori reading) and 胤 'heir, lineage, seed' (tane). Samurai formal-name style; 胤 is a classic nanori element of the Chiba lineage. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Isoemon
explanation: Isoemon - This name pays tribute to the Blessing of the Tide Rocks, a coastal calendar event that emphasizes gratitude to the sea and the safe return of boats. People choose this name to reflect their values for the shore that feeds them and the guardianship of those who work it.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 磯右衛門: 磯 'rocky seashore' (iso) plus 右衛門 'guard of the right gate' (emon), the Edo commoner name ending. Commoner/everyday style, typical of a fishing or coastal village.

name: Gonnojo
explanation: Gonnojo means "deputy's assistant" or "provisional aide", which can suggest a man who holds office in another's name or one who does the work while another takes the title. People with this name may be diligent, unassuming and quietly indispensable.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo village registers (Kiyose) and among early and late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 権之丞: 権 'provisional authority, deputy' (gon), 之 'of' (no), 丞 'assistant, aide' (jo), a name built from old court-office titles as Edo commoners commonly did. Commoner/everyday style of the -nojo type.

name: Noriyori
explanation: Noriyori - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Younger Brother's Campaign, in which a modest commander held the western front for a year so that a more famous sibling could win the battle everyone remembers. It reflects qualities such as reliability, humility, and being a model others can lean on.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura through Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 範頼: 範 'model, example' (nori) and 頼 'rely on, trust' (yori). Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Minamoto no Noriyori, brother of Yoritomo and Yoshitsune.

name: Shoshichi
explanation: Shoshichi - This name represents the seventh child of a manor household and is often chosen by those who are born late into a large farming family or who are expected to take up whatever work the estate still needs done.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and among Azuchi-Momoyama and late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 庄七: 庄 'manor, estate, village' (sho) and 七 'seven' (shichi), a birth-order name. Commoner/everyday style.

name: Hachirobei
explanation: Hachirobei - Stemming from the word "hachiro", which denotes an eighth son, this name embodies the spirit of the last-born who still stands guard for the household. It resonates with those who are dependable, unassuming, and used to earning their place.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 八郎兵衛: 八郎 'eighth son' (hachiro) plus 兵衛 'palace guard' (bei), the Edo commoner name ending. Commoner/everyday style of the -bei type.

name: Genjuro
explanation: Genjuro - Derived from the phrase "a source that never runs dry", this name embodies the idea of a wellspring of strength that feeds a whole family. It is often associated with those who provide quietly for many and expect no thanks.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, used as a tsusho (everyday name) rather than a formal nanori. Kanji 源十郎: 源 'source, wellspring' (gen) plus 十郎 'tenth son' (juro), a birth-order name. Commoner/everyday style, also borne as an everyday name by samurai. Modern association: the potter Genjuro in Mizoguchi's film Ugetsu.

name: Kaneto
explanation: Kaneto - This name pays tribute to the Day of Appointments, an event that emphasizes the moment each spring when magistrates and clerks receive the year's postings and duties. People choose this name to reflect their values for service, competence, and the willingness to carry more than one charge at once.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 兼任: 兼 'combine, hold concurrently' (kane) and 任 'duty, appointment' (to is a nanori reading; the word 兼任 read kennin means 'holding two posts at once'). Samurai formal-name style; the 任 = to reading is stylized and worth flagging.

name: Sadamichi
explanation: Sadamichi - This name pays tribute to the Opening of the Roads, an event that emphasizes the spring day when the Imperial roads are declared clear of snow and the year's travel begins. People choose this name to reflect their values for constancy, safe passage, and keeping to the road one has chosen.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura through Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 貞通: 貞 'constancy, fidelity' (sada) and 通 'pass through, road' (michi). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Tokitomo
explanation: Tokitomo - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Morning Audience, in which a young courtier arrived at the palace gate before dawn every day for a year until the Emperor finally asked who stood there. It reflects qualities such as patience, punctuality, and faith that the right hour will come.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 時朝: 時 'time, hour' (toki) and 朝 'morning, court' (tomo is a nanori reading; the everyday reading is asa). Samurai formal-name style; the 朝 = tomo reading is a standard nanori convention.

name: Hanshichi
explanation: Hanshichi - This name means "half of seven". It represents the old counting-house joke of a boy born in the middle of a large family, neither first nor last, who is expected to make his own luck.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers, Edo village registers (Kiyose) and among Azuchi-Momoyama and late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 半七: 半 'half' (han) and 七 'seven' (shichi), typically a birth-order name with the first element taken from a father's name. Commoner/everyday style. Modern association: Hanshichi, the Edo detective of Okamoto Kido's Hanshichi Torimonocho stories.

name: Kichibei
explanation: The name Kichibei is inspired by the Shrine of the Lucky Ford, known for its safe crossing where the river runs wide and slow. The name reflects the good fortune of the place and is often chosen by those who value luck earned by caution and a watchful eye on the water.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 吉兵衛: 吉 'good luck' (kichi) plus 兵衛 'palace guard' (bei), the Edo commoner name ending. Commoner/everyday style of the -bei type.

name: Fusamasa
explanation: The name Fusamasa is inspired by the granary town at the head of the Crane rice lands, known for its full storehouses and its markets that never go quiet. The name reflects the plenty of the place and is often chosen by those who value prosperity shared across a whole household.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Muromachi and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 総昌: 総 'whole, all, general' (fusa is a nanori reading; the everyday reading is so) and 昌 'prosperous, flourishing' (masa). Samurai formal-name style; the 総 = fusa reading is stylized and worth flagging.

name: Otogoro
explanation: The name Otogoro is associated with the famous Muster of the Younger Sons, in which the second and fifth sons of a flooded province were called up to hold the levees while their elder brothers were away at war. Those who choose this name try to embody values of readiness, humility, and doing the unglamorous work.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, used as a tsusho (everyday name). Kanji 乙五郎: 乙 'second, younger, the latter' (oto) plus 五郎 'fifth son' (goro), a birth-order name. Commoner/everyday style, also borne as an everyday name by low-ranking samurai.

name: Kagemune
explanation: Kagemune means "scenery of the lineage" or "light of the ancestral house", which can suggest a view worth guarding or a brightness passed down from the founders. People with this name may be proud of their house and mindful of what they inherit.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian through Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 景宗: 景 'view, scenery, light' (kage) and 宗 'sect, lineage head, ancestral' (mune). Samurai formal-name style; 景 is a classic nanori element of the Taira and Kajiwara lines.

name: Shigeyoshi
explanation: Shigeyoshi - A name that means "righteousness accomplished", evoking the retainer who does not merely profess duty but sees it through.
notes: Attested pre-modern name, Heian through early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia; recorded in our sources as a Buddhist name, though the same kanji are also read Shigeyoshi as a samurai nanori. Kanji 成義: 成 'become, accomplish' (shige is a nanori reading; the on reading is jo) and 義 'righteousness' (yoshi). As a monk's name the on reading would be Jogi; as given here it is samurai formal-name style.

name: Hachibei
explanation: Hachibei - Derived from the phrase "eighth guardsman", this name embodies the idea of an ordinary man taking an old title of the palace guard as his own. It is often associated with those who are late-born, hardworking and proud of a name that sounds grander than their station.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Conventional kanji 八兵衛: 八 'eight' (hachi) plus 兵衛 'palace guard' (bei), the Edo commoner name ending; 鉢 'bowl' is an uncommon alternative first element. Commoner/everyday style of the -bei type.

name: Jirozaemon
explanation: Jirozaemon means "the son who governs, of the left gate" or, in its commoner spelling, "second son of the left gate", which can suggest a family's hope for an orderly heir or simply a record of birth order. People with this name may be steady, unhurried, and used to standing watch.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers, Edo village registers (Kiyose) and among Kamakura through late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji as recorded 治郎左衛門: 治 'govern, heal' (ji) and 郎 'son' (ro) plus 左衛門 'guard of the left gate' (zaemon); the more usual spelling is 次郎 'second son'. Commoner/everyday style of the -zaemon type.

name: Motokazu
explanation: Motokazu means "foundation of the company" or "one who counts from the base", which can suggest the member every group is built around or a careful reckoner who starts from first principles. People with this name may be dependable and exacting.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 基員: 基 'foundation, base' (moto) and 員 'member, number' (kazu is a nanori reading; the on reading is in). Samurai formal-name style; the 員 = kazu reading is stylized and worth flagging.

name: Katsunaga
explanation: The name Katsunaga is associated with the famous Long Victory, in which a provincial army won a single battle and then spent seven years holding the ground it had taken rather than marching on. Those who choose this name try to embody values of endurance and of winning by keeping what one has won.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 勝長: 勝 'victory' (katsu) and 長 'long, chief' (naga). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Genroku
explanation: Genroku - This name means "sixth son of the wellspring". It represents the source that keeps giving however many draw from it, a hope pinned on the sixth boy of a crowded farmhouse.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and among Sengoku and late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 源六: 源 'source, wellspring' (gen) plus 六 'six' (roku), a birth-order name. Commoner/everyday style. Not to be confused with the Genroku era (元禄, 1688-1704), which uses different kanji.

name: Magosaku
explanation: Magosaku - A name derived from the fusion of "grandchild" and "craft", reflecting a balance between honoring the elders who came before and doing the work of one's own hands. It is often embraced by those who strive for skill worthy of their grandparents.
notes: Attested pre-modern name, Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia; recorded as a nanori in our sources though the form is that of an everyday name. Kanji 孫作: 孫 'grandchild' (mago) and 作 'make, work, craft' (saku). Reads as commoner/everyday style, of the kind also used as an everyday name by rural samurai.

name: Fusayoshi
explanation: Fusayoshi - A name that means "wholly refined", evoking a cultivation that runs through every part of a person rather than sitting on the surface.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 総彬: 総 'whole, all' (fusa is a nanori reading; the everyday reading is so) and 彬 'refined, cultivated' (yoshi is a nanori reading; akira is more usual). Samurai formal-name style; both readings are stylized nanori conventions.

name: Sadayuki
explanation: Sadayuki - Stemming from the word "sada", which denotes constancy, this name embodies the spirit of good fortune that comes to those who do not waver. It resonates with those who are steadfast, loyal, and quietly content.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura through early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 貞幸: 貞 'constancy, fidelity' (sada) and 幸 'happiness, good fortune' (yuki). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Magojiro
explanation: Magojiro - Composed of the elements "grandchild" and "second son", this name symbolizes a place in the family line recorded plainly at birth. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of continuity and the hope that the line will go on.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo village registers (Nihonjin) and among Muromachi through Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 孫次郎: 孫 'grandchild' (mago) plus 次郎 'second son' (jiro), a birth-order name. Commoner/everyday style. Modern association: Magojiro is also the name of a classic Noh mask of a young woman.

name: Tadayoshi
explanation: Tadayoshi - This name represents loyalty rewarded with good fortune and is often chosen by those who are sworn to a lord's service or who are expected to bring luck to the house through their faithfulness.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian through early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 忠吉: 忠 'loyalty' (tada) and 吉 'good luck' (yoshi). Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Tadayoshi was the name of a celebrated line of Hizen swordsmiths.

name: Harumasa
explanation: The name Harumasa is inspired by the hilltop seat of a provincial governor, known for its clear skies and its reputation for even-handed rule. The name reflects the fair weather of the place and is often chosen by those who value clarity in governance and judgment untroubled by storms.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 晴政: 晴 'clear sky, fair weather' (haru) and 政 'governance' (masa). Samurai formal-name style. Best-known bearer: Nanbu Harumasa, Sengoku daimyo of Mutsu.

name: Yoshifuyu
explanation: Yoshifuyu chose their name in honor of the famous Matsu Yoshifuyu, who marched a relief column through a blizzard to break the siege of a starving town and refused any reward beyond a bowl of the rice they had brought.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Muromachi and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 義冬: 義 'righteousness' (yoshi) and 冬 'winter' (fuyu). Samurai formal-name style; the 義 element is characteristic of Ashikaga-line nanori.

name: Eizo
explanation: Eizo - This name pays tribute to the Sealing of the Storehouses, an event that emphasizes the autumn day when the harvest is counted, recorded, and locked away for winter. People choose this name to reflect their values for thrift, prosperity, and a household that will not go hungry.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers. Kanji 栄藏: 栄 'prosper, flourish' (ei) and 藏 'storehouse' (zo), the older form of 蔵; -zo names were common among late-Edo townsmen. Commoner/everyday style.

name: Tokimune
explanation: Tokimune - Stemming from the word "toki", which denotes time or the appointed hour, this name embodies the spirit of a lineage that meets its moment. It resonates with those who are composed under pressure and ready when the hour comes.
notes: Attested pre-modern name, Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and Sengoku name articles; our sources file it as a Buddhist name because 時宗 is also the Ji-shu sect (read Jishu), but the given name Tokimune is a samurai nanori. Kanji 時宗: 時 'time, hour' (toki) and 宗 'sect, lineage' (mune). Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Hojo Tokimune, the regent who faced the Mongol invasions.

name: Jobutsu
explanation: Jobutsu - This name represents the attainment of enlightenment and is often chosen by those who are entering a monastery late in life or who are expected to find peace at the end of a hard road.
notes: Attested pre-modern Buddhist name, Kamakura-period bearer in Edo-era register compilations (Nihonjin). Kanji 成仏: 成 'become, attain' (jo) and 仏 'Buddha' (butsu), the ordinary Japanese word for attaining Buddhahood, also used of the dead finding rest. Monk's name, on reading, not a lay given name.

name: Jizaemon
explanation: Jizaemon means "the one who governs the left gate" or "healer of the left gate", which can suggest a household hoping for a son who keeps order or one who mends what is broken. People with this name may be practical, patient, and trusted with keys.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers, Edo village registers (Kiyose) and among early and late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 治左衛門: 治 'govern, heal' (ji) plus 左衛門 'guard of the left gate' (zaemon), the Edo commoner name ending. Commoner/everyday style of the -zaemon type.

name: Kiemon
explanation: Kiemon - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of kyogen comic theater, this name represents the joy that a well-timed jest brings to a hall. It is often chosen by those who appreciate laughter that lightens a heavy day and have a deep respect for the players who know exactly when to deliver it.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers, Edo village registers (Kiyose) and among Sengoku and late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 喜右衛門: 喜 'joy, delight' (ki) plus 右衛門 'guard of the right gate' (emon), the Edo commoner name ending. Commoner/everyday style of the -emon type.

name: Kyubei
explanation: The name Kyubei is inspired by the old guardhouse at a long-settled crossroads, known for its worn stones and the same family keeping its watch for nine generations. The name reflects the endurance of the place and is often chosen by those who value long service and things that last.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers. Kanji 久兵衛: 久 'long-lasting, enduring' (kyu) plus 兵衛 'palace guard' (bei), the Edo commoner name ending. Commoner/everyday style of the -bei type. Modern association: Kyubei is a frequent stock name for shopkeepers and merchants in Edo-period fiction.

name: Jingoro
explanation: Jingoro - Composed of the elements "greatly" and "fifth son", this name symbolizes a late child whose arrival was welcomed all the same. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of abundance and a family large enough to count on.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and among late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 甚五郎: 甚 'very, greatly' (jin) plus 五郎 'fifth son' (goro), a birth-order name. Commoner/everyday style. Modern association: Hidari Jingoro, the legendary Edo sculptor credited with the sleeping cat at Nikko.

name: Motohiro
explanation: Motohiro chose their name in honor of the famous Ikoma Motohiro, who opened the first road across a wide marsh and gave the land it drained to the villagers who had dug it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 元広: 元 'origin, source' (moto) and 広 'wide, broad' (hiro). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Matasaburo
explanation: Matasaburo - This name is inspired by the natural element of the returning wind, symbolizing the "again" (mata) that comes round each season and the place of a third son (saburo) who follows two elder brothers. It is often chosen for its connection to the winds that return faithfully every year and its representation of dependability and welcome return.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears as a commoner and everyday name in Edo merchant registers, Sengoku name articles, late-Edo village registers and on Japanese Wikipedia, with bearers from Kamakura through late Edo. Kanji 又三郎: 又 "again, also" + 三郎 "third son", the plain birth-order compound. A commoner and everyday (tsusho) style, never a samurai formal name. Modern association: "Kaze no Matasaburo" (Wind Matasaburo), the 1934 children's story by Miyazawa Kenji.

name: Toshimichi
explanation: Toshimichi means "talented and far-reaching" or "versed in every road", which can suggest a courtier whose reputation travels ahead of him or an official who knows every path of trade and law. People with this name may be quick-witted and widely traveled.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 俊通: 俊 "talented, excellent" + 通 "pass through, far-reaching, versed in"; both are standard nanori readings (toshi, michi). Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Okubo Toshimichi (大久保利通, different kanji), one of the three great statesmen of the Meiji Restoration.

name: Fusahira
explanation: Fusahira - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A house is judged by the balance of its rooms", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value fairness within a household and even-handed judgment among those they command.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura- and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 房衡: 房 "chamber, house wing, cluster" (nanori reading fusa) + 衡 "balance, scales, to weigh" (nanori reading hira); the reading hira for 衡 is a name-only reading and would look unusual to a modern reader. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Kyujiro
explanation: Kyujiro - Derived from the phrase "long at peace under good rule" (hisashiku osamaru), this name embodies the idea of a household that stays orderly for generations. It is often associated with those who keep a shop or a farm running quietly for a lifetime.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo merchant registers and among late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 久治郎: 久 "long-lasting" + 治 "govern, heal, put in order" + 郎 "son, young man"; the kyu-ji-ro reading is the ordinary on reading of all three. Commoner and everyday style, typical of Edo townsmen and villagers. No notable modern association.

name: Ushinosuke
explanation: Ushinosuke - This name represents the helper of the ox, the child born into a house whose wealth is its draft animals, and is often chosen by those who are farmers with a plow team or who are expected to carry a heavy load without complaint.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: an early-Edo everyday (tsusho) name recorded on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 牛之助: 牛 "ox" + 之 "of" + 助 "help, assistant", a common -nosuke pattern; the reading is completely regular. Commoner and everyday style, rustic in flavor. No notable modern association.

name: Chozaburo
explanation: Chozaburo - With origins in the legend of Chozaburo the ferryman, who held the river crossing alone for three days so that a fleeing village could escape a bandit army, this name evokes a sense of stubborn endurance and quiet service. It appeals to those who admire the commoner who does more than duty asks.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo merchant registers and Sengoku name articles. Kanji 長三郎: 長 "long, elder, chief" + 三郎 "third son"; the cho reading is the on reading of 長, regular in such compounds. Commoner and everyday style. No notable modern association.

name: Heiemon
explanation: Heiemon - Stemming from the word "hei", which denotes calm, level ground and peace, this name embodies the spirit of the steady gatekeeper who keeps trouble outside the wall. It resonates with those who are unhurried, reliable and slow to anger.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo merchant registers, the 1774 Noshio and related village registers and on Japanese Wikipedia, with Sengoku and late-Edo bearers. Kanji 平右衛門: 平 "peace, flat, calm" + 右衛門 "right gate guard", the old palace-guard title that became a common name ending. Commoner and everyday style; -emon names were among the most frequent Edo commoner names. No notable modern association.

name: Sadachika
explanation: Sadachika - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Faithful Retainer, in which a samurai stayed beside his dying lord through a winter siege when every other retainer had slipped away, and was found still kneeling at the bedside when the relief column arrived. It reflects qualities such as constancy, filial closeness and loyalty that does not count the cost.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura- and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 貞親: 貞 "constancy, chastity, fidelity" (nanori sada) + 親 "parent, intimate, close" (nanori chika); both readings are standard for names. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Ryuzo
explanation: The name Ryuzo is inspired by the Three Dragon Gorge in the northern mountains, known for its three waterfalls that are said to be the coils of one dragon. The name reflects the untamed power of the place and is often chosen by those who value strength, persistence and a love of high wild country.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: a Sengoku-period everyday (tsusho) name from Sengoku name articles. Kanji 龍三: 龍 "dragon" + 三 "three", read with the plain on readings ryu and zo (the zo reading of 三 is the ordinary voiced form in names such as Shinzo or Kenzo). Commoner and everyday style, though dragon names were used by all castes. No notable modern association.

name: Masakata
explanation: Masakata means "truly wise" or "genuine and virtuous", which can suggest a person of honest judgment or one whose goodness is not a pose. People with this name may be trusted as arbiters and sought out for plain advice.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Sengoku and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 真賢: 真 "true, genuine" (nanori masa) + 賢 "wise, virtuous"; the reading kata for 賢 is a name-only (nanori) reading rather than its everyday reading ken or kashiko-, so it looks stylized to a modern eye. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Kagetoshi
explanation: Kagetoshi - A name derived from the fusion of "light and scenery" and "order and record", reflecting a balance between the beauty of the moment and the discipline that sets it down for posterity. It is often embraced by those who strive for a life worth recording and the patience to record it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 景紀: 景 "scenery, view, light" (nanori kage) + 紀 "chronicle, order, era" (nanori toshi); both are established name readings, though toshi for 紀 is name-only. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Sakuemon
explanation: Sakuemon chose their name in honor of the famous Yasuki Sakuemon, who built the granary that carried a whole province through the two-year famine and refused every reward but a plaque over its door.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo merchant registers and the Kiyose village registers of the late Edo period. Kanji 作右衛門: 作 "make, craft, cultivate" + 右衛門 "right gate guard", the old guard title turned common name ending; saku is the plain on reading. Commoner and everyday style, very much a farmer and craftsman name. No notable modern association.

name: Kojiro
explanation: Kojiro can be written with two different kanji. One means "fortunate second son", and the other means "little second son". The choice of kanji could reflect how a family regarded the boy, such as a blessing that arrived after the heir was secured or simply the younger brother, small only in years.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo merchant registers and on Japanese Wikipedia across every period from Heian to late Edo. Kanji 幸次郎: 幸 "fortune, happiness" + 次郎 "second son"; the alternate spelling 小次郎 "little second son" is the more famous one. Commoner and everyday style, though as a tsusho it was carried by samurai too. Modern association: the Sengoku swordsman Sasaki Kojiro (小次郎), Musashi's opponent at Ganryujima.

name: Yoshiteru
explanation: Yoshiteru - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A good deed shines farther than a lantern", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value quiet virtue over display and who trust that right conduct will be seen in time.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Sengoku and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 良輝: 良 "good, fine" (nanori yoshi) + 輝 "shine, radiance" (nanori teru); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: the shogun Ashikaga Yoshiteru is written 義輝 with a different first character.

name: Sozaburo
explanation: Sozaburo - This name signifies the third son who belongs to the whole village rather than to one house, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values community, shared labor and the good of the many over the one.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo merchant registers of the late Edo period. Kanji 惣三郎: 惣 "all, whole, general" (the character of the medieval village commune, the so) + 三郎 "third son"; so is its regular on reading. Commoner and everyday style, an unmistakably townsman or villager name. No notable modern association.

name: Mitsusue
explanation: The name Mitsusue is associated with the famous Lantern Vigil of the Winter Court, in which the youngest son of a besieged household kept a single light burning in the gate tower all night so that the returning army would know the castle had not fallen. Those who choose this name try to embody values of hope, steadfastness and the duty of the youngest to hold what the eldest have won.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Heian, Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 光季: 光 "light" (nanori mitsu) + 季 "season, youngest" (nanori sue, the character used for the youngest brother); both readings are standard in names. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Moritaka
explanation: Moritaka - This name signifies "flourishing prosperity", and may suggest that the one who chooses it values a house that keeps rising and an heir who will not let it settle.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 盛隆: 盛 "flourish, prosper, heap up" (nanori mori) + 隆 "prosperity, eminence" (nanori taka); both are standard name readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Jochiku
explanation: Jochiku - This name is inspired by the natural element of bamboo, symbolizing the constancy of a stalk that stays green through the winter and bends without breaking. It is often chosen for its connection to the mountain groves where monks cut their walking staves and its representation of humility, uprightness and endurance.
notes: Attested Buddhist name, with Muromachi and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 常竹: 常 "constant, ever" (jo) + 竹 "bamboo" (chiku), both plain on readings as is usual for a monk's name. A monk's name (homyo) rather than a samurai or commoner style; a samurai who took the tonsure might have borne it. No notable modern association.

name: Naoshige
explanation: Naoshige - With origins in the legend of the Upright Magistrate, who weighed the case of their own lord against a peasant and found for the peasant, then offered their head for the offense, this name evokes a sense of honesty that will not bend and of weight carried without complaint. It appeals to those who admire justice done at personal cost.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 直重: 直 "upright, straight, honest" (nanori nao) + 重 "weighty, grave, layered" (nanori shige); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: the Sengoku daimyo Nabeshima Naoshige is written 直茂 with a different second character.

name: Iefusa
explanation: Iefusa - This name pays tribute to the Rite of the Household Hearth, an event that emphasizes the renewal of the home at the turn of the year and the rooms in which a family gathers. People choose this name to reflect their values for domestic harmony, hospitality and the ordering of a house.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 家房: 家 "house, family" (nanori ie) + 房 "chamber, house wing, cluster" (nanori fusa); both readings are standard, with the Ie- prefix a marker of the Tokugawa-era and earlier warrior naming tradition. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Yoshimori
explanation: Yoshimori chose their name in honor of the famous Matsu Yoshimori, who guarded a mountain pass with forty soldiers against an army for six days until the harvest behind them was safely in.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Heian, Kamakura, Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 義守: 義 "righteousness, duty" (nanori yoshi) + 守 "protect, guard" (nanori mori); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: the Kamakura warrior Wada Yoshimori is written 義盛 with a different second character.

name: Yorimasa
explanation: Yorimasa - This name signifies government that can be relied upon, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values trustworthiness, sound administration and the confidence of those they lead.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and in Sengoku name articles. Kanji 頼政: 頼 "rely, trust" (nanori yori) + 政 "government, rule" (nanori masa); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Minamoto no Yorimasa (源頼政), the Heian warrior-poet who raised the first revolt against the Taira in 1180 and is the archetype of the samurai seppuku death.

name: Shojiro
explanation: Shojiro - This name represents "the son who governs the manor" and is often chosen by those who are farmers or village headmen or who are expected to keep an estate's fields in good order.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo merchant registers, the Kiyose village registers and on Japanese Wikipedia, with Azuchi-Momoyama and late-Edo bearers. Kanji 庄治郎: 庄 "manor, estate" + 治 "govern, put in order" + 郎 "son"; all three take their plain on readings. Commoner and everyday style, typical of a farmer or village headman. No notable modern association.

name: Ieuji
explanation: Ieuji - A name that means "house and clan", evoking the whole line of a family gathered under one roof and one name.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura- and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 家氏: 家 "house, family" (ie) + 氏 "clan, lineage" (uji); both are ordinary readings. No notable modern association.

name: Iekage
explanation: Iekage - Derived from the phrase "the light of the house" (ie no kage), this name embodies the idea of the son who is the family's brightness and its good name. It is often associated with those who carry the reputation of their ancestors and are expected to add to it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura- and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 家景: 家 "house, family" (ie) + 景 "light, scenery, view" (nanori kage; note that in modern usage kage 影 means shadow, but 景 is the sunlit view). Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Takakiyo
explanation: Takakiyo - This name pays tribute to the Mountain Purification, an event that emphasizes climbing to a high shrine before dawn to wash in the first spring meltwater. People choose this name to reflect their values for purity, lofty aspiration and the clarity that comes from being above the smoke of the world.
notes: Attested name with Kamakura, Muromachi, Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia; our source classifies it as a Buddhist name, though in form it is an ordinary samurai nanori and it was most likely a lay name carried into religion. Kanji 高清: 高 "high, lofty" (nanori taka) + 清 "pure, clear" (nanori kiyo); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style, also usable by a monk who kept a lay name. No notable modern association.

name: Ryosho
explanation: Ryosho - With origins in the legend of the monk Ryosho, who lit the lamps of a mountain temple every night for sixty years so that travelers lost on the pass could find the gate, this name evokes a sense of patient goodness and quiet illumination. It appeals to those who admire service that asks for no witness.
notes: Attested Buddhist name, Heian-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 良照: 良 "good, fine" (ryo) + 照 "illuminate, shine" (sho), both plain on readings as is usual for a monk's name. A monk's name (homyo), not a samurai or commoner style. No notable modern association.

name: Narihide
explanation: Narihide - This name means "to attain excellence". It represents the hope that a child will grow into distinction through their own accomplishment rather than by birth alone.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Muromachi- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 就秀: 就 "attain, settle into, take up a post" (nanori nari, the reading familiar from Mori Motonari 元就) + 秀 "excel, surpass" (nanori hide); nari for 就 is a name-only reading. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Akikuni
explanation: Akikuni chose their name in honor of the famous Ikoma Akikuni, who as governor of a war-ruined province rebuilt every bridge and granary within ten years and left it brighter than they found it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian- and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 明国: 明 "bright, clear" (nanori aki) + 国 "country, province" (kuni); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Ienaga
explanation: Ienaga - This name means "head of the household". It represents the eldest son who will one day speak for the whole family and answer for it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Heian, Kamakura, Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 家長: 家 "house, family" (ie) + 長 "chief, elder, long" (nanori naga); as a common noun the same characters read kacho, "family head". Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: the historian Ienaga Saburo, though there it is a surname.

name: Nobuchika
explanation: Nobuchika - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the tea ceremony, this name represents the trust that grows between host and guest in a small room. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the intimacy of shared ritual and have a deep respect for the masters who make strangers into friends over a single bowl.
notes: Attested name with Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia; our source classifies it as a Buddhist name, but in form it is an ordinary samurai nanori. Kanji 信親: 信 "trust, faith" (nanori nobu) + 親 "parent, intimate, close" (nanori chika); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Chosokabe Nobuchika (長宗我部信親), the heir killed at the battle of Hetsugigawa in 1587.

name: Sadamune
explanation: Sadamune - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The constant root outlives the tallest branch", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value fidelity to the family line and the patient keeping of what was inherited.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 貞宗: 貞 "constancy, fidelity" (nanori sada) + 宗 "lineage, sect, principal" (nanori mune); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Sadamune (相州貞宗), the Kamakura-period swordsmith regarded as the pupil of Masamune.

name: Takakuni
explanation: Takakuni - With origins in the legend of the governor Takakuni, who raised a province from famine to plenty by walking every one of its valleys on foot, this name evokes a sense of elevated ambition bound to the land. It appeals to those who admire the high-minded ruler who does not rule from a distance.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 高国: 高 "high, lofty" (nanori taka) + 国 "country, province" (kuni); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Hosokawa Takakuni (細川高国), the Muromachi kanrei who dominated the shogunate in the 1520s.

name: Hachirogoro
explanation: Hachirogoro - A name that means "eighth son, fifth son", evoking the stacked birth-order names of a large warrior household in which the fifth son of an eighth son needed a name of his own.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: a Sengoku-period everyday (tsusho) name recorded on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 八郎五郎: 八郎 "eighth son" + 五郎 "fifth son", a doubled birth-order compound of the kind used to tell a junior line apart from the senior one; the reading is fully regular. Commoner and everyday style in form, though as a tsusho it was borne by samurai. No notable modern association.

name: Yoshitada
explanation: Yoshitada - Composed of the elements "righteousness" and "loyalty", this name symbolizes the two virtues a lord asks of a retainer before all others. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of duty done rightly and faith kept.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with bearers in every period from Heian to early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 義忠: 義 "righteousness, duty" (nanori yoshi) + 忠 "loyalty" (nanori tada); both readings are standard and the pairing is a classic bushido compound. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Kinnojo
explanation: Kinnojo - This name is inspired by the natural element of gold, symbolizing wealth drawn from the earth and made useful by a steady hand. It is often chosen for its connection to the ore washed from mountain streams and its representation of worth that is proven by service rather than by shine.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: a late-Edo everyday (tsusho) name recorded on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 金之丞: 金 "gold, metal, money" + 之 "of" + 丞 "assistant, aide", the old office title turned name ending; the reading is regular. Commoner and everyday style, with the merchant flavor that 金 gives it. No notable modern association.

name: Nagamichi
explanation: Nagamichi - This name signifies a long stretch of land and the long road across it, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values patience, the wide view and the endurance to see a journey through.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 長陸: 長 "long, elder" (nanori naga) + 陸 "land, dry land, mainland" (nanori michi); the reading michi for 陸 is a name-only reading and would puzzle a modern reader who expects riku. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Kiyosada
