explanation: Kiyosada - A name derived from the fusion of "purity" and "settled resolve", reflecting a balance between a clean heart and a fixed purpose. It is often embraced by those who strive for honesty that does not waver.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 清定: 清 "pure, clear" (nanori kiyo) + 定 "settle, decide, fix" (nanori sada); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Kiyonaga
explanation: Kiyonaga - A name that means "pure and enduring", evoking a clear stream that has run the same course since before the village was built.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Muromachi, Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 清長: 清 "pure, clear" (nanori kiyo) + 長 "long, enduring, chief" (nanori naga); both readings are standard. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Torii Kiyonaga (鳥居清長), the late-Edo ukiyo-e master of tall bijin prints.

name: Ukon
explanation: Ukon - This name means "of the Right Guard". It represents the old palace title of the Right Inner Guard, worn as a name by a man whose family once claimed a place at the gate of the Emperor.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears on Japanese Wikipedia and in late-Edo village registers, with Kamakura and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers. Kanji 右近: 右 "right" (u) + 近 "near, close" (kon), short for 右近衛 (Ukon-e), the Right Inner Palace Guard; the source string carries a stray iteration mark ゝ that is a transcription artifact and not part of the name. An everyday and commoner style derived from a court office title, borne by samurai and villagers alike. Modern association: Takayama Ukon (高山右近), the Sengoku Christian daimyo beatified in 2017.

name: Yukimasa
explanation: Yukimasa - This name signifies good conduct in government, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values administration carried out with honesty and the discipline to see a policy through.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Sengoku and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 行政: 行 "go, conduct, carry out" (nanori yuki) + 政 "government, rule" (nanori masa); as a common noun the same characters read gyosei, "administration", which a modern reader will notice first. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Matazaemon
explanation: Matazaemon - Derived from the phrase "again at the gate", this name embodies the idea of the guard who returns to their post no matter how often they are relieved. It is often associated with those who are dependable to a fault and are always found where they were left.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo merchant registers and on Japanese Wikipedia, with Sengoku and late-Edo bearers. Kanji 又左衛門: 又 "again, also" + 左衛門 "left gate guard", the old palace-guard title that became one of the commonest Edo name endings; the reading is regular. Commoner and everyday style, though as a tsusho it was carried by samurai. Modern association: Matazaemon was the everyday name of the Sengoku general Maeda Toshiie.

name: Akie
explanation: Akie - This name is inspired by the natural element of autumn, symbolizing the season when a house gathers in what the year has grown. It is often chosen for its connection to the harvest fields and its representation of a family whose fortunes are stored with care and shared under one roof.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian- and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 秋家: 秋 "autumn" (aki) + 家 "house, family" (ie); both readings are ordinary. Samurai formal-name style. Note that Akie is a common modern female given name written with different kanji (such as 明恵), so a modern reader will assume a woman; the pre-modern male name is unrelated.

name: Heiroku
explanation: Heiroku - A name derived from the fusion of "peace" and "six", reflecting a balance between a calm temperament and the plain fact of being the sixth child at the table. It is often embraced by those who strive for contentment with a modest place in a crowded house.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo merchant registers and on Japanese Wikipedia, with Heian, Kamakura and late-Edo bearers. Kanji 平六: 平 "peace, flat, calm" (hei) + 六 "six" (roku), both plain on readings; the Hei- element in older bearers often marked descent from the Taira (平) clan rather than a wish for peace. Commoner and everyday style, a classic birth-order name. No notable modern association.

name: Akimitsu
explanation: Akimitsu - A name derived from the fusion of "shining" and "light", reflecting a balance between the brightness one shows to the world and the light one carries within. It is often embraced by those who strive for a reputation that is as clear in private as it is in public.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 昭 (aki, "bright, shining") + 光 (mitsu, "light"); aki for 昭 is a standard nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style.

name: Kinzo
explanation: Kinzo - This name is inspired by the natural element of gold, symbolizing what is precious enough to be stored away and guarded. It is often chosen for its connection to the metal drawn from the hills and its representation of thrift, stewardship, and wealth kept safe for the household.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and the Kiyose village register. 金 (kin, "gold") + 蔵 (zo, "storehouse"); 金蔵 is also the ordinary word for a treasury. Commoner everyday style, typical of a merchant household.

name: Fusamoto
explanation: Fusamoto - This name pays tribute to the Festival of First Fruits, an event that emphasizes gratitude for the earliest heavy clusters of the orchard and the labor that brought them in. People choose this name to reflect their values for humility, thankfulness, and returning to the source of every good thing.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 房 (fusa, "cluster, chamber") + 元 (moto, "origin, source"). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Sadayasu
explanation: Sadayasu - Stemming from the word "sadame", which denotes a thing fixed and settled by decree, this name embodies the spirit of calm resolution. It resonates with those who are steady, unhurried, and at peace once a matter is decided.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 定 (sada, "settle, fix") + 安 (yasu, "peace, ease"). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Masakazu
explanation: Masakazu - This name represents prosperity in harmony and is often chosen by those who are raised to manage a thriving estate or who are expected to keep peace among quarreling kin.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 昌 (masa, "prosperous, flourishing") + 和 (kazu, "harmony"); kazu for 和 is a nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style.

name: Gisho
explanation: Gisho - This name pays tribute to the Ceremony of the Passed Lamp, an event that emphasizes the handing-on of a master's teaching to a chosen disciple before the assembled brotherhood. People choose this name to reflect their values for righteous inheritance and the duty to carry forward what they have received.
notes: Attested Buddhist monastic name, a Muromachi bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. 義 (gi, "righteousness") + 承 (sho, "receive, inherit"); on-readings throughout, as monastic names are. Monk's name; in this setting suited to any caste who has taken vows.

name: Naoie
explanation: Naoie - This name signifies an honest house whose dealings are straight, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values plain speech and a family reputation kept clean.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura through Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 直 (nao, "straight, honest") + 家 (ie, "house, family"). Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: the Sengoku warlord Ukita Naoie (1529-1582).

name: Iehira
explanation: Iehira - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of flower arrangement, this name represents a household held in balance like stems set against one another in a single vase. It is often chosen by those who appreciate restraint and proportion and have a deep respect for masters who make three stems say what a garden cannot.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian and Kamakura bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 家 (ie, "house") + 衡 (hira, "balance, scales"); hira for 衡 is a nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Kiyohara no Iehira of the Later Three Years War.

name: Ichiemon
explanation: Ichiemon - Composed of the elements "market" and "gate guard", this name symbolizes the townsman who keeps order at the place where trade is done. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of honest dealing, watchfulness, and a settled place among the shopkeepers of a town.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers, the Kiyose village register, and on Japanese Wikipedia. 市 (ichi, "market") + 右衛門 (emon, from the old Right Gate Guard title, worn as a name suffix); the u of uemon is elided in ordinary reading. Commoner everyday style of the -emon type.

name: Shigetsuna
explanation: Shigetsuna - This name signifies the mainstay rope that holds a task through to completion, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values finishing what is begun.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, bearers from Heian through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. 成 (shige, "accomplish, become") + 綱 (tsuna, "rope, mainstay"); shige for 成 is a nanori reading, unusual outside names. Samurai formal-name style.

name: Jugoro
explanation: Jugoro - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Fifth Son and the Stone Gate, in which the youngest of five brothers shoulders the fallen gate-beam his elders could not lift and holds it until the village has passed beneath. It reflects qualities such as quiet strength and doing the heavy work without complaint.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: late-Edo merchant registers, with an Azuchi-Momoyama bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. 重 (ju, "heavy, layered") + 五郎 (goro, "fifth son"). Commoner everyday style of the numbered-son type.

name: Rokurotaro
explanation: Rokurotaro - This name represents the eldest son of a sixth son and is often chosen by those who are born into a large and branching family or who are expected to carry a junior line's name with pride.
notes: Attested everyday name (tsusho), a Kamakura bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. 六郎 (rokuro, "sixth son") + 太郎 (taro, "eldest son"), a stacked birth-order name meaning the eldest son of a man called Rokuro. Commoner or low-samurai everyday style, not a formal nanori.

name: Masataka
explanation: Masataka - Stemming from the word "matsurigoto", which denotes the work of governing, this name embodies the spirit of rising through good administration. It resonates with those who are diligent, orderly, and ambitious in service.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, bearers from Kamakura through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. 政 (masa, "governance") + 隆 (taka, "rise, prosper"). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Hikosaburo
explanation: Hikosaburo - A name that means "the fine third son", evoking the handsome younger boy of a family who must make his own way.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and the Kiyose village register. 彦 (hiko, "fine young man") + 三郎 (saburo, "third son"). Commoner everyday style of the numbered-son type. Modern association: the kabuki actor lineage Bando Hikosaburo.

name: Yoshichika
explanation: Yoshichika - Rooted in the ancient proverb "Righteousness is learned at a parent's hearth", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value filial duty and the home as the first school of honor.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, bearers from Heian through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia and in Sengoku name lists. 義 (yoshi, "righteousness") + 親 (chika, "parent, intimate"). Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Minamoto no Yoshichika, the Heian rebel.

name: Kanshichiro
explanation: Kanshichiro - A name that means "the seventh son of keen reckoning", evoking a quick-witted younger brother who counts the odds before he acts.
notes: Attested everyday name (tsusho), a Sengoku bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. 勘 (kan, "intuition, reckoning") + 七郎 (shichiro, "seventh son"). Commoner or low-samurai everyday style, not a formal nanori.

name: Munekiyo
explanation: The name Munekiyo is inspired by the Clearwater Springs beneath the Dragon foothills, known for its cold, pure pools that a founding line of shrine-keepers has tended for generations. The name reflects the purity of the place and is often chosen by those who value clean lineage and unmuddied conduct.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian, Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 宗 (mune, "lineage, main line") + 清 (kiyo, "pure, clear"). Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Taira no Munekiyo, who spared the young Yoritomo.

name: Gonbei
explanation: Gonbei - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the rice-planting song, this name represents the steady voice that keeps a line of planters moving together. It is often chosen by those who appreciate humble work done in rhythm and have a deep respect for the elders who lead the singing.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: early- and late-Edo merchant and village registers (Kiyose) and Japanese Wikipedia. 権 (gon, "authority, provisional") + 兵衛 (bei, from the old palace-guard title, worn as a name suffix). Commoner everyday style of the -bei type. Modern association: "Nanashi no Gonbei" is the Japanese equivalent of John Doe, so the name reads as the archetypal peasant.

name: Shosaburo
explanation: Shosaburo - This name means "third son of the manor". It represents a boy born to a farming village who must make his own way, since the fields will pass to his elder brothers, and the steadiness expected of one who works land he will not inherit.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and the Kiyose village register. 庄 (sho, "manor, village") + 三郎 (saburo, "third son"). Commoner everyday style of the numbered-son type.

name: Kyusuke
explanation: Kyusuke - With origins in the legend of the Long-Serving Retainer, who kept a ruined household running for forty years until its heir returned, this name evokes a sense of loyalty that outlasts hope. It appeals to those who admire endurance in service.
notes: Attested everyday name (tsusho), an early-Edo bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. 久 (kyu, "long-lasting") + 助 (suke, "help"). Commoner everyday style. Modern association: in Japanese, "kyusuke" is also the trade word for broken rice crackers sold cheap.

name: Akiuji
explanation: Akiuji - This name means "clan of light". It represents a family line that expects to shine in the eyes of its lord.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 光 (aki, "light") + 氏 (uji, "clan"); aki for 光 is a nanori reading, the ordinary readings being hikari or mitsu. Samurai formal-name style.

name: Kagetomo
explanation: Kagetomo - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Morning View, in which a sentry who watched the dawn every day from a castle wall was the only one to notice the enemy banners rising with the sun. It reflects qualities such as vigilance and the reward of unglamorous duty.
notes: Attested name with Kamakura through Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia; our data classes it as Buddhist, but the kanji are an ordinary samurai-style pair, so treat it as a formal name that a bearer kept after taking vows. 景 (kage, "view, scenery, bright") + 朝 (tomo, "morning, court"); tomo for 朝 is a nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style.

name: Ujikata
explanation: The name Ujikata is associated with the famous Concord of the Standards, in which the banners of two feuding vassal houses were planted side by side before their daimyo and neither was allowed to stand a hand higher. Those who choose this name try to embody values of loyalty to the clan above the branch.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 氏 (uji, "clan") + 方 (kata, "side, direction"). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Munetoki
explanation: The name Munetoki is inspired by the Hour-Bell Shrine of the eastern coast, known for its great bronze bell that a single family has rung at every watch for centuries. The name reflects the constancy of the place and is often chosen by those who value duty kept on time and lineage kept unbroken.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian, Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 宗 (mune, "lineage, main line") + 時 (toki, "time"). Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Hojo Munetoki, elder brother of the second Kamakura regent.

name: Gonjiro
explanation: Gonjiro - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Second Son Who Kept the Ledger, in which a younger brother, given no land, ran the family accounts so well that the magistrate made him headman over his elders. It reflects qualities such as diligence and authority earned by competence.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in the Kiyose village register and in Kamakura-period name lists. 権 (gon, "authority, provisional") + 治郎 (jiro, "second son", a common variant spelling of 次郎 with 治 "govern"). Commoner everyday style of the numbered-son type.

name: Kiyoshige
explanation: Kiyoshige - A name that means "pure and flourishing", evoking a clear stream running through thick summer growth.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, bearers from Kamakura through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. 清 (kiyo, "pure, clear") + 茂 (shige, "luxuriant"). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Katsuyori
explanation: Katsuyori - Rooted in the ancient proverb "Victory that leans on one shoulder falls when that shoulder tires", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value shared burdens and the danger of relying on a single strength.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 勝 (katsu, "victory") + 頼 (yori, "rely on"). Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Takeda Katsuyori, whose defeat at Nagashino ended his house.

name: Katsumasa
explanation: Katsumasa - With origins in the legend of the Just Champion, who won a duel and then conceded the prize because his opponent's blade had been tampered with, this name evokes a sense of victory that refuses to be stained. It appeals to those who admire winning only by right means.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 勝 (katsu, "victory") + 正 (masa, "correct, just"). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Ushiwakamaru
explanation: Ushiwakamaru chose their name in honor of the famous Akodo Ushiwakamaru, who as a boy slipped past the gate guards of a besieged castle and carried word of its plight to the relieving army.
notes: Attested childhood name (yomyo), Heian, from Sengoku-era name articles. 牛 (ushi, "ox") + 若 (waka, "young") + 丸 (maru, the suffix of boys' childhood names). A child's name, given before coming of age; in this setting a boy of any caste might bear it, though the -maru form is especially samurai. Famous bearer: the childhood name of Minamoto no Yoshitsune, a fixture of folklore and kabuki.

name: Ieyoshi
explanation: Ieyoshi - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A righteous house needs no locks", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value a family reputation that guards itself.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 家 (ie, "house") + 義 (yoshi, "righteousness"). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Nariharu
explanation: Nariharu - A name that means "to take up governing", evoking the retainer who accepts an office and brings a province to order under it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 就 (nari, "take up, accomplish") + 治 (haru, "govern, heal"); both are nanori readings, nari for 就 being the hallmark of the Mori house (as in Motonari). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Tokikiyo
explanation: Tokikiyo - This name signifies a time kept pure, an hour unmuddied by haste or scheming, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values clear judgment in the moment it is needed.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian and Kamakura bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 時 (toki, "time") + 清 (kiyo, "pure, clear"). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Motofusa
explanation: Motofusa - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the First Chamber, in which a young regent, offered the grandest hall in the palace, chose instead the small room where his grandfather had first studied, and governed from there. It reflects qualities such as humility and fidelity to one's origins.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura through Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 元 (moto, "origin") + 房 (fusa, "chamber, cluster"). Samurai formal-name style, also used in court-noble houses. Famous bearer: the Heian regent Matsudono Motofusa.

name: Narikane
explanation: Narikane - This name means "to accomplish and to hold together". It represents a leader who finishes what is begun while keeping the many strands of a house in one hand.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 就 (nari, "take up, accomplish") + 兼 (kane, "combine, hold together"); nari for 就 is a nanori reading typical of the Mori house. Samurai formal-name style.

name: Otojiro
explanation: Otojiro - Derived from the phrase "the second son listens for the sound", this name embodies the idea of attentiveness in one who is not first in line. It is often associated with those who hear what others miss and speak only when it is worth the hearing.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: late-Edo merchant registers, with further bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 音 (oto, "sound") + 次郎 (jiro, "second son"). Commoner everyday style of the numbered-son type. Modern association: Kawakami Otojiro, the Meiji actor and showman. The phrase in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Norimochi
explanation: Norimochi - With origins in the legend of the Model Governor, who ruled a poor province so well that its customs were copied across the Empire, this name evokes a sense of good example that spreads. It appeals to those who admire leadership by pattern rather than by command.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 範 (nori, "model, pattern") + 茂 (mochi, "flourish"); mochi for 茂 is a nanori reading, the ordinary one being shige. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Fujiwara no Norimochi, executed after the Jokyu War.

name: Heisaburo
explanation: Heisaburo means "peaceful third son" or "third son of the plain", which can suggest a boy born into calm times or a family of the open lowlands. People with this name may be even-tempered and easy in company.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: Kamakura- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and in period name lists. 平 (hei, "flat, peaceful") + 三郎 (saburo, "third son"). Commoner everyday style of the numbered-son type.

name: Zaemonsaburo
explanation: Zaemonsaburo - A name derived from the fusion of "guardian of the left gate" and "third son", reflecting a balance between inherited office and humble birth order. It is often embraced by those who strive for a post worth holding even as a younger son.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: a Muromachi bearer in period name lists. 左衛門 (zaemon, from the old Left Gate Guard title, worn as a name element) + 三郎 (saburo, "third son"), a stacked name of the kind common before the Edo period. Commoner everyday style.

name: Sadatomo
explanation: Sadatomo - A name derived from the fusion of "constancy" and "morning", reflecting a balance between steadfastness and fresh beginnings. It is often embraced by those who strive for loyalty that renews itself each day.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura through early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 貞 (sada, "constancy, chastity") + 朝 (tomo, "morning, court"); tomo for 朝 is a nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style.

name: Toshishige
explanation: Toshishige - This name means "keen and weighty". It represents a sharp mind anchored by gravity of character.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian, Muromachi and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 利 (toshi, "sharp, advantage") + 重 (shige, "weight, layered"); toshi for 利 is a nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style.

name: Tokimoto
explanation: The name Tokimoto is inspired by the Well of the First Hour in the old capital, known for its water that is said to have been drawn at the very moment the city was founded. The name reflects the timelessness of the place and is often chosen by those who value returning to first principles.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 時 (toki, "time") + 元 (moto, "origin"). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Takatada
explanation: Takatada - With origins in the legend of the Rising Retainer, who began as a gate guard and rose to command his lord's army without once being caught in a lie, this name evokes a sense of loyalty rewarded with elevation. It appeals to those who admire advancement through faithful service.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. 隆 (taka, "rise, prosper") + 忠 (tada, "loyalty"). Samurai formal-name style.

name: Nobuhide
explanation: Nobuhide - Composed of the elements "trust" (nobu) and "excellence" (hide), this name symbolizes a man whose word can be relied upon and whose deeds stand above those of his fellows. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of sincerity and distinguished service to a lord.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 信 (trust, faith) + 秀 (excel, surpass); both are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Oda Nobuhide, the Sengoku lord who was father of Oda Nobunaga.

name: Ujinari
explanation: Ujinari - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Lineage Restored, in which the last son of a disgraced house labored twenty years as a common clerk until his careful records exposed the forger who had ruined his family, and the Emperor returned the name to him. It reflects qualities such as patience, diligence, and loyalty to one's ancestors.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura, Sengoku and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 氏 (clan, lineage) + 業 (deed, work, vocation), read uji + nari; nari for 業 is a nanori reading rather than the everyday gyo/waza. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Morimune
explanation: Morimune - This name represents a flourishing lineage and is often chosen by those who are heirs to an old and honored house or who are expected to restore a family's fortunes and carry its traditions forward.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 盛 (flourish, prosper) + 宗 (lineage, main line, founding principle); mori and mune are conventional nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Nagaharu
explanation: Nagaharu - With origins in the legend of Nagaharu the Steward, who governed a famine-struck province for his absent lord so evenly that not one village rose in revolt, this name evokes a sense of steadiness and long peace. It appeals to those who admire quiet, enduring good governance over battlefield glory.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 長 (long, lasting; also chief) + 治 (govern, bring to peace), read naga + haru; haru is the nanori reading of 治. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Bessho Nagaharu, the Sengoku lord of Miki castle who held out against Hashiba Hideyoshi in a long siege.

name: Naganobu
explanation: Naganobu - A name that means "lasting faith", evoking trust that holds through a generation of hard winters without once being withdrawn.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 長 (long, lasting) + 信 (trust, faith); naga and nobu are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Yukitsugu
explanation: Yukitsugu - This name signifies conduct carried forward from those who came before, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values continuity, the example of their ancestors, and the duty to pass a way of life on unbroken.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 行 (go, conduct, practice) + 継 (succeed to, inherit, continue); yuki and tsugu are conventional nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Masasada
explanation: Masasada - A name that means "constant governance", evoking a magistrate whose rulings do not shift with the season or the standing of the petitioner.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 政 (governance, administration) + 貞 (constancy, steadfastness); masa and sada are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Hidetsuna
explanation: Hidetsuna - This name represents an excellence that others can hold onto like a rope, and is often chosen by those who are already the mainstay of their household or who are expected to become the one their comrades rely on in a hard fight.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from Heian through Sengoku on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 秀 (excel, surpass) + 綱 (rope, mainstay, guiding principle); hide and tsuna are conventional nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Yukiyasu
explanation: Yukiyasu - Composed of the elements "conduct" (yuki) and "peace" (yasu), this name symbolizes a life that brings calm to those around it. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of steady bearing and a household at ease.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura, Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 行 (go, conduct) + 泰 (peace, calm, security); yasu for 泰 is a nanori reading (the everyday reading is tai). Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Kichijiro
explanation: Kichijiro - This name signifies a lucky second son, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values good fortune, an orderly household, and the modest hope that a younger child will find his own place in the world.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and in Edo village registers (kiyose). Kanji 吉 (good luck) + 治 (govern, settle) + 郎 (son, young man); the -jiro ending marks a second son and 治郎 is a common variant of the more usual 次郎. Commoner/everyday style, never a samurai formal name. Modern association: Kichijiro (written 吉次郎) is the wavering apostate in Endo Shusaku's novel Silence and its 2016 film.

name: Sadakuni
explanation: Sadakuni - Composed of the elements "constancy" (sada) and "province" (kuni), this name symbolizes a land held steady by the man who governs it. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of reliable stewardship and a lord's duty to the domain.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 貞 (constancy, steadfastness) + 国 (country, province, domain); sada and kuni are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Ujitsuna
explanation: Ujitsuna - With origins in the legend of Ujitsuna the Binder, who after his father's death held together a dozen quarreling vassal houses by marriage, oath and patient arbitration until they were one clan, this name evokes a sense of cohesion and dependable strength. It appeals to those who admire the work of holding a family together rather than winning it glory.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 氏 (clan, lineage) + 綱 (rope, mainstay); uji and tsuna are conventional nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Hojo Ujitsuna, second head of the Later Hojo of Odawara, whose real career the explanation loosely echoes.

name: Enshu
explanation: The name Enshu is associated with the famous Sealing of the Cracked Bell, in which a monk of a mountain temple, finding the great bell split by frost, refused to let it be recast and instead taught the brothers to ring the flaw so that its uneven note became the temple's call to prayer. Those who choose this name try to embody values of acceptance, completeness found in imperfection, and devotion to the doctrine over the object.
notes: Attested Buddhist monastic name: Heian-period bearers in the issendai Buddhist name lists. Kanji 円 (circle, perfection, completeness) + 宗 (doctrine, sect, main principle), both in their on readings en + shu (shū). A monk's religious name, not a samurai formal name or a commoner name. Modern association only by sound: the tea master Kobori Enshu writes his name 遠州, different kanji.

name: Ietsuna
explanation: Ietsuna - A name derived from the fusion of "house" and "mainstay", reflecting a balance between the private duty owed to one's own family and the public duty of being the rope others hold. It is often embraced by those who strive for a household that stands as a support to its lord and neighbors.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian, Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 家 (house, family) + 綱 (rope, mainstay); ie and tsuna are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Tokugawa Ietsuna, the fourth Tokugawa shogun (a later, Edo-period bearer than those in our lists).

name: Kaneyoshi
explanation: Kaneyoshi - A name derived from the fusion of "combining" and "ability", reflecting a balance between breadth and mastery. It is often embraced by those who strive for competence in many arts rather than fame in one.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Kamakura through Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, recorded in our metadata as a Buddhist name, though in shape it is an ordinary two-element warrior formal name. Kanji 兼 (combine, hold concurrently) + 能 (ability, skill); kane and yoshi are nanori readings. Suits either a samurai formal name or a monk who kept a lay-style name. No notable modern association.

name: Sukenobu
explanation: Sukenobu - Rooted in the ancient proverb "Heaven helps those whose word is whole", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value sincerity and the belief that the Fortunes favor an honest man.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 祐 (divine help, blessing) + 信 (trust, faith); suke for 祐 is a nanori reading (the everyday reading is yū). Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: the Edo ukiyo-e artist Nishikawa Sukenobu (same kanji).

name: Ujitada
explanation: Ujitada - Stemming from the word "chu", which denotes loyalty to one's lord, this name embodies the spirit of a lineage defined by faithful service. It resonates with those who are steadfast, dutiful, and proud to be counted among the retainers of an old house.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura, Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 氏 (clan, lineage) + 忠 (loyalty, read chu in isolation and tada as a nanori reading); uji is standard. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Toshiro
explanation: Toshiro - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the noh stage, this name represents the quick, precise intelligence a performer needs to hold a mask's stillness and a chorus's timing at once. It is often chosen by those who appreciate restraint and exact movement and have a deep respect for the years of drilling behind a single graceful step.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers, in Sengoku name articles (bryant) and in Japanese Wikipedia biographies. Kanji 敏 (quick, clever, alert) + 郎 (son, young man); toshi is a nanori-style reading of 敏 and -ro (-rō) is the common son-name ending. Commoner/everyday (tsusho) style rather than a formal name. Modern association: the actor Mifune Toshiro (三船敏郎, same kanji), the star of Seven Samurai and Yojimbo.

name: Yukimune
explanation: Yukimune - This name signifies conduct that honors the founding line of a house, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values orthodoxy, the teachings of their school, and a life lived by the principles their ancestors set down.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 行 (go, conduct, practice) + 宗 (lineage, main line, founding principle); yuki and mune are conventional nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Toshitane
explanation: Toshitane - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A keen blade is nothing without an heir to carry it", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value the continuation of their line as much as their own accomplishments.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 利 (advantage, profit; also sharp, keen) + 胤 (heir, offspring, lineage); toshi and tane are nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Kazuyuki
explanation: The name Kazuyuki is inspired by the First Ford, known for its single stone causeway where every traveler from the eastern provinces must cross the same river by the same path. The name reflects the unity of the place and is often chosen by those who value single-mindedness and a shared road with their comrades.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 一 (one, first) + 之 (the possessive particle "of"), read kazu + yuki; both are stylized nanori readings, 之 as yuki being a purely name-only convention with no independent meaning beyond "of" or "this". Samurai formal-name style; the same sounds are also written 和幸 or 一幸 in later names. No notable modern association.

name: Tametoki
explanation: The name Tametoki is associated with the famous Waiting at the Gate, in which a provincial governor passed over for office stood at the palace gate through three seasons of petitions until the Emperor, moved by a single poem he submitted, granted him the post. Those who choose this name try to embody values of patience, the worth of learning, and acting when the moment is right.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Heian and Kamakura bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, recorded in our metadata as a Buddhist name, though in shape it is a court-noble formal name. Kanji 為 (to do, to act, for the sake of) + 時 (time, the right moment); tame and toki are standard nanori readings. Suits a samurai or courtier formal name, or a man who took orders late in life and kept it. Famous bearer: Fujiwara no Tametoki, the Heian scholar-official and father of Murasaki Shikibu, whose real story the explanation echoes.

name: Ichirobei
explanation: Ichirobei - This name pays tribute to the Opening of the Spring Market, an event that emphasizes the first day of trading after the thaw, when the eldest son of each stall-keeping household carries the family's tally board to the market square. People choose this name to reflect their values for honest dealing, the pride of a first son, and a household's good name in the marketplace.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and in Edo village registers (kiyose). Kanji 市 (market, town) + 郎 (son) + 兵衛 (a fossilized palace-guard title used as an ordinary name suffix among Edo commoners); ichi-ro marks a first son. Commoner/everyday style, typical of an Edo shopkeeper or village householder. No notable modern association.

name: Iemoto
explanation: Iemoto means "foundation of the house" or "root of the family", which can suggest a first son on whom the line rests or a father's wish that this child anchor the household. People with this name may be steady, dutiful, and reluctant to leave home.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 家 (house, family) + 基 (foundation, base); ie and moto are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association by sound only: iemoto (家元, different second kanji) is the term for the hereditary head of a school of tea, flower arranging or noh.

name: Yataro
explanation: Yataro - With origins in the legend of Yataro the Ferryman, who carried an entire village across a flooding river through one night, going back for each household in turn until the water took the last boat, this name evokes a sense of tireless, ever-growing effort. It appeals to those who admire a man who keeps returning to the work until it is done.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Heian and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 弥 (increasingly, ever more) + 太 (great) + 郎 (son); ya, ta and ro are standard readings. Although recorded under nanori in our metadata, this is an everyday (tsusho) style name of the kind samurai used before or alongside their formal name, and equally at home on a commoner. Famous bearer: Iwasaki Yataro, the Meiji founder of Mitsubishi.

name: Chikamori
explanation: Chikamori - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of armor lacing, this name represents the close, protective binding of plate to plate that keeps a warrior whole. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the patient craft of the armorer and have a deep respect for those who guard others with their own hands.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian, Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 親 (parent, kin; also close, intimate) + 守 (protect, guard); chika for 親 is a nanori reading and mori is the standard name reading of 守. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Yukisada
explanation: Yukisada - A name derived from the fusion of "conduct" and "constancy", reflecting a balance between action and steadiness. It is often embraced by those who strive for a life in which what they do never wavers from what they have sworn.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 行 (go, conduct) + 貞 (constancy, steadfastness); yuki and sada are conventional nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Toshinari
explanation: Toshinari can be written with two different kanji. One means "quick-witted achievement", and the other means "talented achievement". The choice of kanji could reflect what a family hopes a son will become, such as a sharp and alert magistrate or a gifted poet in the courtly tradition.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia with the kanji 敏成. Kanji 敏 (quick, clever, alert) + 成 (become, achieve); the alternate spelling 俊成 uses 俊 (talented, outstanding) with the same reading. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: the Heian poet Fujiwara no Toshinari (俊成), better known by the on reading Shunzei.

name: Genshichi
explanation: Genshichi - Derived from the phrase "seven springs from one source", this name embodies the idea of a single wellspring feeding many streams. It is often associated with those who are the source of a large family's livelihood or the seventh child of a house with deep roots.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and in Japanese Wikipedia biographies (Sengoku). Kanji 源 (source, origin; also the Minamoto surname character) + 七 (seven); gen and shichi are on readings and number-names of this kind commonly marked birth order. Commoner/everyday style. No notable modern association.

name: Chujiro
explanation: The name Chujiro is associated with the famous Raising of the Long Bridge, in which the second son of a village carpenter, when the master builders despaired at a river too wide to span, laid the piers in the dry season by his own reckoning and was named bridge-warden for life. Those who choose this name try to embody values of practical ingenuity, humility of birth, and work that outlasts its maker.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 長 (long, chief) + 次 (next, second) + 郎 (son); 長 here takes its on reading chō, so the strict romanization is Chōjirō and "Chujiro" is a macron-dropped, slightly stylized spelling. Commoner/everyday style. Modern association: Chōjirō (長次郎), the sixteenth-century founder of the Raku family of tea-bowl potters.

name: Oniwakamaru
explanation: Oniwakamaru - Composed of the elements "demon" and "young", this name symbolizes the fierce child whose strength outruns his years. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of untamed vigor, a fearsome look that hides a loyal heart, and the hope that a wild boy will grow into a guardian.
notes: Attested pre-modern childhood name (yomyo): recorded in Sengoku name articles (bryant) as a Heian-period bearer. Kanji 鬼 (demon, ogre) + 若 (young) + 丸 (the -maru suffix used for boys' childhood names); oni, waka and maru are the ordinary readings. A childhood name, not a formal adult name of any caste; flagged here as peasant-usable because -maru names were not caste-bound. Famous bearer: Oniwakamaru was the childhood name of the warrior-monk Musashibo Benkei.

name: Senjiro
explanation: Senjiro - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The hermit's second son still carries water up the mountain", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value humble labor over lofty detachment.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and in Japanese Wikipedia biographies. Kanji 仙 (hermit, mountain immortal) + 次 (next, second) + 郎 (son); sen, ji and ro are the ordinary readings and -jiro marks a second son. Commoner/everyday style. No notable modern association. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Zenhachi
explanation: Zenhachi - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of temple carving, this name represents the goodness that a craftsman hopes to cut into every one of the eight faces of a shrine lantern. It is often chosen by those who appreciate humble, devotional craftsmanship and have a deep respect for the carvers who work unsigned in the service of the Fortunes.
notes: Attested pre-modern everyday name (tsusho): a Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 善 (good, virtue) + 八 (eight); zen and hachi are on readings, and number-names of this shape marked birth order among commoners and low-ranking samurai alike. Commoner/everyday style. No notable modern association.

name: Mitsuyuki
explanation: Mitsuyuki chose their name in honor of the famous Doji Mitsuyuki, who walked the length of the Imperial road on foot to deliver a poem of condolence to a grieving rival house, and by that light-footed courtesy ended a feud of three generations.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 光 (light, shine) + 行 (go, conduct); mitsu and yuki are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Notable bearer: Minamoto no Mitsuyuki, a Kamakura-period poet and scholar of the Tale of Genji.

name: Sadafusa
explanation: Sadafusa means "settled chamber" or "fixed abode", which can suggest a household that has put down roots or a man whose place in the world is firmly decided. People with this name may be homebodies of the best kind, loyal to a single lord and a single hearth.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 定 (settle, fix, decide) + 房 (chamber, house; also tuft); sada and fusa are conventional nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Kinmitsu
explanation: Kinmitsu - Stemming from the word "kin", which denotes what is public and open to all, this name embodies the spirit of conduct that hides nothing from the court. It resonates with those who are fair, transparent, and comfortable being watched.
notes: Attested court nanori: Heian and Kamakura bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 公 (public; lord, duke) + 光 (light); kin for 公 is a stylized nanori reading used almost exclusively in the names of Heian court nobles (the Fujiwara and their branches), and mitsu is standard. A courtier-style samurai formal name. No notable modern association.

name: Sadaharu
explanation: Sadaharu - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the Settled Waters, an event that emphasizes the day the spring floods are declared past and the magistrates walk the repaired dikes. People choose this name to reflect their values for steady governance, the calm after hardship, and a land kept in order.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 貞 (constancy, steadfastness) + 治 (govern, bring to peace); sada is standard and haru is the nanori reading of 治. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: the baseball player Oh Sadaharu (王貞治, same kanji), holder of the world professional home-run record.

name: Motosato
explanation: Motosato - Rooted in the ancient proverb "However far the road, the village you were born in walks beside you", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value their origins and the home that shaped them.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 元 (origin, source) + 郷 (home village, native place); moto is standard and sato is the kun reading of 郷. Samurai formal-name style, uncommon. No notable modern association.

name: Shohachi
explanation: Shohachi - This name signifies the eighth child of a manor household, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values a large family, the land his house works, and the contentment of a modest place in a settled order.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 庄 (manor, estate; a common element in rural place names) + 八 (eight), on readings sho (shō) + hachi; number-names of this kind marked birth order. Commoner/everyday style, typical of a village or shop householder. No notable modern association.

name: Motoji
explanation: Motoji - A name derived from the fusion of "foundation" and "lineage", reflecting a balance between what a man builds himself and what he inherits. It is often embraced by those who strive for a house whose future rests on more than its name.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 基 (foundation) + 氏 (clan, lineage); the fuller reading is Motouji, and "Motoji" is a contracted, somewhat stylized rendering of the same kanji. Samurai formal-name style. Notable bearer: Ashikaga Motouji (基氏), first Kamakura kubo of the Muromachi period.

name: Heishichi
explanation: Heishichi - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of tatami weaving, this name represents the flat, even surface a craftsman lays down seven rushes at a time. It is often chosen by those who appreciate quiet, level workmanship and have a deep respect for the weavers whose floors every house stands on.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 平 (flat, level; peace; also the Taira surname character) + 七 (seven), on readings hei + shichi; number-names of this shape marked birth order. Commoner/everyday style. No notable modern association.

name: Yoshitake
explanation: Yoshitake - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the sword dance, this name represents righteousness expressed through martial form. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the discipline that turns a weapon into ceremony and have a deep respect for the warriors who perform it before the shrine.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 義 (righteousness, duty) + 武 (martial, military); yoshi and take are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Chikaie
explanation: Chikaie - This name pays tribute to the Gathering of the Hearths, an event that emphasizes the midwinter night when every branch of a family returns to the main house to eat from one pot. People choose this name to reflect their values for kinship, closeness between the generations, and a house that stays whole.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura, Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 親 (parent, kin; close, intimate) + 家 (house, family); chika for 親 is a nanori reading and ie is standard. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Harukiyo
explanation: Harukiyo - This name means "clear and pure". It represents a sky washed clean after rain and a heart with nothing hidden in it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 晴 (clear sky, fine weather) + 清 (pure, clean); haru and kiyo are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Iesada
explanation: Iesada - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Unmoved House, in which a lord whose castle was besieged for a full year refused every offer to abandon his vassals' families and buy his own escape, and was rewarded when the besiegers, running out of rice first, withdrew. It reflects qualities such as steadfastness, duty to dependents, and the settled resolve of a household that will not be shaken.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from Heian through Azuchi-Momoyama on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 家 (house, family) + 定 (settle, fix, decide); ie and sada are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Tokugawa Iesada, the thirteenth Tokugawa shogun (a later bearer than those in our lists).

name: Yoshimura
explanation: Yoshimura - This name represents righteousness practiced in the village rather than at court and is often chosen by those who are raised among the farmers of their family's lands or who are expected to govern a domain by knowing the villagers who feed it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 義 (righteousness, duty) + 村 (village); yoshi is a standard nanori reading and mura is the kun reading of 村. Samurai formal-name style, though the same kanji are far more familiar today as a surname. Notable bearer: Miura Yoshimura, a Kamakura-period gokenin.

name: Tametsune
explanation: Tametsune - Composed of the elements "to act" (tame) and "to govern" (tsune), this name symbolizes a man who takes up the work of ordering the world rather than merely studying it. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of practical administration and the scriptural learning that underlies it.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Heian, Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, recorded in our metadata as a Buddhist name, though in shape it is a court or warrior formal name. Kanji 為 (to do, to act, for the sake of) + 経 (sutra; pass through; govern, manage); tame is standard and tsune is a nanori reading of 経 (its everyday reading is kei or kyō). Suits a samurai formal name or a courtier who later took the tonsure. No notable modern association.

name: Koretsuna
explanation: Koretsuna - Derived from the phrase "think, then bind", this name embodies the idea of careful thought made fast in action, like a knot tied only after the rope has been measured. It is often associated with those who deliberate before they commit and hold firm once they have.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Kamakura bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 惟 (think, consider; also an emphatic particle) + 縄 (rope, cord); kore for 惟 is a stylized nanori reading found in Heian court and early warrior names, and tsuna for 縄 is likewise a name-only reading (the everyday reading is nawa). Samurai formal-name style, archaic in flavor. No notable modern association.

name: Ushimatsu
explanation: Ushimatsu - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The ox is slow, but the earth is patient", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value steady labor over quick reward and the endurance of the pine through every winter.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in a late-Edo village register (kiyose). Kanji 牛松, ushi (ox) + matsu (pine), both plain readings; an ox-and-pine compound of the animal-and-plant kind rural Edo commoners bore. Commoner everyday-name style, suitable for a farmer or laborer. Ushimatsu is also the name of the protagonist of Shimazaki Toson's 1906 novel Hakai (The Broken Commandment).

name: Yoshikane
explanation: Yoshikane means "to hold righteousness" or "duty doubled", which can suggest a man who keeps to what is right or one who bears two obligations at once. People with this name may be steadfast under conflicting demands.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian, Kamakura and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 義兼, yoshi (righteousness, duty) + kane (to combine, to hold two things at once), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style; 兼 is a classic second element in warrior-house name lineages. No notable modern association.

name: Mitsukane
explanation: Mitsukane means "light combined" or "holding light together", which can suggest one who gathers many small virtues into a single radiance or one who serves two masters honorably at once. People with this name may be steady, versatile retainers trusted with more than one charge.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 光兼, mitsu (light) + kane (to combine, to hold concurrently), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style, a typical two-element warrior compound. No notable modern association.

name: Sadatoshi
explanation: Sadatoshi chose their name in honor of the famous Lion magistrate Sadatoshi, who sat in judgment for forty years and was never once shown to have ruled from favor or fear.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 貞俊, sada (constancy, chastity, steadfastness) + toshi (talented, quick-witted), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Nichijo
explanation: Nichijo - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Monk Who Rode the Sun, in which a wandering brother, told he could not cross a flooded river before dark, sat in meditation until the sun itself carried his shadow to the far bank. It reflects qualities such as patience, faith in the Tao, and the calm that outlasts any obstacle.
notes: Attested Buddhist name: a Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 日乗, nichi (sun, day) + jo (to ride, to mount), both on-readings, as is normal for a dharma name. Monk's name style, of the Nichiren-lineage kind that takes 日 as its first element; not a lay name. No notable modern association.

name: Yorisuke
explanation: Yorisuke - This name signifies a reliable source of support, the one on whom others depend and who supplies what the household lacks, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values loyalty, provision for others, and being worthy of trust.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 頼資, yori (to rely on, to trust) + suke (resources, assets, to aid), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style, of the courtly Heian-Kamakura kind. No notable modern association.

name: Chikamitsu
explanation: Chikamitsu - Stemming from the word "chika", which denotes closeness and kinship, this name embodies the spirit of light shared among those bound together. It resonates with those who are warm toward their kin, generous with their household, and bright in the eyes of those nearest them.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 親光, chika (intimate, parent, close kin) + mitsu (light), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Mitsushige
explanation: Mitsushige - This name means "light layered upon light". It represents an honor that accumulates generation by generation, each bearer adding weight to the family's brilliance.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from Heian through Azuchi-Momoyama on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 光重, mitsu (light) + shige (heavy, to pile up), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Yasoji
explanation: Yasoji - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The eightieth koku is counted like the first", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value diligence in the smallest transaction and honesty at the end of a long ledger as much as at its start.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers (issendai-merchants). Kanji 彌惣次 as the register wrote it; 彌 (ya, the old form of 弥, increasingly) + 惣 (so, all, the whole) + 次 (ji, next, second son). This is a merchant-house everyday name of the three-element kind, with no dictionary meaning beyond auspicious fullness and a birth-order suffix; commoner style, suitable for a shopkeeper or clerk. No notable modern association.

name: Toshihide
explanation: The name Toshihide is associated with the famous Contest of the Thousand Brushes, in which the Emperor summoned the finest calligraphers of every clan and the winner was a young provincial scribe whose hand was quick, clear, and unadorned. Those who choose this name try to embody values of native talent, clarity of mind, and excellence that needs no ornament.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 俊秀, toshi (talented, quick-witted) + hide (excellent, outstanding), both standard nanori readings; as a common noun shunshu means a person of outstanding talent. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Sukekuro
explanation: Sukekuro - A name derived from the fusion of "help" and "ninth son", reflecting a balance between the duty to assist and the humility of coming last. It is often embraced by those who strive for usefulness without expecting any inheritance in return.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: late-Edo merchant registers (issendai-merchants) and a Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 助九郎, suke (to help, to assist) + kuro (九郎, ninth son), a standard tsusho reading. Commoner everyday-name style, of the birth-order -ro kind borne by townsmen and low-ranking retainers alike. No notable modern association.

name: Kagehira
explanation: Kagehira - A name derived from the fusion of "shadow and scenery" and "peace and evenness", reflecting a balance between the quiet observer and the calm hand that keeps order. It is often embraced by those who strive for a level temper and an eye that misses nothing.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 景平, kage (view, scenery; also shadow, light) + hira (flat, level, peaceful), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style; 景 as kage is the classic Kamakura-Sengoku warrior reading. No notable modern association.

name: Naoyasu
explanation: Naoyasu chose their name in honor of the famous Crane courtier Naoyasu, who kept the peace between two feuding provinces for a decade by refusing to carry a single false word between them.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: an Azuchi-Momoyama-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia, plus one of undetermined period. Kanji 直保, nao (straight, honest, upright) + yasu (to protect, to preserve), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Beijiro
explanation: Beijiro - A name that means "second son of the guard", evoking a household of soldiers in which the younger boy follows his father to the gate.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Kamakura and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and in a Japanese-name compilation (nihonjin-name). Kanji 兵衞次郎, hyoe (兵衞, old form of 兵衛, a palace-guard office title) + jiro (次郎, second son). READING FLAG: the conventional reading of 兵衞次郎 is Hyoejiro; Beijiro is a contracted or dialectal reading of the same kanji and is unusual. Commoner everyday-name style, a title-plus-birth-order compound of the kind common among warrior retainers and villagers alike. No notable modern association.

name: Iemasa
explanation: Iemasa - This name represents the governance of a household and is often chosen by those who are heirs to an established family or who are expected to manage a domain's affairs with a firm and orderly hand.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from Kamakura through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 家政, ie (house, family, lineage) + masa (government, administration), both standard nanori readings; as a common noun kasei means household management. Samurai formal-name style, of the kind used by heads of established houses. No notable modern association.

name: Yasuhide
explanation: Yasuhide - Stemming from the word "yasu", which denotes calm, peace, and broad tranquility, this name embodies the spirit of excellence achieved without agitation. It resonates with those who are composed, quietly outstanding, and untroubled under pressure.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 泰秀, yasu (peaceful, calm, grand) + hide (excellent), both standard nanori readings; 泰 as yasu is a nanori reading rather than the everyday tai. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Ichijuro
explanation: The name Ichijuro is associated with the famous Market of the Tenth Day, in which a river town, its granaries emptied by flood, was fed for a month by merchants who reopened trade on the tenth day of the month with no expectation of profit. Those who choose this name try to embody values of commerce as service, first to arrive when help is needed, and generosity in lean seasons.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Edo merchant registers (issendai-merchants) and early- and late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 市十郎, ichi (market; also one) + juro (十郎, tenth son), standard tsusho readings. Commoner everyday-name style, of the birth-order -ro kind typical of townsmen and merchant houses. No notable modern association.

name: Chikasada
explanation: Chikasada chose their name in honor of the famous Crab commander Chikasada, who held his brother's fortress for a full winter after his brother fell and never once let the garrison see him doubt.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 親定, chika (intimate, close kin, parent) + sada (to settle, to fix, constancy), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Shigemune
explanation: Shigemune means "accomplished head of the line" or "one who becomes the origin", which can suggest a founder who builds something that outlasts them or an heir who completes what their ancestors began. People with this name may be ambitious, dutiful, and mindful of the lineage they carry.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian, Kamakura and Azuchi-Momoyama-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 成宗, shige (to become, to accomplish; a nanori reading of 成, more usually nari) + mune (origin, head of a lineage, sect), both attested nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style; 宗 as mune is a classic warrior-house element. No notable modern association.

name: Kunihira
explanation: Kunihira - This name means "peaceful province". It represents the wish that the bearer's home country stay level and calm, and the duty of a warrior to keep it so.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 国平, kuni (country, province) + hira (flat, level, peace), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Kunihira is also a well-known name among historical Japanese swordsmiths, notably the Kamakura-era Rai Kunihira.

name: Sadanobu
explanation: Sadanobu - Composed of the elements "constancy" and "proclamation", this name symbolizes a word given once and never withdrawn. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of firm judgment, reliability, and a voice that carries authority because it does not waver.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, plus one of undetermined period. Kanji 貞宣, sada (constancy, steadfastness) + nobu (to proclaim, to declare), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. The better-known modern association is with the Edo statesman Matsudaira Sadanobu, whose name is written 定信 with different kanji.

name: Tamemune
explanation: Tamemune - A name derived from the fusion of "for the sake of" and "the origin of the line", reflecting a balance between service to others and loyalty to one's own house. It is often embraced by those who strive for a life spent in the family's cause.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 為宗, tame (for the sake of, to do; a standard nanori reading of 為) + mune (origin, head of lineage, sect), both attested nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style; 為 as a first element marks several Heian-Kamakura warrior lineages. No notable modern association.

name: Tameyuki
explanation: Tameyuki - Derived from the phrase "act for the sake of another", this name embodies the idea of deeds done in service rather than for one's own name. It is often associated with those who go where they are sent and do what is needed without asking who will be credited.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian, Kamakura and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 為行, tame (for the sake of, to do) + yuki (to go, to act, conduct), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Sadamasa
explanation: Sadamasa means "settled and correct" or "fixed in righteousness", which can suggest a judge whose rulings hold for generations or a retainer whose loyalty was decided long ago and has never needed revisiting. People with this name may be firm, upright, and hard to sway.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers in every period from Heian through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia, one of the most durable warrior compounds. Kanji 定正, sada (to settle, to fix) + masa (correct, righteous), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Chikayuki
explanation: Chikayuki chose their name in honor of the famous Unicorn scout Chikayuki, who rode the near roads of the border every night for a year so that no raider could approach a village unseen.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 近行, chika (near, close) + yuki (to go, conduct), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Korezumi
explanation: Korezumi - This name signifies purity of thought, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values an unmixed loyalty and a heart kept clean by deliberate care.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 惟純, kore (this, to think; a nanori reading of 惟) + zumi (pure, unmixed; sumi voiced in compound), both attested nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style, of the courtly Heian kind that used 惟 as a lineage element. No notable modern association.

name: Ujiaki
explanation: Ujiaki means "bright clan" or "the lineage made clear", which can suggest a house whose name shines at court or a bearer who brings their family's affairs into the light of honest dealing. People with this name may be proud of their descent and open in their conduct.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 氏明, uji (clan, lineage) + aki (bright, clear), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style; 氏 as a first element is the mark of certain Sengoku warrior houses, notably the Hojo of Odawara. No notable modern association.

name: Ujimitsu
explanation: Ujimitsu - This name signifies a lineage brought to fullness, the clan at the height of its strength, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values family prosperity, completeness, and the duty to leave the house fuller than it was found.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 氏満, uji (clan, lineage) + mitsu (full, complete), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style, of the 氏-lineage kind. No notable modern association.

name: Toemon
explanation: Toemon - A name derived from the fusion of "wisteria" and "the guard at the right gate", reflecting a balance between the graceful and the watchful. It is often embraced by those who strive for a steady post honorably kept and a household that flowers in peace.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, late-Edo merchant registers (issendai-merchants), and a late-Edo village register (kiyose). Kanji 藤右衛門, to (wisteria, the 藤 of Fujiwara, read to in on-reading) + emon (右衛門, the Right Gate Guard office title, a stock ending of Edo commoner names). Commoner everyday-name style, one of the most common -emon names of village and merchant registers. No notable modern association.

name: Yorinaka
explanation: Yorinaka - A name derived from the fusion of "reliance" and "the middle", reflecting a balance between being leaned upon and standing between parties as a mediator. It is often embraced by those who strive for trustworthiness and fair dealing.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 頼仲, yori (to rely on, to trust) + naka (middle, relations between), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style, of the 頼-lineage kind associated with Minamoto houses. No notable modern association.

name: Koreyasu
explanation: Koreyasu - Composed of the elements "to think" and "peace", this name symbolizes a tranquility that is reasoned rather than merely felt. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of a contemplative mind and a household kept calm by good judgment.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 惟安, kore (this, to think; a nanori reading of 惟) + yasu (peace, ease, tranquility), both attested nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style, of the courtly 惟-lineage kind. No notable modern association.

name: Heizaemon
explanation: Heizaemon - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Gatekeeper Who Would Not Sleep, in which a common guard at a lord's left gate stood his post through a three-day siege while the samurai within slept in shifts, and was granted a sword for it. It reflects qualities such as humble steadfastness, vigilance, and honor earned at a low station.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and late-Edo merchant registers (issendai-merchants). Kanji 平左衛門, hei (flat, peaceful; the 平 of the Taira, read hei in on-reading) + zaemon (左衛門, the Left Gate Guard office title, voiced in compound). Commoner everyday-name style, one of the stock -zaemon names of Edo townsmen and villagers. No notable modern association.

name: Nobumichi
explanation: Nobumichi - This name signifies faith that swells and grows the more it is tested, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values conviction, abundance of spirit, and the Tao's promise that trust rightly placed is never wasted.
notes: Attested name: a Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia (tagged buddhist in our sources), plus one of undetermined period. Kanji 信彭, nobu (faith, trust) + 彭 (to swell, to be abundant; also the surname Peng). READING FLAG: 彭 is a rare character in names and michi is a nanori reading found in name dictionaries rather than an everyday one; treat the reading as stylized. Despite the source tag, the name has the shape of a samurai nanori rather than a monk's dharma name; suitable for either. No notable modern association.

name: Yoritoshi
explanation: Yoritoshi - Stemming from the word "yori", which denotes trust and reliance, this name embodies the spirit of talent that others can depend upon. It resonates with those who are quick, capable, and asked for first when something must be done well.
notes: Attested name: Heian, Kamakura and Azuchi-Momoyama-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia (tagged buddhist in our sources). Kanji 頼俊, yori (to rely on, to trust) + toshi (talented, quick-witted), both standard nanori readings. The shape is that of a samurai formal name of the 頼-lineage kind; a monk bearing it would most likely have kept it from before taking vows. No notable modern association.

name: Kisaburo
explanation: Kisaburo - Derived from the phrase "a third joy", this name embodies the idea of a third son welcomed as gladly as the first. It is often associated with those who are cheerful, unenvious of their elders, and content with a place they did not choose.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: late-Edo merchant registers (issendai-merchants) and bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 喜三郎, ki (joy, rejoicing) + saburo (三郎, third son), standard tsusho readings. Commoner everyday-name style, of the birth-order -ro kind. No notable modern association.

name: Magoshiro
explanation: The name Magoshiro is inspired by the four-cornered market town of Yotsuya, known for its generations of merchant families where a grandson inherits the stall his grandfather kept. The name reflects the continuity of the place and is often chosen by those who value family trade, respect for elders, and a fourth son's willingness to carry on.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Kamakura and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and in a Japanese-name compilation (nihonjin-name), and late-Edo merchant registers (issendai-merchants). Kanji 孫四郎, mago (grandchild) + shiro (四郎, fourth son), standard tsusho readings. Commoner everyday-name style, of the birth-order -ro kind also borne as a tsusho by warriors. The Yotsuya in the explanation is a Rokugani invention, not a reference to the Edo district. No notable modern association.

name: Ennin
explanation: Ennin - This name represents perfect benevolence, the circle of compassion with no gap in it, and is often chosen by those who are entering a monastery or who are expected to carry the Tao's teaching to distant provinces.
notes: Attested Buddhist name: a Heian-period bearer in our Buddhist-name list (issendai-buddhist). Kanji 円仁, en (circle, perfect, complete) + nin (benevolence, humaneness), both on-readings, as is standard for a dharma name. Monk's name style, not a lay name. The historical Ennin (794-864) was a Tendai patriarch famous for his diary of travels in Tang China.

name: Akinobu
explanation: Akinobu - Stemming from the word "aki", which denotes what is made manifest and evident, this name embodies the spirit of faith that can be seen in deeds. It resonates with those who are open, sincere, and whose word is plainly kept.
notes: Attested name: Heian, Kamakura and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia (tagged buddhist in our sources). Kanji 顕信, aki (manifest, evident; a nanori reading of 顕) + nobu (faith, trust), both attested nanori readings. The shape is that of a samurai formal name; the same kanji read kenshin would be a dharma name, so a monk bearing it is plausible either way. No notable modern association.

name: Hanzo
