explanation: Hanzo - With origins in the legend of the half-hidden retainer Hanzo, who guarded his lord's storehouse for thirty years and was seen by no thief who lived to describe him, this name evokes a sense of quiet menace, discretion, and unshakable loyalty. It appeals to those who admire service done in shadow and a reputation built from silence.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: late-Edo merchant registers (issendai-merchants) and bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 半藏 as the register wrote it, the old form of 半蔵; han (half) + zo (storehouse), a standard reading. Commoner everyday-name style of the -zo kind, also borne as a tsusho by warriors. The famous modern association is Hattori Hanzo, the Sengoku-period Tokugawa retainer turned pop-culture ninja, whose name gives Tokyo's Hanzomon its name.

name: Noritoki
explanation: Noritoki chose their name in honor of the famous Phoenix teacher Noritoki, who kept a school open through a famine year and taught the children of samurai and commoner alike to read the calendar so that no planting would be missed.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 教時, nori (to teach, doctrine; a nanori reading of 教) + toki (time, season), both attested nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style; 時 as a second element is a classic Hojo-lineage marker. No notable modern association.

name: Nagamoto
explanation: Nagamoto - A name derived from the fusion of "long-lasting" and "office", reflecting a balance between the endurance of a post and the duties it demands. It is often embraced by those who strive for a career of steady service and an office held without scandal.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura, Muromachi and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, plus one of undetermined period. Kanji 長職, naga (long, chief) + moto (office, duty, employment; a nanori reading of 職, more usually shoku), both attested nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Ujimasa
explanation: Ujimasa - A name derived from the fusion of "the clan" and "governance", reflecting a balance between loyalty to one's lineage and the impartial administration of a domain. It is often embraced by those who strive for a house well ruled and a province well kept.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 氏政, uji (clan, lineage) + masa (government, administration), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style, of the 氏-lineage kind. The best-known historical bearer is Hojo Ujimasa, fourth lord of Odawara, who died in 1590 at its fall.

name: Jirokichi
explanation: Jirokichi - Rooted in the ancient proverb "Good fortune visits the second son who sweeps the shop", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value humble diligence and the luck that follows those who do not wait for it.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: late-Edo merchant registers (issendai-merchants) and a late-Edo village register (kiyose). Kanji 次郎吉, jiro (次郎, second son) + kichi (good luck, auspicious), standard tsusho readings. Commoner everyday-name style, a birth-order name with an auspicious -kichi suffix typical of Edo townsmen. The best-known bearer is Nezumi Kozo Jirokichi, the Edo-period thief of folklore and kabuki.

name: Umasaburo
explanation: Umasaburo - With origins in the legend of the stable-hand Umasaburo, who as a third son with no inheritance tamed the wild horse no samurai could ride and was raised to the saddle for it, this name evokes a sense of grit, low-born talent, and skill that outranks birth. It appeals to those who admire the horseman and the outsider who earns a place.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Muromachi and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and in a Japanese-name compilation (nihonjin-name). Kanji 右馬三郎, uma (右馬, the Right Stables office of the old court, read uma) + saburo (三郎, third son). READING FLAG: 右馬 is conventionally read uma as a title, so Umasaburo is a plausible reading but the compound is a title-plus-birth-order name rather than the word for horse alone. Commoner everyday-name style borne by warrior retainers as a tsusho. No notable modern association.

name: Hideuji
explanation: Hideuji - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of lineage recitation, in which a herald names every generation of a house before a duel or a marriage, this name represents a clan whose roll of ancestors is its finest ornament. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the weight of a name well kept and have a deep respect for the heralds who remember them all.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku, Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 秀氏, hide (excellent, outstanding) + uji (clan, lineage), both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style; 秀 as a first element was widely granted in the Toyotomi era. No notable modern association.

name: Magozaemon
explanation: Magozaemon - A name that means "the grandson at the left gate", evoking a family whose men have kept the same post for three generations.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and late-Edo merchant registers (issendai-merchants). Kanji 孫左衛門, mago (grandchild) + zaemon (左衛門, the Left Gate Guard office title, voiced in compound). Commoner everyday-name style, one of the stock -zaemon names of Edo townsmen, also borne by warriors as a tsusho. No notable modern association.

name: Kintoki
explanation: The name Kintoki is inspired by the Hour-Bell Terrace of a lordly castle town, known for its great bronze bell that has marked the lord's hours for generations. The name reflects the steady, public timekeeping of the place and is often chosen by those who value punctuality and service that the whole domain can rely upon.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura- and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 公 (public, lord) + 時 (time, hour); 公 read as "kin" is a nanori reading rather than the ordinary on-reading "ko", which is conventional in formal names but worth flagging. Samurai formal-name style. The best-known bearer is the legendary Heian retainer Sakata no Kintoki, the adult form of the folk hero Kintaro.

name: Yaheiji
explanation: Yaheiji - Derived from the phrase "ever more peace, and the next in line", this name embodies the idea of a household whose calm grows with each generation. It is often associated with those who keep the family shop or fields steady and hand them on in better order than they found them.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and in the Kiyose village registers. Kanji 弥 (ever more, increasingly) + 平 (peace, level) + 次 (next, second); read ya-hei-ji, all standard readings. Commoner everyday style of the numeral-and-suffix type, common among shopkeepers and farmers. No notable modern bearer.

name: Zenzaemon
explanation: Zenzaemon - With origins in the legend of a gatekeeper who stood his post through a night of fire and let no looter pass, this name evokes a sense of quiet goodness and unshaken duty. It appeals to those who admire steadfast service done without any hope of reward.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: a Sengoku-period everyday (tsusho) name borne by figures on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 善 (good, virtuous) + 左衛門 (Left Gate Guard, an old palace-guard title that became a stock name ending); read zen-za-e-mon, standard. Commoner/everyday style, though samurai also used such -zaemon names as their common names alongside a formal nanori. No notable modern bearer.

name: Shigesato
explanation: Shigesato - A name that means "a village set at peace", evoking the samurai whose presence alone quiets a restless countryside.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 鎮 (to pacify, calm, garrison) + 里 (village, hamlet); 鎮 read as "shige" is a nanori reading (the ordinary reading is "chin" or "shizu"), so the reading is stylized in the way formal names often are. Samurai formal-name style. The modern game designer Shigesato Itoi bears the name with different kanji.

name: Shigenobu
explanation: Shigenobu can be written with two different kanji. One means "pacified trust", and the other means "weighty trust". The choice of kanji could reflect what a house wished to say about its heir, such as a peace secured by a reliable word or a faith that carries real weight between lord and retainer.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Kamakura through Azuchi-Momoyama periods on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 鎮 (pacify, calm) + 信 (trust, faith); 鎮 as "shige" is a nanori reading (ordinary reading "chin"), standard in formal names. Samurai formal-name style. Shigenobu remains a common given name in modern Japan, usually with other kanji such as 重信.

name: Fusakatsu
explanation: Fusakatsu - Composed of the elements "household" and "victory", this name symbolizes a family whose fortunes rise together. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of shared success and a lineage that wins as one.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, plus some of undated period. Kanji 房 (house, chamber; also a cluster or tassel) + 勝 (victory); 房 read "fusa" is its regular kun reading, 勝 "katsu" standard. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer.

name: Jiroemon
explanation: Jiroemon - This name represents the second son who stands guard at the right-hand gate and is often chosen by those who are younger sons expected to serve rather than inherit or who are expected to keep watch over the family's affairs while the heir carries its name.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in early- and late-Edo merchant registers, the Kiyose village registers, and on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 二郎 (second son) + 右衛門 (Right Gate Guard, an old guard title turned stock name ending); read ji-ro-e-mon, standard. Commoner everyday style, extremely common among Edo farmers and townsmen. No notable modern bearer.

name: Kotaro
explanation: Kotaro - This name pays tribute to the Festival of First Incense, an event that emphasizes the offering of the year's first fragrant smoke to the ancestors and the naming of firstborn sons before the family altar. People choose this name to reflect their values for filial devotion and a household that begins each year by honoring those who came before.
notes: Attested pre-modern name with bearers from the Heian period through late Edo on Japanese Wikipedia and in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 香 (fragrance, incense) + 太郎 (eldest son); read ko-ta-ro, standard, though 香 is an unusual choice - the common spelling is 小太郎 (little eldest son), and this fragrance spelling should be treated as a rarer variant. Commoner everyday style. Kotaro remains a very common modern given name.

name: Kazaemon
explanation: Kazaemon means "auspicious gate guard" or "the joyful one who keeps the left gate", which can suggest a man whose service brings luck to his household or a cheerful temperament that lightens hard duty. People with this name may be steady workers whose good humor makes them welcome wherever they are posted.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 嘉 (auspicious, joyful, praiseworthy) + 左衛門 (Left Gate Guard, an old guard title turned stock name ending); read ka-za-e-mon, standard. Commoner everyday style of the -zaemon type. No notable modern bearer.

name: Yashiro
explanation: Yashiro - Stemming from the word "shiro", which denotes the fourth son in the old counting names, this name embodies the spirit of the boy who must make his own way because three brothers stand ahead of him. It resonates with those who are ambitious, adaptable, and unafraid to leave home to find their place.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Kamakura- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 弥 (ever more) + 四郎 (fourth son); read ya-shi-ro, standard. Although recorded among formal names, the numeral shape is an everyday (tsusho) style that samurai and commoners both used; note that the same romaji also spells 社 (shrine), an entirely different word. No notable modern bearer.

name: Motosada
explanation: Motosada - Derived from the phrase "settled at the root", this name embodies the idea of a man whose foundations are fixed before he builds anything upon them. It is often associated with those who master the basics of their school so thoroughly that nothing later can shake them.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 元 (origin, root) + 定 (settled, fixed); read moto-sada, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer.

name: Kintsuna
explanation: Kintsuna means "the lord's rope" or "public discipline", which can suggest the cord that binds a domain together under its lord or the rule of law that holds regardless of who is in power. People with this name may be rigorous administrators who see themselves as the binding that keeps a province from coming apart.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura- and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 公 (public, lord) + 綱 (rope, cord; by extension a guiding principle or discipline); 公 as "kin" is a nanori reading (ordinary on-reading "ko"), standard in formal names but stylized. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer.

name: Choemon
explanation: Choemon chose their name in honor of the famous village headman Choemon, who walked three days to the provincial capital to lay his village's tax ledger before the magistrate and prove that the collector had been skimming rice.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and in the Kiyose village registers. Kanji 長 (chief, elder, long) + 右衛門 (Right Gate Guard, an old guard title turned stock name ending); read cho-e-mon, standard. Commoner everyday style of the -emon type, very common among Edo headmen and merchants. No notable modern bearer.

name: Jingobei
explanation: Jingobei - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the festival drum, this name represents the fifth and loudest beat that closes a measure. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the exuberance of a well-struck rhythm and have a deep respect for the drummers who carry a whole procession on their backs.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: an early-Edo everyday (tsusho) name borne by figures on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 甚 (exceedingly, greatly) + 五 (five) + 兵衛 (soldier guard, an old guard title turned stock name ending); read jin-go-be-e, standard. Commoner/everyday style of the -bei type, used by townsmen and as the common name of low-ranking samurai. No notable modern bearer.

name: Kyuemon
explanation: Kyuemon - Derived from the phrase "the gate long kept", this name embodies the idea of a post held faithfully for a lifetime. It is often associated with those who serve one house from boyhood to old age and are trusted with its keys.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and the Kiyose village registers, with Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 久 (long-lasting, enduring) + 右衛門 (Right Gate Guard, an old guard title turned stock name ending); read kyu-e-mon, standard. Commoner everyday style of the -emon type. No notable modern bearer.

name: Nobutsuna
explanation: Nobutsuna - Derived from the phrase "trust is the rope that binds the household", this name embodies the idea of many strands made strong together. It is often associated with those who hold a family or a company of retainers in one piece.
notes: Attested pre-modern name with bearers from the Heian period through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia; our source records it as a Buddhist name, but the shape is that of a standard samurai nanori (compare Takeda Nobutsuna), so it should be treated chiefly as a formal samurai name. Kanji 信 (trust, faith) + 縄 (rope, cord); read nobu-tsuna, both standard. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer. The phrase in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Koretoshi
explanation: Koretoshi chose their name in honor of the famous Crane courtier Koretoshi, who untangled a thirty-year boundary dispute between two provinces in a single afternoon by producing a land survey everyone else had forgotten existed.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian- and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 維 (to uphold, to bind; also a copula "this") + 敏 (quick, clever, alert); 維 read "kore" is a nanori reading (ordinary on-reading "i"), standard in the Heian-style formal names that use it. Samurai formal-name style with an aristocratic, court-era flavor. No notable modern bearer.

name: Mitsutsugu
explanation: Mitsutsugu - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the lamp-bearer of the mountain shrine, in which a dying priest hands his lantern to a boy who carries it unextinguished through a storm so the shrine's flame is never lost. It reflects qualities such as continuity, reverence for what one has been given, and the humility to be a link rather than the origin.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Kamakura through Sengoku periods on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 光 (light) + 継 (to succeed, to carry on); read mitsu-tsugu, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer.

name: Masamori
explanation: Masamori - A name that means "governance that flourishes", evoking the prosperous province whose lord rules well enough that the fields fill and the granaries overflow.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Heian period through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 政 (governance, administration) + 盛 (to flourish, prosper); read masa-mori, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Taira no Masamori, grandfather of Kiyomori, is the best-known historical bearer.

name: Hikohachi
explanation: Hikohachi - Stemming from the word "hiko", which denotes a fine young man in the old poetic tongue, this name embodies the spirit of the eighth child who is welcomed as warmly as the first. It resonates with those who are good-natured, hardworking, and secure in a large family's affection.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 彦 (a fine young man, an old honorific for males) + 八 (eight); read hiko-hachi, standard. Commoner everyday style of the numeral type. No notable modern bearer.

name: Chikatsuna
explanation: Chikatsuna - This name represents the close bond of kinship drawn tight like a rope and is often chosen by those who are heads of large households or who are expected to hold a fractious family together through a succession.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Azuchi-Momoyama-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 親 (parent, kin, intimate) + 綱 (rope, cord; by extension a guiding principle); read chika-tsuna, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer.

name: Yasufuji
explanation: Yasufuji - This name signifies the calm of wisteria hanging still on a windless spring day, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values serenity, refinement, and a peace that is cultivated rather than merely found.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 泰 (peace, calm, great) + 藤 (wisteria); read yasu-fuji, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style; names ending in -fuji often signaled a connection to the Fujiwara line in the Heian and Kamakura eras. No notable modern bearer.

name: Narimori
explanation: Narimori - Stemming from the word "nari", which denotes one's deeds and the work one leaves behind, this name embodies the spirit of accomplishment that grows year upon year. It resonates with those who are industrious, patient, and determined that their labor will amount to something lasting.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 業 (deeds, work, vocation; also karma) + 盛 (to flourish, prosper); 業 read "nari" is a nanori reading (ordinary readings "gyo" and "waza"), standard in formal names but stylized. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer.

name: Shigehide
explanation: The name Shigehide is associated with the famous Weighing of the Grain, in which an Imperial inspector uncovered a generation of falsified rice tallies by insisting that every sack in a provincial storehouse be weighed in front of the assembled headmen. Those who choose this name try to embody values of weighty diligence and excellence in the unglamorous work that keeps an Empire honest.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Kamakura period through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia, plus some of undated period. Kanji 重 (weighty, important) + 秀 (to excel, outstanding); read shige-hide, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Ogiwara Shigehide, the Edo finance commissioner who debased the coinage, is the best-known historical bearer.

name: Genpachi
explanation: Genpachi - A name that means "eighth of the source", evoking the youngest son of an old line who carries the family's wellspring forward when his elders have scattered.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: Sengoku-period bearers in Bryant's name articles and late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 源 (source, origin; also the Minamoto clan name) + 八 (eight); read gen-pachi, standard. Commoner everyday style of the numeral type. The name has a stock-character feel in kabuki and period fiction but no single famous bearer.

name: Ujinao
explanation: Ujinao - A name that means "the clan set straight", evoking the heir who inherits a house in disorder and makes it upright again.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 氏 (clan, lineage) + 直 (upright, honest, straight); read uji-nao, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style; the 氏 element was the hereditary name character of the later Hojo lords. Hojo Ujinao, last lord of Odawara, is the best-known bearer.

name: Sadamitsu
explanation: Sadamitsu - Composed of the elements "constancy" and "light", this name symbolizes a fidelity that shines without flickering. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of unwavering loyalty and a virtue visible to everyone who meets its bearer.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Heian period through Sengoku on Japanese Wikipedia, plus some of undated period. Kanji 貞 (constancy, chastity, fidelity) + 光 (light); read sada-mitsu, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Usui Sadamitsu, one of the legendary four retainers of Minamoto no Yorimitsu, is the best-known bearer.

name: Masashige
explanation: Masashige - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the honest steward, in which a castle steward refuses to shave a single measure from the rice owed to his lord's ashigaru even when his own family goes hungry, and is rewarded when the soldiers hold the wall for him in the siege that follows. It reflects qualities such as correctness, gravity, and the weight that a truly upright man carries in the eyes of others.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Kamakura period through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 正 (correct, upright) + 重 (weighty, important); read masa-shige, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. The famous loyalist Kusunoki Masashige spells his name 正成, with a different second character.

name: Kichinojo
explanation: The name Kichinojo is inspired by the Lucky Ferry Crossing on a broad lowland river, known for its ferrymen who have never lost a passenger in living memory. The name reflects the dependable good fortune of the place and is often chosen by those who value being the steady helper others can count on when the water runs high.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: a late-Edo everyday (tsusho) name borne by figures on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 吉 (good luck, auspicious) + 之 (of, possessive) + 丞 (assistant, an old bureaucratic rank); read kichi-no-jo, standard. Commoner/everyday style of the -nojo type, also used as the common name of low-ranking samurai and popular among kabuki actors. No notable modern bearer.

name: Motomitsu
explanation: Motomitsu - Rooted in the ancient proverb "Light returns to its source", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value remembering the origin of whatever brightness they enjoy.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Heian period through Sengoku on Japanese Wikipedia. Conventional kanji 元光: 元 (origin, root) + 光 (light), read moto-mitsu, both standard nanori readings; the alternate 基光 (foundation + light) is also a real spelling. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Kansuke
explanation: Kansuke - Derived from the phrase "the helper who sees through things", this name embodies the idea of a shrewd assistant whose intuition catches what his master misses. It is often associated with those who serve as advisors, clerks, or scouts and whose judgment is worth more than their rank suggests.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in early- and late-Edo merchant registers, the Kiyose village registers, and Sengoku name articles, with bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 勘 (intuition, perception, to investigate) + 助 (help, assistant); read kan-suke, standard. Commoner everyday style of the -suke type, also used as a common name by samurai. The Sengoku strategist Yamamoto Kansuke, hero of a famous Taiga drama, is the best-known bearer.

name: Shigemitsu
explanation: Shigemitsu - This name represents fullness carried with gravity and is often chosen by those who are heirs to a house of long standing or who are expected to bring a family's fortunes to completion.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Heian period through Sengoku on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 重 (weighty, important) + 満 (full, complete); 満 read "mitsu" is a nanori reading (ordinary reading "man" or "michi"), standard in formal names but stylized. Samurai formal-name style. Modern bearers usually spell it 重光, as with the diplomat Shigemitsu Mamoru's surname.

name: Jirotaro
explanation: Jirotaro - A name that means "second son, eldest son", evoking the boy raised as heir after the first-born was lost.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in the Kamakura-period village name lists. Kanji 二郎 (second son) + 大郎 (eldest son, in the old spelling with 大 rather than the later 太); read ji-ro-ta-ro, standard; the alternate 次郎太郎 uses the same readings with the later conventional characters. Commoner everyday style, a doubled numeral name of a kind seen in medieval registers. No notable modern bearer.

name: Mitsukuni
explanation: The name Mitsukuni is associated with the famous Lighting of the Provinces, in which a newly enthroned Emperor ordered signal beacons lit on every mountain of the Empire in a single night so that each province could see its neighbors' fires and know it was not alone. Those who choose this name try to embody values of unity, illumination, and the duty of the strong to be a light to the whole realm.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Heian through Muromachi periods on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 光 (light) + 国 (country, province); read mitsu-kuni, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Tokugawa Mitsukuni, the Edo lord of Mito famous as the wandering hero Mito Komon, spelled his name 光圀 with a rare variant of the second character.

name: Jujiro
explanation: Jujiro - This name signifies the second son who is nonetheless the family's weight-bearing beam, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values responsibility taken up willingly rather than by right of birth.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and the Kiyose village registers, with Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 重 (weighty, important) + 次郎 (second son); read ju-ji-ro, with 重 in its on-reading "ju", standard. Commoner everyday style of the numeral type. No notable modern bearer.

name: Masazumi
explanation: Masazumi - This name means "flourishing purity". It represents the hope that a man may prosper without the slightest stain on his conduct.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Muromachi period through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia, plus some of undated period. Kanji 昌 (flourishing, bright) + 純 (pure, unmixed); 昌 read "masa" is a nanori reading (ordinary reading "sho"), standard in formal names. Samurai formal-name style. Honda Masazumi, a senior counselor to the early Tokugawa shoguns, is the best-known bearer.

name: Hirohide
explanation: Hirohide - This name means "broad excellence". It represents the well-rounded samurai who excels in the court, the dojo, and the field alike rather than in one narrow art.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku- and early-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 広 (broad, wide) + 秀 (to excel, outstanding); read hiro-hide, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer.

name: Kiyotaka
explanation: Kiyotaka - This name represents purity raised to a lofty height and is often chosen by those who are born to high station or who are expected to hold themselves to a standard above the ordinary run of their peers.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Kamakura through Azuchi-Momoyama periods on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 清 (pure, clear) + 高 (high, lofty); read kiyo-taka, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Kiyotaka remains a common modern given name.

name: Naohira
explanation: Naohira - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the level road, in which a young magistrate is ordered to build a highway through a mountain and, refusing every bribe to bend it around the estates of the wealthy, drives it straight and flat so that the poorest carter can use it. It reflects qualities such as honesty, evenhandedness, and a refusal to let a straight path be crooked for anyone's convenience.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 直 (upright, straight, honest) + 平 (level, peaceful); read nao-hira, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer.

name: Hachizaemon
explanation: Hachizaemon - A name derived from the fusion of "eight" and "gate guard", reflecting a balance between a lowly place in the order of things and the faithfulness of standing one's post. It is often embraced by those who strive for steady service in a station no one else wanted.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and the Kiyose village registers. Kanji 八 (eight) + 左衛門 (Left Gate Guard, an old guard title turned stock name ending); read hachi-za-e-mon, standard. Commoner everyday style of the -zaemon type. No notable modern bearer.

name: Haruaki
explanation: The name Haruaki is associated with the famous Clearing of the Ledgers, in which a provincial governor opened every tax record of their domain to public reading so that no headman could claim to have been cheated and no collector could hide a theft. Those who choose this name try to embody values of transparent governance and a rule that is bright enough for all to see.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from the Heian period through Sengoku on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 治 (to govern, to heal) + 明 (bright, clear); 治 read "haru" is a nanori reading (ordinary readings "ji" and "osamu"), standard in formal names but stylized. Samurai formal-name style. Modern bearers usually spell the name 春明 (spring + bright).

name: Shokichi
explanation: Shokichi - This name pays tribute to the Manor Rent Festival, an event that emphasizes the day each year when a village's tenants bring their rice to the estate storehouse with music and drink and are feasted in return. People choose this name to reflect their values for the good luck of a fair landlord and a harvest that leaves something over for celebration.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 庄 (manor, estate, village) + 吉 (good luck, auspicious); read sho-kichi, standard. Commoner everyday style of the -kichi type, common among Edo farmers and shop apprentices. No notable modern bearer.

name: Daizosuke
explanation: Daizosuke means "assistant of the great storehouse" or "clerk of the treasury", which can suggest a family of granary keepers or a line that once served in the ministry that counts the Emperor's rice. People with this name may be careful with accounts and trusted with what belongs to others.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: a late-Edo everyday (tsusho) name borne by figures on Japanese Wikipedia. Conventional kanji 大蔵助: 大蔵 (great storehouse; also the Treasury ministry of the old court) + 助 (assistant, a low court rank), read dai-zo-suke, standard and echoing an actual ancient office title; the alternate 大造助 (great construction + assistant) is a plausible variant. Commoner/everyday style, also used as a common name by minor samurai. No notable modern bearer.

name: Hikojiro
explanation: Hikojiro means "fine second son" or "the handsome younger boy", which can suggest a family's open pride in a child who will not inherit or a mother's affection for the son who stays closest to her. People with this name may be easygoing charmers who never had to compete for the family's name and so never learned to be hard.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and late-Edo merchant registers, plus some of undated period. Kanji 彦 (a fine young man, an old honorific for males) + 次郎 (second son); read hiko-ji-ro, standard. Commoner everyday style of the numeral type. No notable modern bearer.

name: Moritsugu
explanation: Moritsugu - With origins in the legend of a second son who took over a bankrupt estate from his elder brother and made it the richest in the province within ten years, this name evokes a sense of prosperity that is inherited and then earned twice over. It appeals to those who admire the heir who improves on what he was given rather than merely keeping it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian- and Azuchi-Momoyama-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 盛 (to flourish, prosper) + 次 (next, to succeed, second); read mori-tsugu, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern bearer.

name: Hiromasa
explanation: Hiromasa - With origins in the legend of a wandering magistrate who traveled the breadth of the Empire settling disputes so justly that both parties thanked them, this name evokes a sense of wide-ranging fairness and a judgment that fits each case exactly. It appeals to those who admire the arbiter whose rulings are broad in reach yet precise in their justice.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: late-Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, plus some of undated period. Kanji 広 (broad, wide) + 當 (fitting, proper, to hit the mark; the old form of 当), with 當 read "masa" as a nanori reading (ordinary reading "to"), so this spelling is stylized and rare - the common spelling is 広正 or 博雅. Samurai formal-name style. Minamoto no Hiromasa (博雅), the Heian court musician of ghost-story fame, is the best-known bearer, with different kanji.

name: Takayasu
explanation: Takayasu - Derived from the phrase "prosper and protect", this name embodies the idea that wealth is worth having only so that one may guard what depends on it. It is often associated with those who rise high in a lord's service and use their station to shelter their retainers and kin.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian- and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, plus some of undated period. Kanji 隆 (to prosper, to rise, eminent) + 保 (to protect, to keep); read taka-yasu, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Takayasu is also a modern sumo ring name and a common surname in Okinawa.

name: Nobumitsu
explanation: Nobumitsu - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of lacquerware, this name represents the deep, trustworthy luster that only many patient coats can produce. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the slow accumulation of a finish that cannot be faked and have a deep respect for the artisans who give years to a single perfect surface.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura- and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 信 (trust, faith) + 光 (light); read nobu-mitsu, both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Nobumitsu remains a modern given name, usually with the same kanji.

name: Gozaemon
explanation: Gozaemon - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the Five Gates, an event that emphasizes the vigilance of the guards who stand watch through the five nights before the new year. People choose this name to reflect their values for steadfast watchfulness and the humble duty of the one who keeps the gate.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and among early and late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 五左衛門: 五 (go, five) plus 左衛門 (saemon, the old Left Palace Gate Guard office, long fossilized into a name suffix). A commoner everyday-name style; the -zaemon ending was worn by townsmen and villagers with no connection to the office. No notable modern association.

name: Daihachiro
explanation: The name Daihachiro is associated with the famous Muster of the Eight Sons, in which a widowed farmer of the river provinces sent all eight of her sons to serve the daimyo's levy and the youngest, called Great Eighth, carried the banner home when the rest had fallen. Those who choose this name try to embody values of family duty, endurance, and carrying on what others began.
notes: Attested pre-modern tsusho (everyday name), with Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 大八郎: 大 (dai, great, big), 八 (hachi, eight) and 郎 (ro, son, young man), a birth-order name meaning great eighth son. Commoner and everyday style; samurai also used such names as tsusho alongside a formal nanori. No notable modern association.

name: Kagenobu
explanation: Kagenobu - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A bright prospect is seen only by a trusting eye", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value faith in their lord and the clear sight that comes of an untroubled heart.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Heian and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 景信: 景 (kage, view, prospect, bright scenery) and 信 (nobu, trust, faith, sincerity). Both are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Yukitsuna
explanation: The name Yukitsuna is associated with the famous Crossing of the Rope Bridge, in which a lone samurai walked a single cord across a gorge to carry a treaty to a besieged castle before its garrison starved. Those who choose this name try to embody values of resolve in action and holding fast to the principles that bind a samurai to their duty.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Heian, Kamakura and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 行綱: 行 (yuki, to go, conduct) and 綱 (tsuna, rope, cord; by extension a cardinal principle or guiding rule). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Jirosaburo
explanation: Jirosaburo - Derived from the phrase "the second son's third son", this name embodies the idea of a lineage remembered in the name itself. It is often associated with those who know exactly where they stand in a large family and take quiet pride in that place.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in the Nihonjin name register and among Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 二郎三郎: 二郎 (Jiro, second son) stacked on 三郎 (Saburo, third son), a compound birth-order name of the kind that marked a father's own name in the son's. Commoner everyday-name style; samurai also bore such names as childhood or everyday names. No notable modern association.

name: Aritsune
explanation: The name Aritsune is inspired by the Temple of the Standing Sutras, known for its library where every scroll of the Tao has been copied and kept unbroken since the temple's founding. The name reflects the enduring possession of teaching of the place and is often chosen by those who value learning that is kept rather than merely acquired.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 有経: 有 (ari, to have, to exist) and 経 (tsune, sutra, scripture; also to pass through, to endure). The reading tsune for 経 is a nanori reading and should be flagged as slightly stylized; the meaning is read as possessing or keeping the sutras. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Harutane
explanation: Harutane - Composed of the elements "clear sky" and "lineage", this name symbolizes a bloodline under fair weather, an heir born with nothing clouding his prospects. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of good fortune and a house that expects to continue.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 晴胤: 晴 (haru, clear weather, fair sky) and 胤 (tane, seed, offspring, heir of a lineage). Standard nanori readings; 胤 as tane is a classic name element marking descent. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Terumasa
explanation: The name Terumasa is inspired by the Shining Provincial Court of the southern coast, known for its magistrates whose rulings were said to be as clear as the light off the bay. The name reflects the illuminated governance of the place and is often chosen by those who value fair administration and visible justice.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 輝政: 輝 (teru, to shine, radiance) and 政 (masa, government, administration). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Ikeda Terumasa, the Azuchi-Momoyama and early Edo lord who built Himeji Castle's present keep.

name: Munetsugu
explanation: The name Munetsugu is associated with the famous Reunification of the Split House, in which two branches of a family that had fought one another for three generations were rejoined under a single heir by decree of the Emperor. Those who choose this name try to embody values of continuity, reconciliation, and the unbroken line.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Azuchi-Momoyama and early Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 統続: 統 (mune, to unify, to govern a line) and 続 (tsugu, to continue, to succeed). The reading mune for 統 is a nanori reading rather than an everyday one and should be treated as slightly stylized. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Manjiro
explanation: Manjiro - Composed of the elements "ten thousand" and "second son", this name symbolizes a younger son given a limitless number as his portion, since he will inherit no land. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of abundance and of making one's own fortune.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers, the Kiyose village register, and among late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 万次郎: 万 (man, ten thousand, myriad), 次 (ji, next, second) and 郎 (ro, son). Commoner everyday-name style. Famous bearer: Nakahama Manjiro, the late Edo castaway fisherman who was rescued by an American whaler and later served as an interpreter.

name: Gensuke
explanation: Gensuke - A name derived from the fusion of "source" and "help", reflecting a balance between where one comes from and what one gives to others. It is often embraced by those who strive for usefulness without forgetting their origins.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and among Sengoku and late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 源助: 源 (gen, source, origin, spring) and 助 (suke, help, assistant). Commoner everyday-name style; -suke names were among the most common for townsmen and villagers. No notable modern association.

name: Shokuro
explanation: Shokuro - Derived from the phrase "the ninth son works the manor's fields", this name embodies the idea of earning one's rice from the soil when nothing is left to inherit. It is often associated with those who rise by labor rather than by birth.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and among early and late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 庄九郎: 庄 (sho, manor, estate, farming village) plus 九郎 (kuro, ninth son), a birth-order name. Commoner everyday-name style. Historical association: Saito Dosan, the Sengoku warlord of Mino, used Shokuro as an everyday name during his rise from oil merchant to daimyo. The phrase in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Jinsuke
explanation: Jinsuke - Composed of the elements "exceedingly" and "help", this name symbolizes a man who is very much a help to his household. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of reliability and of a hand that is always there when needed.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers, the Kiyose village register, and among Azuchi-Momoyama and late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 甚助: 甚 (jin, very, exceedingly) and 助 (suke, help, assistant). Commoner everyday-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Nobuyasu
explanation: Nobuyasu - This name represents faith and peace and is often chosen by those who are trusted to keep a household calm or who are expected to hold a lord's confidence through troubled years.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and in Sengoku name articles; one source lists it among names borne by a Buddhist monk, but its form is that of a samurai nanori. Kanji 信康: 信 (nobu, trust, faith) and 康 (yasu, peace, health, ease). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Matsudaira Nobuyasu, eldest son of Tokugawa Ieyasu, ordered to commit seppuku in 1579.

name: Takamoto
explanation: The name Takamoto is inspired by the High Foundation Shrine of the northern mountains, known for its stone platform raised above the snowline on which nothing has ever been permitted to fall. The name reflects the lofty and unshakable base of the place and is often chosen by those who value ambition built on firm ground.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Sengoku and early Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 高基: 高 (taka, high, lofty) and 基 (moto, foundation, base). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Mochimoto
explanation: The name Mochimoto is associated with the famous Laying of the Foundation Stone, in which a young lord rebuilt his family's castle upon the original footings after a fire rather than on a more convenient hill. Those who choose this name try to embody values of building on what one has been given and honoring the base laid by one's ancestors.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 以基: 以 (mochi, by means of, using) and 基 (moto, foundation). The reading mochi for 以 is a nanori reading, common in medieval warrior names but unusual today, and should be flagged as stylized. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Motonori
explanation: Motonori - Stemming from the word "nori", which denotes a teaching or doctrine, this name embodies the spirit of instruction traced back to its source. It resonates with those who are studious, respectful of their teachers, and mindful of where a lesson came from.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 元教: 元 (moto, origin, source, beginning) and 教 (nori, teaching, doctrine). Standard nanori readings; 教 as nori is a classic name element. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Chikamasa
explanation: Chikamasa means "close and upright" or "a parent's righteousness", which can suggest a man whose justice begins at home or the correctness a father passes to his children. People with this name may be strict but fair, and loyal first to their own kin.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 親正: 親 (chika, parent; also intimate, close) and 正 (masa, correct, righteous, just). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Historical bearer: Ikoma Chikamasa, Sengoku lord of Sanuki.

name: Kunitoki
explanation: Kunitoki - This name pays tribute to the Provincial Reckoning, an event that emphasizes the day each province presents its harvest accounts to the Emperor's ministers and the season turns from labor to tribute. People choose this name to reflect their values for service to the realm and knowing the proper time for every duty.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura and late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 国時: 国 (kuni, country, province, realm) and 時 (toki, time, season, hour). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Tomomura
explanation: Tomomura - With origins in the legend of the Morning Headman, who walked every lane of his village before sunrise so that no household's trouble went unseen by the time the sun was up, this name evokes a sense of diligence and quiet care. It appeals to those who admire leaders who serve before they are asked.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 朝村: 朝 (tomo, morning; also the imperial court) and 村 (mura, village). The reading tomo for 朝 is a nanori reading (the everyday readings are asa and cho) and should be flagged as stylized. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Naotsugu
explanation: The name Naotsugu is associated with the famous Honest Succession, in which a dying daimyo passed over his own eldest son and named a plain-spoken nephew heir because the nephew alone had told him the truth about a lost battle. Those who choose this name try to embody values of candor and the worthiness to inherit.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 直継: 直 (nao, straight, honest, direct) and 継 (tsugu, to succeed, to inherit, to carry on). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Seigoro
explanation: Seigoro - This name means "pure fifth son". It represents a clean-living temperament in a boy far down the order of brothers, who has nothing to inherit but his own good name.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and among Sengoku and late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Conventional kanji 清五郎: 清 (sei, pure, clear) plus 五郎 (goro, fifth son); the alternate 政五郎 uses 政 (sei, government). Commoner everyday-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Narikatsu
explanation: Narikatsu - Derived from the phrase "take up the task and win", this name embodies the idea of victory that comes from accepting a duty rather than seeking glory. It is often associated with those who finish what they are assigned.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 就勝: 就 (nari, to take up a post, to accomplish) and 勝 (katsu, to win, victory). The reading nari for 就 is a nanori reading and should be flagged as stylized. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Tamenari
explanation: Tamenari - Stemming from the word "tame", which denotes acting for the sake of another, this name embodies the spirit of achievement in service. It resonates with those who are selfless and measure their success by what they have accomplished for their lord or family.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: a Heian-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia; the source lists it under Buddhist names, though its form is that of a samurai or courtier nanori. Kanji 為成: 為 (tame, for the sake of, to do) and 成 (nari, to become, to achieve). Standard nanori readings. Formal-name style, usable for samurai or a monk who kept his lay name. No notable modern association.

name: Daisuke
explanation: Daisuke can be written with two different kanji. One means "great help", and the other means "great assistant". The choice of kanji could reflect what a family expected of the boy, such as a generous hand offered to neighbors or a lifetime of service in a master's shop.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers and among late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 大助: 大 (dai, great, big) and 助 (suke, help, assistant). Commoner everyday-name style in this spelling. Modern association: one of the most common Japanese male given names of the late twentieth century, usually written 大輔 or 大介 today.

name: Nobushige
explanation: Nobushige means "weighty trust" or "layered faith", which can suggest a man whose word carries weight or a loyalty built up over many years. People with this name may be grave, dependable, and slow to give their confidence.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Muromachi, Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 信重: 信 (nobu, trust, faith) and 重 (shige, heavy, weighty; also layered, repeated). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Sanada Nobushige, better known as Yukimura, who died at the siege of Osaka in 1615.

name: Jirokuro
explanation: Jirokuro - With origins in the legend of the Ninth Son of the Second Son, who was so far down the line of inheritance that he left home with nothing and returned as the magistrate of the province, this name evokes a sense of humble beginnings and earned rank. It appeals to those who admire men who make their own place.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in the Nihonjin name register and among Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 次郎九郎: 次郎 (Jiro, second son) stacked on 九郎 (Kuro, ninth son), a compound birth-order name marking the father's name in the son's. Commoner everyday-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Chojuro
explanation: Chojuro - This name means "eldest and weighty son". It represents a first-born whose responsibilities were felt from the day he was named.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers, the Kiyose village register, and among early and late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 長重郎: 長 (cho, long, chief, eldest), 重 (ju, heavy, weighty) and 郎 (ro, son); the more common spelling of the name is 長十郎 (tenth son), so the 重 form is worth flagging. Commoner everyday-name style. Modern association: Chojuro (長十郎) is a well-known variety of Japanese pear.

name: Hikozaemon
explanation: Hikozaemon - A name that means "fine young man of the Left Gate", evoking a handsome youth standing his first watch at the palace gate.
notes: Attested pre-modern tsusho (everyday name), with Azuchi-Momoyama and early Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and in Sengoku name articles. Kanji 彦左衛門: 彦 (hiko, a fine young man, an old honorific for men) plus 左衛門 (zaemon, the Left Palace Gate Guard office fossilized into a name suffix). Everyday-name style used by samurai and commoners alike. Famous bearer: Okubo Hikozaemon, the blunt Tokugawa retainer of folk tale and kabuki.

name: Mitsuyasu
explanation: Mitsuyasu - This name signifies peaceful light, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values a calm clarity of mind and a household untroubled by shadows.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Heian, Muromachi, Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 光安: 光 (mitsu, light, radiance) and 安 (yasu, peace, calm, ease). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Takeyoshi
explanation: Takeyoshi - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the sword, this name represents martial skill paired with good fortune. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the discipline of the dojo and have a deep respect for the swordmasters whose luck was earned by practice.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 武吉: 武 (take, martial, warrior) and 吉 (yoshi, good luck, auspicious). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Famous bearer: Murakami Takeyoshi, the Sengoku lord of the Inland Sea pirate fleets.

name: Nagayasu
explanation: Nagayasu - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Long Peace, in which a magistrate refused every provocation to war for forty years and was mocked as a coward until the neighboring provinces, exhausted by their feuds, came begging for his terms. It reflects qualities such as patience, restraint, and peace that lasts.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura, Sengoku and early Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 長泰: 長 (naga, long, lasting) and 泰 (yasu, peace, calm, tranquility). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Morifusa
explanation: The name Morifusa is inspired by the Flourishing Terraces of the western hills, known for their rice paddies that step up the slopes and yield the finest grain in the province. The name reflects the abundant excellence of the place and is often chosen by those who value hard-won prosperity.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Heian-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 盛英: 盛 (mori, to flourish, to prosper) and 英 (fusa, excellent, outstanding, hero). The reading fusa for 英 is a nanori reading (the everyday reading is ei) and should be flagged as stylized. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Nobukuni
explanation: Nobukuni - This name represents faith in one's homeland and is often chosen by those who are sworn to hold a province for their lord or who are expected to keep the trust between a domain and the house that rules it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Heian and late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 信邦: 信 (nobu, trust, faith) and 邦 (kuni, homeland, country). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Nobukuni is also the name of a lineage of Kyoto swordsmiths, though usually written 信国.

name: Hironaga
explanation: Hironaga - This name means "wide and eternal". It represents generosity that stretches across a province and endures beyond the giver's lifetime.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 広永: 広 (hiro, wide, broad) and 永 (naga, eternal, long-lasting). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Yasumura
explanation: Yasumura - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Peaceful Village, in which a hamlet on the border between two warring lords was spared by both armies because its headman had fed every traveler who passed through for thirty years. It reflects qualities such as hospitality, calm, and the safety that kindness buys.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 泰村: 泰 (yasu, peace, calm) and 村 (mura, village). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Historical bearer: Miura Yasumura, the Kamakura-period lord destroyed in the Hoji Rebellion of 1247.

name: Koremoto
explanation: The name Koremoto is associated with the famous Founding of the First Library, in which a scholar-lord had every scroll in his province copied onto stone tablets so that no fire could take them, declaring that thought was the only foundation worth building on. Those who choose this name try to embody values of learning preserved and ideas that outlast their thinkers.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Heian-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 惟基: 惟 (kore, to think, to consider; also only) and 基 (moto, foundation). The reading kore for 惟 is a classic Heian nanori reading and should be flagged as stylized. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Tahei
explanation: Tahei - This name represents a great guardsman and is often chosen by those who are big and reliable or who are expected to stand at the door of a household and keep it safe.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late Edo merchant registers. Kanji 太兵衛: 太 (ta, great, thick, stout) plus 兵衛 (hei, the old Palace Guard office fossilized into a name suffix; the usual full reading is Tahyoe, contracted to Tahei). Commoner everyday-name style; -bei and -hei names were staples of Edo townsmen. No notable modern association.

name: Kihachiro
explanation: Kihachiro - This name represents a joyful eighth son and is often chosen by those who are cheerful in a crowded house or who are expected to bring gladness late in their parents' lives.
notes: Attested pre-modern tsusho (everyday name), with Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 喜八郎: 喜 (ki, joy, delight) plus 八郎 (hachiro, eighth son), a birth-order name. Commoner and everyday style, also used by samurai as a tsusho beside a formal nanori. Modern association: Okura Kihachiro, the Meiji industrialist who founded the Okura zaibatsu.

name: Koremori
explanation: Koremori chose their name in honor of the famous Doji Koremori, who held a mountain pass for nine days with forty men while the Emperor's court withdrew to safety behind him.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Heian and Kamakura bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 惟守: 惟 (kore, to think, to consider; also only) and 守 (mori, to protect, guardian). The reading kore for 惟 is a classic Heian nanori reading and should be flagged as stylized. Samurai formal-name style. Historical note: the more famous Taira no Koremori of the Heike wars wrote his name 維盛 with different kanji.

name: Yasushige
explanation: Yasushige - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Heavy Peace, in which a lord who had won every war of his youth found the burden of keeping the peace afterward heavier than any campaign, and bore it anyway. It reflects qualities such as endurance, gravity, and the weight of responsibility carried without complaint.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Kamakura and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 泰重: 泰 (yasu, peace, calm) and 重 (shige, heavy, weighty). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Tadataka
explanation: The name Tadataka is associated with the famous Loyal Ascent, in which a retainer carried his wounded lord up a mountain through a night of snow and, having delivered him to the shrine at the summit, was rewarded with lands that made his house prosperous for ten generations. Those who choose this name try to embody values of loyalty and the prosperity that flows from it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with bearers from the Heian period through the early Edo period on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 忠隆: 忠 (tada, loyalty, devotion) and 隆 (taka, prosperity, rising high). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: the surveyor Ino Tadataka who mapped Japan wrote his name 忠敬 with a different second kanji.

name: Magoemon
explanation: Magoemon - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The grandson keeps the gate the grandfather opened", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value continuity and the duty owed to those who came before.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo merchant registers, the Kiyose village register, and among early and late Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 孫右衛門: 孫 (mago, grandchild) plus 右衛門 (emon, the Right Palace Gate Guard office fossilized into a name suffix). Commoner everyday-name style. No notable modern association. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Munesue
explanation: Munesue - Composed of the elements "main house" and "youngest", this name symbolizes the last-born son who still belongs to the lineage. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of loyalty to the family's head and contentment with a modest share.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, with Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 宗季: 宗 (mune, lineage, main house; also sect) and 季 (sue, season; also youngest, last-born). Standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Chozaemon
explanation: Chozaemon - This name means "elder of the left gate guard". It represents the steady senior man of a household, the one trusted to keep the door and the accounts, and it is borne with quiet pride by heads of merchant houses and village elders alike.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 長左衛門 - 長 "long, elder, chief" + 左衛門 "left palace gate guard", the fossilized Heian office title that became a stock ending for commoner names; the reading Chozaemon is the standard one. A commoner everyday name of the -zaemon type, typical of shopkeepers and prosperous farmers, never a samurai formal name. No notable modern association.

name: Heibei
explanation: Heibei - This name signifies calm, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values an even temper that keeps the peace of the shop and the household.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers, with bearers of unknown period on Japanese Wikipedia. Conventional kanji 平兵衛 - 平 "level, calm, peace" + 兵衛 "palace guard", a stock commoner ending; the alternative 丙兵衛 uses 丙 (hei, the third calendar stem) and is a plausible but far rarer spelling. A commoner everyday name of the -bei type, the sort found on shop signs and village rosters. No notable modern association.

name: Jirobei
explanation: Jirobei - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the Mended Dike, an event that emphasizes the second son's duty to take up the work when the eldest is called away. People choose this name to reflect their values for steady labor, healing what is broken and guarding the village's ordinary days.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in early- and late-Edo merchant registers and on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji as recorded 治郎兵衛 - 治 "govern, heal, set in order" + 郎 "son, young man" + 兵衛 "palace guard"; the far more common spelling is 次郎兵衛 with 次 "second", and 治郎 is a variant that keeps the sound while adding the sense of good order. A commoner everyday name of the -bei type. No notable modern association.

name: Bunjiro
explanation: Bunjiro - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the First Brushstroke, an event that emphasizes the moment a child first writes a character under a teacher's eye. People choose this name to reflect their values for learning, letters and the hope that a second son might rise by his brush rather than his inheritance.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 文次郎 - 文 "writing, letters, learning" + 次郎 "second son"; the reading is the standard one. A commoner everyday name of the numbered-son type, common among clerks and shop apprentices. No notable modern association.

name: Morofuyu
explanation: Morofuyu - This name is inspired by the natural element of winter, symbolizing the season that teaches endurance to everything living. It is often chosen for its connection to the hard months on a mountain domain and its representation of a master whose authority comes from having borne the worst himself.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 師冬 - 師 "master, teacher, army" (moro is a nanori reading) + 冬 "winter"; the reading is unusual to a modern eye but regular for warrior formal names of the period. A samurai formal-name style, of the two-element nanori type. No notable modern association.

name: Takatomo
explanation: Takatomo - This name means "lofty morning". It represents the early hour when a samurai is already at practice while the household sleeps, and the high standard a family sets for the son who bears it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura-, Muromachi- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 高朝 - 高 "high, lofty" + 朝 "morning, court" (tomo is a nanori reading of 朝). A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Mitsumori
explanation: Mitsumori - A name derived from the fusion of "light" and "flourishing", reflecting a balance between a bright reputation and the prosperity that sustains it. It is often embraced by those who strive for a house that shines as well as it thrives.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Conventional kanji 光盛 - 光 "light" + 盛 "flourish, prosper"; the alternative 満盛 uses 満 "full". A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Moritane
explanation: Moritane - Stemming from the word "tane", which denotes a seed or the line that springs from it, this name embodies the spirit of a house's hope for its posterity. It resonates with those who are conscious of being heirs and eager to see the family spread.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura-, Sengoku- and Azuchi-Momoyama-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Conventional kanji 盛胤 - 盛 "flourish, prosper" + 胤 "lineage, heir, seed"; the alternative 守胤 uses 守 "protect". A samurai formal-name style, 胤 being a hereditary element in several warrior houses. No notable modern association.

name: Shigetane
explanation: Shigetane - This name means "weighty lineage". It represents the burden of an old house carried on a single heir's shoulders, and the expectation that he will add another layer to what his ancestors built.
notes: Attested samurai nanori with bearers from Heian through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia; our source tagged one bearer as a Buddhist name, but the form is a plain two-element warrior nanori. Kanji 重胤 - 重 "heavy, layered, important" + 胤 "lineage, heir"; the reading is regular. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Takayuki
explanation: Takayuki - Stemming from the word "takashi", which denotes what is high and prosperous, this name embodies the spirit of rising with due respect for those above. It resonates with those who are ambitious without arrogance and courteous even at the top of the ladder.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 隆恭 - 隆 "prosper, rise high" + 恭 "respectful, reverent"; yuki is a nanori reading of 恭 and would not be guessed from the character alone, so flag as stylized. A samurai formal-name style. The sound Takayuki is very common in modern Japan, usually with different kanji.

name: Kinbei
explanation: Kinbei - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Golden Gatekeeper, in which a poor guard refused a bribe of gold to open a gate at night and was found the next morning with a single gold coin in his hand, left by the Fortune of Wealth himself. It reflects qualities such as incorruptibility, patience and reward that comes unlooked for.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers, with an Azuchi-Momoyama bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 金兵衛 - 金 "gold, metal, money" + 兵衛 "palace guard"; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name of the -bei type, the auspicious 金 marking it as a merchant's name. No notable modern association.

name: Raitan
explanation: Raitan - This name is inspired by the natural element of dawn, symbolizing the light a monk relies on to begin each day's devotions. It is often chosen for its connection to the first hour of morning and its representation of a faith renewed with every sunrise.
notes: Attested Buddhist name, Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 頼旦 - 頼 "rely, trust" + 旦 "dawn, morning", read in on-yomi as is normal for a monk's name. A monk's name, the sort taken at ordination; a samurai would not carry it as a formal name. No notable modern association.

name: Genzaburo
explanation: Genzaburo chose their name in honor of the famous Yasuki Genzaburo, who as a third son with no inheritance built a rice brokerage from a single borrowed cart and fed a starving coastal province through two failed harvests.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers, with an Azuchi-Momoyama bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 源三郎 - 源 "source, origin" + 三郎 "third son"; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name of the numbered-son type, also used as a samurai's tsusho. No notable modern association.

name: Magoshichi
explanation: Magoshichi - This name means "seventh grandchild". It represents the plainest kind of village reckoning, a boy known by his place in a large and growing family.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 孫七 - 孫 "grandchild" + 七 "seven"; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name, a numeral name of the plainest village-register kind. No notable modern association.

name: Yoshito
explanation: Yoshito - A name that means "righteousness that reaches far", evoking a duty whose reach extends past the household to the whole domain.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian-, Kamakura- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Conventional kanji 義遠 - 義 "righteousness, duty" + 遠 "far, distant", where to is a nanori reading of 遠 and should be flagged as stylized; the alternative 良人 "good person" is the everyday modern spelling. A samurai formal-name style in the 義遠 spelling. The sound Yoshito is common in modern Japan.

name: Hiroyuki
explanation: Hiroyuki - Stemming from the word "hiroi", which denotes what is wide and open, this name embodies the spirit of a generous reach that takes in the whole province rather than one village. It resonates with those who are broad-minded, welcoming and slow to draw a narrow line.
notes: Attested samurai nanori with bearers from Heian through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 広之 - 広 "wide, broad" + 之 "of, this", a possessive particle used as a name filler with the nanori reading yuki; the reading is conventional for the pair. A samurai formal-name style. The sound Hiroyuki is very common in modern Japan.

name: Yorinobu
explanation: Yorinobu - Composed of the elements "reliance" and "faith", this name symbolizes a lord in whom retainers can rest their whole trust. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of dependability, kept promises and the bond between a house and those sworn to it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian- and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and in Sengoku name articles. Kanji 頼信 - 頼 "rely, trust" + 信 "faith, sincerity"; the reading is regular. A samurai formal-name style, 頼 being a hereditary element of the Minamoto line. Historically borne by Minamoto no Yorinobu, the Heian warrior ancestor of the Kawachi Genji.

name: Heisuke
explanation: Heisuke chose their name in honor of the famous Yoritomo Heisuke, who as a magistrate's humble assistant kept the peace of a river town for forty years without once drawing the short sword he was permitted to carry.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Kamakura-period biographies on Japanese Wikipedia and in early- and late-Edo merchant and village registers. Kanji 平介 - 平 "level, peace" + 介 "assistant, mediator", the old title of a provincial vice-governor turned into a stock name ending; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name of the -suke type, also used as a samurai's tsusho. No notable modern association.

name: Naotomo
explanation: Naotomo - This name pays tribute to the Dawn Audience, an event that emphasizes the moment each new year when a lord's retainers present themselves at first light to speak plainly of the year past. People choose this name to reflect their values for honesty before their superiors and the courage to be upright in the morning court.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Muromachi- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 直朝 - 直 "upright, straight, honest" + 朝 "morning, court" (tomo is a nanori reading of 朝). A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Takaie
explanation: Takaie chose their name in honor of the famous Shinjo Takaie, who rebuilt his burned family hall higher on the hill than before so that every rider on the steppe road could see that the house still stood.
notes: Attested samurai nanori with bearers from Heian through Sengoku on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 高家 - 高 "high" + 家 "house, family"; the reading is regular. A samurai formal-name style, and the same characters read koke were also a rank of high-status hereditary families under the shogunate. Historically borne by Fujiwara no Takaie, the Heian noble who repelled the Toi invasion of Kyushu.

name: Takichi
explanation: Takichi - Rooted in the ancient proverb "great luck comes to the door that is swept each morning", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value diligence in small things and believe fortune favors the tidy shop.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 太吉 - 太 "great, stout" + 吉 "good luck"; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name of the auspicious two-character kind that villagers and shop boys bore. No notable modern association.

name: Gorosaburo
explanation: Gorosaburo - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The fifth son's third son still keeps the shop", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value a house name passed down through birth order and trade.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers, with bearers of unknown period on Japanese Wikipedia. Conventional kanji 五郎三郎 - 五郎 "fifth son" + 三郎 "third son", a doubled numbered-son name of the kind that passed down a house as a hereditary shop name; the alternative 五良三郎 uses 良 "good" for the same sound. A commoner everyday name, also used as a samurai's tsusho. No notable modern association. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Asaemon
explanation: Asaemon - Composed of the elements "shallow" and "right gate guard", this name symbolizes the man who stands in the shallows of the river ford and keeps the crossing. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of watchfulness, modesty about one's own depth and reliable service at the threshold.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 浅右衛門 - 浅 "shallow" + 右衛門 "right palace gate guard", a stock commoner ending; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name of the -emon type, also carried by low-ranking samurai as a tsusho. Historically the hereditary name of Yamada Asaemon, the shogunate's sword-testers and executioners, which gives it a grim ring in period fiction.

name: Shichiemon
explanation: Shichiemon - Derived from the phrase "seven at the right gate", this name embodies the idea of the seventh child who still finds a post to hold. It is often associated with those who come late to a crowded household and make themselves useful anyway.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 七右衛門 - 七 "seven" + 右衛門 "right palace gate guard"; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name of the -emon type, a numeral name of the plainest kind. No notable modern association.

name: Shigechika
explanation: Shigechika - A name that means "weighty kinship", evoking the duty a son owes his parents and the seriousness with which a stern house names it.
