notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku- and Azuchi-Momoyama-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Conventional kanji 重親 - 重 "heavy, important" + 親 "parent, kin, intimate"; the alternative 茂親 uses 茂 "luxuriant". A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Moritsuna
explanation: Moritsuna - This name represents a flourishing bond, the rope that holds a house together as it grows, and is often chosen by those who are heirs to a rising family or who are expected to bind new retainers to an old lord.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian- and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 盛綱 - 盛 "flourish, prosper" + 綱 "rope, bond, principle"; the reading is regular. A samurai formal-name style. Historically borne by Sasaki Moritsuna, the Genpei-war warrior remembered for fording a strait on horseback.

name: Tomonaga
explanation: Tomonaga - Composed of the elements "fully furnished" and "eternal", this name symbolizes a household provisioned for all time. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of completeness, preparation and a legacy that lacks nothing.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian-, Kamakura- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 具永 - 具 "furnish, equip, complete" (tomo is a nanori reading) + 永 "eternal, long"; the reading of 具 should be flagged as stylized. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Tarobei
explanation: The name Tarobei is associated with the famous Stand at the Rice Bridge, in which a village headman's eldest son held a narrow bridge with a bamboo spear against bandits until the magistrate's yoriki arrived. Those who choose this name try to embody values of an eldest son's responsibility, plain courage and loyalty to one's neighbors.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose), with an Azuchi-Momoyama bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 太郎兵衛 - 太郎 "eldest son" + 兵衛 "palace guard"; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name of the -bei type, one of the most ordinary village-register names there is. No notable modern association.

name: Umasuke
explanation: Umasuke - Composed of the elements "Right Stables" and "assistant", this name symbolizes the retainer whose place is among the lord's horses. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of a court office held or claimed and of a groom's plain devotion to his animals.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears as a Kamakura-period tsusho on Japanese Wikipedia. Conventional kanji 右馬助 - 右馬 "Right Horse Bureau" + 助 "assistant", an Imperial court office title (properly read Umanosuke) that warriors adopted as an everyday name; the shortened reading Umasuke is a stylized one and should be flagged, and the alternative 馬助 "horse helper" is a plain commoner spelling. An everyday name rather than a formal nanori, usable by samurai and grooms alike. No notable modern association.

name: Chomatsu
explanation: Chomatsu - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of bonsai, this name represents the long pine trained over decades into a single graceful line. It is often chosen by those who appreciate patience made visible and have a deep respect for the gardeners who work for a beauty they may not live to see.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 長松 - 長 "long, elder" + 松 "pine"; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name of the auspicious two-character kind, 松 being one of the most common village-register elements. No notable modern association.

name: Rokurozaemon
explanation: Rokurozaemon - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the six-stringed koto, this name represents the sixth son who stands guard at the left gate while the music plays within. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the humble post kept faithfully and have a deep respect for the players whose peace the guard makes possible.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears as a Kamakura-period tsusho on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 六郎左衛門 - 六郎 "sixth son" + 左衛門 "left palace gate guard"; the reading is standard. An everyday name of the -zaemon type, used by samurai as a tsusho and by commoners as their only name. No notable modern association.

name: Gengoro
explanation: Gengoro - Composed of the elements "source" and "fifth son", this name symbolizes the spring from which a younger branch of the family flows. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of origin, plenty and the fifth child who starts something of his own.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers, with a Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 源五郎 - 源 "source, origin" + 五郎 "fifth son"; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name of the numbered-son type, also used as a samurai's tsusho. In modern Japanese gengoro is the common word for the diving beetle, said to be named for a man of this name.

name: Kaison
explanation: Kaison - This name is inspired by the natural element of the sea, symbolizing a vastness that is revered because it refuses no river. It is often chosen for its connection to the tides and the deep water off the coast and its representation of humility, patience and a nobility that takes in all who come.
notes: Attested Buddhist name, Heian-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 海尊 - 海 "sea" + 尊 "revered, noble", read in on-yomi as is normal for a monk's name. A monk's name, taken at ordination. Historically borne by Hitachibo Kaison, the warrior-monk companion of Minamoto no Yoshitsune said in legend to have lived for centuries.

name: Hikoemon
explanation: Hikoemon - Rooted in the ancient proverb "a gate is only as strong as the young man who stands at it", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value vigilance, steadiness in humble posts and the honest strength of youth placed in service.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and Edo village registers (Kiyose). Kanji 彦右衛門 - 彦 "fine young man, prince" + 右衛門 "right palace gate guard"; the reading is standard. A commoner everyday name of the -emon type. No notable modern association. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Zenshuku
explanation: Zenshuku - A name that means "complete blessing", evoking the monk who has given everything and asks nothing, and whose prayers therefore lack nothing.
notes: Attested Buddhist name, Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 全祝 - 全 "whole, complete" + 祝 "blessing, celebration", read in on-yomi as is normal for a monk's name. A monk's name, taken at ordination. No notable modern association.

name: Rokurosaburo
explanation: The name Rokurosaburo is inspired by the Six Rivers Ford, known for its three stone piers that let travelers cross where six streams meet. The name reflects the patient reliability of the place and is often chosen by those who value the younger son who becomes the family's crossing-point in hard years.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears as a Kamakura-period tsusho on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 六郎三郎 - 六郎 "sixth son" + 三郎 "third son", a doubled numbered-son name that marks a third son of a sixth son; the reading is standard. An everyday name, used by samurai as a tsusho and by commoners as their only name. No notable modern association.

name: Narisada
explanation: Narisada - This name pays tribute to the Investiture of Office, an event that emphasizes the day a samurai first takes up an appointment and swears to hold it with constancy. People choose this name to reflect their values for accomplishment through duty and a steadiness that does not waver once the post is accepted.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 就貞 - 就 "take up a post, accomplish" (nari is a nanori reading) + 貞 "constancy, chastity, uprightness"; the reading of 就 should be flagged as stylized. A samurai formal-name style, 就 being a hereditary element of the Mori house of Aki. No notable modern association.

name: Kinmune
explanation: Kinmune - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of court calligraphy, this name represents the public hand of a lord whose brushwork sets the style of the main line. It is often chosen by those who appreciate formality carried lightly and have a deep respect for the courtiers whose every stroke is watched.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 公宗 - 公 "public, lord, duke" (kin is a nanori reading used by the Saionji and other court houses) + 宗 "main line, sect, ancestor"; the reading of 公 should be flagged as stylized. A court and samurai formal-name style rather than a commoner name. No notable modern association.

name: Shigehira
explanation: Shigehira - This name means "luxuriant peace". It represents the settled prosperity of a domain where the fields are thick and the roads are quiet, and the lord who is content to keep them so.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian- and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji as recorded 茂平 - 茂 "luxuriant, flourishing" + 平 "level, peace"; the reading is regular. A samurai formal-name style, though 茂平 is also found as a commoner name. The famous Taira no Shigehira of the Genpei war wrote his name 重衡, with different characters.

name: Haruyoshi
explanation: Haruyoshi - This name represents a deep and profound rejoicing and is often chosen by those who are born after a long-awaited good fortune or who are expected to carry a joy with depth and mystery behind it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Sengoku- and Azuchi-Momoyama-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji as recorded 玄慶 - 玄 "deep, profound, dark, mysterious" + 慶 "rejoice, congratulate"; haru for 玄 is a rare nanori reading and yoshi for 慶 a common one, so the whole reading should be flagged as stylized and could be mistaken for the on-reading Genkei. A samurai formal-name style. The sound Haruyoshi is common in modern Japan with different kanji.

name: Koretada
explanation: Koretada - Composed of the elements "only, this" and "loyalty", this name symbolizes a devotion that considers nothing but one's lord. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of single-mindedness, constancy and a fidelity that does not look elsewhere.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura- and Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 惟忠 - 惟 "consider, only, this" (kore is its regular nanori reading) + 忠 "loyalty"; the reading is conventional for Heian and Kamakura names of the 惟- type. A samurai formal-name style. Historically borne by Fujiwara no Koretada, a Heian regent, though the sound is rare today.

name: Tokihira
explanation: Tokihira - Composed of the elements "time" and "balance", this name symbolizes the scale on which the seasons are weighed. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of good timing, fair measure and a judgment that gives each moment its due.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian- and Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji as recorded 時衡 - 時 "time, season" + 衡 "balance, scale, weigh" (hira is a nanori reading of 衡); flag the second element as stylized. A samurai formal-name style. The famous Fujiwara no Tokihira, rival of Sugawara no Michizane, wrote his name 時平 with a different second character.

name: Hirokata
explanation: Hirokata - With origins in the legend of the Broad-Road Magistrate, who widened every path in their district until no farmer's cart had to yield to a samurai's palanquin, this name evokes a sense of generosity and even-handed method. It appeals to those who admire an official whose fairness has a direction and whose reach is wide.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura- and early-Edo-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 弘方 - 弘 "broad, spread wide" + 方 "direction, method, person"; kata is the regular reading of 方 and hiro of 弘. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Hideyasu
explanation: Hideyasu - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Excellent Peace, in which a young champion won a tournament before the Emperor and then asked, as his prize, that his home province be spared a year's levy. It reflects qualities such as excellence turned to the good of others and a peace that is earned rather than merely wished for.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Heian-, Kamakura- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 秀安 - 秀 "excel, surpass" + 安 "peace, ease"; the reading is regular. A samurai formal-name style. Historically borne by Yuki Hideyasu, a son of Tokugawa Ieyasu.

name: Nobufusa
explanation: Nobufusa - Derived from the phrase "faith kept within the house", this name embodies the idea of trust that is tended at home before it is shown abroad. It is often associated with those who hold a household together through quiet reliability.
notes: Attested samurai nanori with bearers from Kamakura through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 信房 - 信 "faith, trust" + 房 "chamber, house, tassel" (fusa is its regular name reading). A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Ujitsugu
explanation: Ujitsugu - A name that means "successor of the clan", evoking the heir who takes up the family name as a duty rather than a prize.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Muromachi- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 氏次 - 氏 "clan, family name" + 次 "next, succeed, second"; the reading is regular. A samurai formal-name style, 氏 being a hereditary element of the Hojo of Odawara and the Imagawa. No notable modern association.

name: Akitaka
explanation: Akitaka - This name means "discerning and lofty". It represents the lord who investigates a matter thoroughly before judging it from on high, and it is favored by houses that prize an inquiring mind alongside rank.
notes: Attested samurai nanori, Kamakura- and Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 詮高 - 詮 "discern, investigate, elucidate" (aki is a nanori reading, as in the Ouchi and Shiba houses) + 高 "high, lofty"; the reading of 詮 should be flagged as stylized. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Kiyonobu
explanation: The name Kiyonobu is inspired by the clear headwaters of a mountain shrine-stream in the Dragon lands, known for its cold, unclouded water and the pilgrims who keep their word to return to it each spring. The name reflects the unclouded faithfulness of the place and is often chosen by those who value sincerity and steadfast trust.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 清信, 清 (kiyo, pure, clear) and 信 (nobu, trust, faith); both are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Yoshimitsu
explanation: Yoshimitsu - This name means "righteousness fulfilled". It represents a samurai whose sense of duty is complete, lacking nothing, the way a full moon lacks no part of its light.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from Heian through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia and in Sengoku name articles. Written 義満, 義 (yoshi, righteousness, duty) and 満 (mitsu, full, fulfilled); standard readings. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, the Muromachi shogun who built the Golden Pavilion, is the famous historical bearer.

name: Terusuke
explanation: Terusuke - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Lantern-Bearer of the Pass, in which a lowly retainer carried the only lamp through a night storm so that his lord's column could cross a mountain road, and was afterward given the lamp as his family crest. It reflects qualities such as quiet service, reliability, and the light one samurai can lend to many.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 輝資, 輝 (teru, to shine, radiance) and 資 (suke, resources, to aid); 資 as suke is a common nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Suketada
explanation: Suketada - Derived from the phrase "aid given in loyalty", this name embodies the idea of support offered to one's lord without being asked. It is often associated with those who serve as stewards, seconds, and trusted lieutenants rather than seeking command themselves.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from Kamakura through Sengoku on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 資忠, 資 (suke, resources, aid) and 忠 (tada, loyalty); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Chikaharu
explanation: Chikaharu - Composed of the elements "kin, intimate" and "to govern, to settle", this name symbolizes the ordering of a household by one close to it. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of a steward's care, a kinsman's fairness and quarrels settled within the family.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 親治, 親 (chika, intimate, kin, parent) and 治 (haru, to govern, to settle); 治 as haru is a standard nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Shigeaki
explanation: Shigeaki can be written with two different kanji. One means "achievement made bright", and the other means "layered brightness". The choice of kanji could reflect a family's hopes for a son, such as a career of visible accomplishment or a character of many-sided clarity.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 成明, 成 (shige, to achieve, to become) and 明 (aki, bright); 成 read shige is a nanori reading rather than the everyday nari, so the reading is stylized but historically attested. The alternate spelling in the explanation is 重明 (重 shige, layered, important). Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Shigeharu
explanation: Shigeharu - Stemming from the word "shige", which denotes growth brought to completion, this name embodies the spirit of an administrator who brings order to what has been built. It resonates with those who are patient, methodical, and content to finish what others began.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku, Azuchi-Momoyama, and early Edo bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 成治, 成 (shige, to achieve, to become) and 治 (haru, to govern); both are nanori readings, with 成 as shige being the less common one. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Takenaka Shigeharu is the formal name of the strategist better known as Takenaka Hanbei.

name: Koretoki
explanation: Koretoki - Composed of the elements "to hold fast" and "time", this name symbolizes a samurai who keeps the hour, the season, and the obligation each brings. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of constancy and good timing.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and Kamakura bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 維時, 維 (kore, to hold, to maintain; also a classical particle) and 時 (toki, time); 維 as kore is a standard nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style, with a distinctly Heian flavor. No notable modern association.

name: Shichizaemon
explanation: Shichizaemon - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the Seventh Night, an event that emphasizes the keeping of watch and the reunion of those long separated. People choose this name to reflect their values for vigilance, patience, and the faith that what is waited for will come.
notes: Attested commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and the Kiyose village register. Written 七左衛門, 七 (shichi, seven) and 左衛門 (zaemon, Left Gate Guard), an old palace-guard title that became a fossilized name suffix among commoners; the seven usually marks a seventh son. Commoner everyday style, the classic townsman and headman pattern. No notable modern association.

name: Shigeru
explanation: The name Shigeru is inspired by the terraced hill-villages of the Crane coast, known for their dense mulberry groves and the silk they yield. The name reflects the luxuriant growth of the place and is often chosen by those who value abundance, diligence, and the slow work of cultivation.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian and undated bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and in Sengoku name articles. Written 茂, a single character meaning luxuriant, thickly growing; shigeru is its plain kun reading. Samurai formal-name style, though the single-character form also passed easily among commoners. Modern association: a very common twentieth-century given name (Yoshida Shigeru, prime minister; Miyamoto Shigeru of Nintendo).

name: Tomofusa
explanation: Tomofusa - Stemming from the word "fusa", which denotes a full cluster or a well-furnished chamber, this name embodies the spirit of a household kept complete and in good order. It resonates with those who are provident, hospitable, and attentive to every detail of their house.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from Kamakura through Sengoku on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 具房, 具 (tomo, to furnish, complete) and 房 (fusa, chamber, tassel, cluster); 具 as tomo is a nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Tadaki
explanation: Tadaki - A name that means "loyal and clear", evoking a retainer whose devotion is as open and untroubled as a bright morning.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from Kamakura through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 忠朗, 忠 (tada, loyalty) and 朗 (aki, clear, cheerful); the full reading would normally be Tadaaki, and Tadaki is a contracted reading of the same kanji, so treat it as stylized. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Chikasue
explanation: Chikasue - A name that means "beloved youngest", evoking the cherished last-born son of a house, raised with affection and expected to hold the family together after his elders.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 愛季, 愛 (chika, love, affection) and 季 (sue, youngest, end of a season); 愛 read chika is a nanori reading rather than the everyday ai. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Ando Chikasue, the Sengoku lord of Dewa, is the famous bearer.

name: Yorihisa
explanation: Yorihisa - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of lacquerwork, this name represents the many thin coats that must each be relied upon before the whole endures. It is often chosen by those who appreciate patient layering and have a deep respect for craftsmen who work for a beauty that outlives them.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from Kamakura through Sengoku on Japanese Wikipedia and in Sengoku name articles. Written 頼尚, 頼 (yori, to rely on) and 尚 (hisa, esteemed, enduring); 尚 as hisa is a standard nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Hanbei
explanation: Hanbei means "half soldier" or "half a guardsman", which can suggest a man of humble martial standing or a clerk who is only half a warrior. People with this name may be sharper than they look, and are often the ones who do the thinking while others swing the sword.
notes: Attested commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and the Kiyose village register, with an Azuchi-Momoyama bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 半兵衛, 半 (han, half) and 兵衛 (bei, soldier guard), an old guard title fossilized as a name suffix. Commoner everyday style, though samurai used it as a tsusho too. Modern association: Takenaka Hanbei, the strategist of Hideyoshi, is the famous bearer.

name: Tosuke
explanation: Tosuke - With origins in the legend of Tosuke the Wisteria-Keeper, who tended a dying vine at a roadside shrine until it flowered and shaded a whole village's rest-stop, this name evokes a sense of humble care and unexpected reward. It appeals to those who admire quiet labor that ripens into shelter for others.
notes: Attested commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and the Kiyose and Nihonjin village registers, with Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 藤介, 藤 (to, wisteria) and 介 (suke, assistant), the second character being an old provincial-office title turned name suffix. Commoner everyday style. No notable modern association.

name: Yukinaga
explanation: The name Yukinaga is inspired by the Long Bridge villages of the southern rice plains, known for their prosperous households and the wooden span that has stood for generations. The name reflects the lasting good fortune of the place and is often chosen by those who value stability, longevity, and steady prosperity.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian, Kamakura, and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 幸長, 幸 (yuki, good fortune, happiness) and 長 (naga, long, chief); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Konishi Yukinaga, the Christian daimyo, is the best-known bearer, though his name uses 行長.

name: Yukitaka
explanation: Yukitaka can be written with two different kanji. One means "to go forth and prosper", and the other means "fortunate and prosperous". The choice of kanji could reflect what a family hoped for a son, such as a life of action and advancement or a life blessed by the Fortunes from the start.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and undated bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 行隆, 行 (yuki, to go, conduct) and 隆 (taka, prosperous, high); the alternate spelling in the explanation is 幸隆 (幸 yuki, good fortune). Both are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Sanada Yukitaka (幸隆), grandfather of Sanada Yukimura.

name: Hirosue
explanation: Hirosue - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of garden design, this name represents the wide vista deliberately placed at the very end of a winding path. It is often chosen by those who appreciate a reward that opens out after patience and have a deep respect for gardeners who plan a view they may never see mature.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 弘季, 弘 (hiro, broad, wide) and 季 (sue, youngest, end of a season); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Tomokiyo
explanation: Tomokiyo - This name signifies friendship kept pure, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values loyalty among companions and honesty in all dealings.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 友清, 友 (tomo, friend) and 清 (kiyo, pure); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Hikoshiro
explanation: Hikoshiro can be written with two different kanji. One means "fine fourth son", and the other means "fine young gentleman". The choice of kanji could reflect a family's circumstances, such as a simple count of sons in a large farming household or a hope that the boy would carry himself above his station.
notes: Attested commoner name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers, with Kamakura and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 彦四郎, 彦 (hiko, fine young man) and 四郎 (shiro, fourth son); the alternate spelling in the explanation is 彦士郎 (士 shi, gentleman, warrior). Commoner everyday style, also used by samurai as a childhood or tsusho name. No notable modern association.

name: Hironori
explanation: Hironori - Derived from the phrase "the law reaches wide", this name embodies the idea of justice that extends to every corner of a domain, not just its castle town. It is often associated with those who serve as magistrates and take pride in hearing the cases of remote villages.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: late-Edo and undated bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 広憲, 広 (hiro, wide, broad) and 憲 (nori, law, constitution); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Tamesuke
explanation: Tamesuke - Rooted in the ancient proverb "Act for the sake of others and you will never lack a helper", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value service, reciprocity, and the bonds between a lord and their retainers.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 為佐, 為 (tame, for the sake of, to do) and 佐 (suke, to assist); both standard nanori readings, the second being an old office title. Samurai formal-name style with a Kamakura flavor. No notable modern association.

name: Sadazane
explanation: Sadazane can be written with two different kanji. One means "settled truth", and the other means "constant sincerity". The choice of kanji could reflect the virtue a family most wanted to emphasize, such as firm judgment or unwavering fidelity.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 定実, 定 (sada, to settle, fixed) and 実 (zane, truth, fruit); the alternate spelling in the explanation is 貞実 (貞 sada, constant, chaste). 実 read zane is a standard nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Uesugi Sadazane, the Sengoku lord of Echigo.

name: Ienari
explanation: Ienari - This name represents the making of a house and is often chosen by those who are founding a new branch family or who are expected to restore a lineage's fortunes after a fall.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 家成, 家 (ie, house, family) and 成 (nari, to become, to achieve); both standard readings. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Tokugawa Ienari, the eleventh and longest-reigning shogun, is the famous historical bearer.

name: Naokatsu
explanation: Naokatsu - This name means "honest victory". It represents winning without deceit, a triumph earned in the open that no one can later call into question.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 直勝, 直 (nao, straight, honest) and 勝 (katsu, victory); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Ii Naokatsu, the son of Ii Naomasa, is a known bearer.

name: Sukechika
explanation: Sukechika - Stemming from the word "suke", which denotes aid and assistance, this name embodies the spirit of help offered to one's own kin. It resonates with those who are loyal retainers, dependable brothers and the sort of samurai who takes a relative's burden as their own.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian, Muromachi, and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 亮親, 亮 (suke, to aid, clear) and 親 (chika, intimate, kin); 亮 read suke is a nanori reading derived from its old use as an office title. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Ito Sukechika, the Heian lord who fostered the young Minamoto Yoritomo.

name: Harunobu
explanation: Harunobu - A name that means "clear-skied faith", evoking a trust as untroubled as a bright day with no cloud on any horizon.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia and in Sengoku name articles. Written 晴信, 晴 (haru, clear sky, fine weather) and 信 (nobu, trust, faith); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. Modern association: Takeda Harunobu is the formal name of Takeda Shingen, and Suzuki Harunobu the ukiyo-e artist.

name: Shigekazu
explanation: Shigekazu means "important member" or "weighty count", which can suggest a man who matters to his household or one whose word is counted carefully in council. People with this name may be steady, dependable, and difficult to move once they have decided.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura, Muromachi, and Azuchi-Momoyama bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 重員, 重 (shige, heavy, important) and 員 (kazu, member, number); 員 read kazu is a nanori reading. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Norisue
explanation: Norisue - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The last to follow the model must still match it", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value tradition, precise form, and the duty of a younger son to uphold the standard his elders set.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Muromachi bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 範季, 範 (nori, model, pattern) and 季 (sue, youngest, end of a season); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Sukeuji
explanation: Sukeuji - This name signifies aid given to one's clan, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values kinship above personal ambition and the strength of the family over the glory of the individual.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 資氏, 資 (suke, resources, aid) and 氏 (uji, clan, lineage); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style with a strong Kamakura flavor. No notable modern association.

name: Sadakiyo
explanation: Sadakiyo - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the tea ceremony, this name represents the constant, purified attention that each unchanging gesture demands. It is often chosen by those who appreciate stillness and precision and have a deep respect for tea masters who find freedom inside strict form.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers from Kamakura through early Edo on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 貞清, 貞 (sada, constant, chaste, upright) and 清 (kiyo, pure); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Shigemichi
explanation: Shigemichi can be written with two different kanji. One means "an important road", and the other means "a flourishing way". The choice of kanji could reflect what a family hoped the boy would become, such as a man of consequence on the great highways of the Empire or one who follows the Tao and thrives along it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 重通, 重 (shige, heavy, important) and 通 (michi, to pass through, road); the alternate spelling in the explanation is 茂道 (茂 shige, luxuriant; 道 michi, way). Both are standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Takatsu
explanation: Takatsu - This name represents lofty generosity and is often chosen by those who are born to high station or who are expected to be open-handed with the wealth and rank they inherit.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi and undated bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 高厚, 高 (taka, high, lofty) and 厚 (atsu, thick, generous); the full reading would normally be Takaatsu, and Takatsu is a contracted reading of the same kanji, so treat it as stylized. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Akiharu
explanation: Akiharu - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of calligraphy, this name represents the moment a stroke makes its meaning plain and brings the whole page into order. It is often chosen by those who appreciate clarity of expression and have a deep respect for calligraphers whose discipline shows in every line.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 顕治, 顕 (aki, manifest, to make plain) and 治 (haru, to govern, to put in order); both standard nanori readings. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Shigeie
explanation: Shigeie chose their name in honor of the famous Crab Shigeie, who held a river-crossing fort with a single household of retainers for forty days until relief came, and never once let the gate be opened for parley.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian, Kamakura, and Sengoku bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 鎮家, 鎮 (shige, to pacify, to hold firm) and 家 (ie, house, family); 鎮 read shige is a nanori reading familiar from the Otomo house of Kyushu. Samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Bunbei
explanation: Bunbei means "letters" or "the learned guardsman", which can suggest a clerk who keeps the tallies or a townsman who stands at his post with a brush rather than a spear. People with this name may be shopkeepers, scribes or the sort of merchant who trusts a written record over memory.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 文兵衛, bun (letters, learning) plus the suffix -bei from 兵衛, the old palace-guard office title that became a stock commoner name ending. A commoner everyday-name style, typical of Edo townsmen and merchants.

name: Bunroku
explanation: Bunroku - This name means "letters, six". It represents a sixth son marked out for learning, the one child in a large household expected to read and keep the accounts.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 文六, bun (letters, learning) plus roku (six), the number suffix common in birth-order names. A commoner everyday-name style. Bunroku is also the name of a Japanese era (1592-1596), which is a historical association rather than a personal one.

name: Bunshiro
explanation: Bunshiro - A name derived from the fusion of "letters" and "fourth son", reflecting a balance between the humility of a younger child and the standing that learning confers. It is often embraced by those who strive for advancement by the brush rather than by birth.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (Kiyose). Kanji 文四郎, bun (letters, learning) plus shiro (fourth son), the standard -shiro birth-order ending. A commoner everyday-name style, though -shiro names were also borne by samurai as common names.

name: Bungoro
explanation: Bungoro - Derived from the phrase "the fifth son learns his letters", this name embodies the idea of a younger child making his way through learning when there is no land left to inherit. It is often associated with those who become clerks, scribes and shopkeepers in a river town.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 文五郎, bun (letters, learning) plus goro (fifth son), a birth-order ending. A commoner everyday-name style; -goro names were extremely common among Edo townsmen.

name: Bunzo
explanation: Bunzo - This name represents a storehouse of learning and is often chosen by those who are clerks or scribes or who are expected to keep a family's records honestly.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers and an Edo village register, with bearers on Japanese Wikipedia as well. Kanji 文蔵, bun (letters, learning) plus zo (storehouse), a very common Edo commoner ending. A commoner everyday-name style. The novelist Kodo Nomura's fictional detective Zenigata Heiji is often paired with his assistant Hachigoro, not Bunzo, but Bunzo remains a stock period-drama townsman name.

name: Eicho
explanation: Eicho - This name means "flourishing morning". It represents the moment when a new dawn is greeted with gratitude, and the hope that one's faith will brighten with each day.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: a Kamakura-period Buddhist monk's name with a bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 栄朝, ei (flourish, glory) plus cho (morning, or dynasty/court). A monk's name style, read entirely in on-reading as monastic names are. Eicho (1165-1247) was a Tendai monk and an early figure in the Zen lineage of Eisai.

name: Ekei
explanation: Ekei - This name is inspired by the natural element of fine jade drawn from a riverbed, symbolizing a blessing that is found rather than made. It is often chosen for its connection to the polished stone of mountain streams and its representation of grace, worth and a gift one is obliged to pass on.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Our metadata lists it as a nanori, but the famous bearer, Ankokuji Ekei (d. 1600), was a Rinzai monk and diplomat for the Mori, so this is a monk's name in on-reading, not a samurai formal name. Kanji 恵瓊, e (blessing, grace) plus kei (fine jade, jewel). The reading is straightforward.

name: Eigen
explanation: Eigen - Derived from the phrase "eternal solemnity", this name embodies the idea of a dignity that does not waver with the years. It is often associated with those who take monastic vows or who retire from office to a life of stern devotion.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 永厳, ei (eternal) plus gen (stern, solemn). An on-reading name of the kind borne by monks and by samurai in retirement, so its style sits between monastic and formal.

name: Eizaburo
explanation: Eizaburo - This name signifies a third son whose family hopes he will flourish, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values prosperity earned in one's own right rather than inherited.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 栄三郎, ei (flourish, glory) plus saburo (third son), a birth-order ending. A commoner everyday-name style, very typical of Edo townsmen.

name: Eihachi
explanation: Eihachi was a deity that was said to have made a poor family's single rice plant branch eight ways after the farmer shared his last bowl with a beggar at the roadside.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed on the attested Edo prefix-plus-suffix pattern of commoner names (Wasuke 和助, Otokichi 乙吉), here the attested prefix Ei- (栄, flourish) with the attested number suffix -hachi (八, eight). Kanji 栄八. A commoner everyday-name style. The name is plausible enough that a real Edo bearer may well exist outside our registers. The deity in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Denkichi
explanation: Denkichi chose their name in honor of the famous Ide Denkichi, who carried a dying magistrate's sealed judgment across three provinces so that a wrongly accused farmer could be freed before the harvest.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 傳吉 (傳 is the old form of 伝), den (transmit, tradition) plus kichi (good luck), the most common of all Edo commoner name endings. A commoner everyday-name style.

name: Denbachi
explanation: Denbachi - This name signifies the eight traditions handed down from father to son, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values continuity, the old ways of a household and the duty to pass on what was received.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 傳八 (傳 is the old form of 伝), den (transmit, tradition) plus hachi (eight), a number suffix; the -b- in Denbachi is the usual voicing after -n. A commoner everyday-name style.

name: Daikuro
explanation: Daikuro - Composed of the elements "great" and "ninth son", this name symbolizes a late-born child of large promise. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of strength and of a house so blessed that even its ninth son is counted a gift.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 大九郎, dai (great) plus kuro (ninth son), a birth-order ending. Though classed as a nanori in our metadata, -kuro names are the everyday-name (tsusho) style that samurai used alongside their formal names, so it reads as a common name for any caste.

name: Domanmaru
explanation: Domanmaru - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Full Road, in which a boy walking the whole of the Emperor's highway found every waystation full and slept instead beneath the stars, where the Fortunes showed him his path. It reflects qualities such as patience, contentment, and trust in the Way.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Muromachi-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 道満丸, do (road, the Way) plus man (full) plus -maru, the childhood-name suffix; despite the nanori tag this is a yomyo, a boy's name borne before coming of age. Its best-known bearer was Domanmaru (d. 1579), a young son of Uesugi Kagetora killed in the Otate succession war. A samurai childhood-name style.

name: Doan
explanation: Doan - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The simple hut holds the deepest learning", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value humility, scholarship, and retreat from the noise of court.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: late-Edo bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 侗庵, do (simple, unlearned, a humility word) plus an (hermitage, thatched hut). This is a scholar's art name (go) rather than a birth name: Koga Doan (1788-1847) was a Confucian scholar of the shogunate's academy. A retired-scholar or monk's name style, not a samurai formal name.

name: Dosei
explanation: Dosei - With origins in the legend of the monk Dosei, who walked westward for forty years toward the paradise of the setting sun and was found seated in peace at the edge of the Empire, this name evokes a sense of serenity and steadfast faith. It appeals to those who admire devotion that outlasts the body.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 道西, do (road, the Way) plus sei (west), the west being the direction of the Pure Land. Names of this shape were taken by lay believers and warriors on entering religion, so despite the nanori tag it is a Buddhist lay-name style rather than a samurai formal name.

name: Rikichi
explanation: Rikichi - Stemming from the word "ri", which denotes reason and the underlying principle of things, this name embodies the spirit of good fortune that follows sound judgment. It resonates with those who are careful, orderly, and lucky in trade.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 理吉, ri (reason, principle) plus kichi (good luck), the commonest Edo commoner ending. A commoner everyday-name style.

name: Rokuzaemon
explanation: Rokuzaemon - A name derived from the fusion of "six" and "guardian of the left gate", reflecting a balance between a humble place in the birth order and a proud old office. It is often embraced by those who strive for steady, unglamorous service.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 六左衛門, roku (six) plus -zaemon from 左衛門, the ancient Left Palace Guard office that became a stock name ending. A commoner everyday-name style, though -zaemon names were borne by samurai as common names too.

name: Rokuemon
explanation: Rokuemon - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of gate-guarding, this name represents the sixth watchman at the right-hand gate. It is often chosen by those who appreciate vigilance and have a deep respect for the old palace guard offices from which such names descend.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 六右衛門, roku (six) plus -emon from 右衛門, the ancient Right Palace Guard office that became a stock name ending. A commoner everyday-name style, also used by samurai as an everyday name.

name: Risuke
explanation: The name Risuke is associated with the famous Reckoning of the Salt Road, in which a merchant's clerk uncovered a decade of false tallies and returned the missing profit to the province rather than keep it. Those who choose this name try to embody values of honesty in gain and helpfulness to one's master.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 利助, ri (profit, advantage) plus suke (help), one of the commonest Edo commoner endings. A commoner everyday-name style, characteristic of merchant houses.

name: Raishun
explanation: Raishun - This name pays tribute to the Festival of Relying Spring, an event that emphasizes trust in the returning year and the talents that ripen with it. People choose this name to reflect their values for reliability and quiet excellence.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period Buddhist bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 頼俊, rai (rely on, trust) plus shun (talented, excellent). A monk's name style in full on-reading; the same kanji read in kun would be the samurai nanori Yoritoshi.

name: Raisho
explanation: Raisho - This name represents a light that can be relied upon and is often chosen by those who are teachers or temple keepers or who are expected to guide others through dark seasons.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period Buddhist bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 頼照, rai (rely on) plus sho (shine, illuminate). A monk's name style in on-reading; read in kun the same kanji give the samurai nanori Yoriteru.

name: Raitoku
explanation: Raitoku - With origins in the legend of Brother Raitoku, a wandering monk who walked from village to village promising each one a virtue not yet visible in it and returning years later to find it grown, this name evokes a sense of hope and patient faith. It appeals to those who admire the trust that sows a seed it may never see harvested.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in a Kamakura-period register (nihonjin-name), written 来とく with the second element in kana; the conventional kanji spelling is 来徳, rai (come, arrive) plus toku (virtue). A commoner name in on-reading, of the religious-sounding kind medieval villagers often bore. The monk in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Otomatsu
explanation: Otomatsu - This name is inspired by the natural element of the pine, symbolizing endurance through every season and the voice of the wind in its branches. It is often chosen for its connection to the evergreen groves around a village shrine and its representation of long life, steadiness and a song that does not fade.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (Kiyose). Kanji 音松, oto (sound) plus matsu (pine), the pine being the standard auspicious suffix for longevity. A commoner everyday-name style.

name: Okiaki
explanation: Okiaki - This name is inspired by the natural element of the rising sun, symbolizing brightness that comes up out of darkness. It is often chosen for its connection to the first light over the eastern hills and its representation of revival, renewed fortune and a clear beginning.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 興明, oki (rise, revive) plus aki (bright). A samurai formal-name (nanori) style in two kun readings.

name: Onaga
explanation: Onaga - This name signifies a hero who endures, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values a courage that lasts longer than a single charge.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 雄長, o (male, hero) plus naga (long, enduring). A samurai formal-name (nanori) style. Onaga is also a common Okinawan surname, an unrelated modern association.

name: Otohisa
explanation: Otohisa - A name that means "lasting sound", evoking a reputation that keeps echoing after the deed is done.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Muromachi-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 音久, oto (sound) plus hisa (long-lasting). A samurai formal-name (nanori) style, with an unusual first element; oto- is rare in nanori and the reading should be flagged as a stylized one.

name: Otokichi
explanation: Otokichi chose their name in honor of the famous Kaiu Otokichi, who kept a castle's kitchens fed through a winter siege by trading his own small fortune for rice.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed on the attested Edo prefix-plus-suffix pattern of commoner names, here the prefix Oto- (乙, second, junior) with the suffix -kichi (吉, good luck). Kanji 乙吉. In honesty the name is real: Otokichi was a common Edo commoner name, the best-known bearer being the castaway Yamamoto Otokichi (1818-1867), though his name was usually written 音吉. A commoner everyday-name style.

name: Otobei
explanation: Otobei was a deity that was said to have stood guard at the second gate of the Heavens after the first gate's keeper fell asleep and let a hungry ghost slip through.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed on the attested Edo prefix-plus-suffix pattern of commoner names (Wasuke 和助, Otokichi 乙吉), here the prefix Oto- (乙, second, junior) with the suffix -bei from 兵衛, the old guard office. Kanji 乙兵衛. A commoner everyday-name style; a real Edo bearer is likely to exist outside our registers.

name: Zendayu
explanation: Zendayu - Derived from the phrase "good master of the house", this name embodies the idea of a benevolent head of household. It is often associated with those who lead a troupe, a guild, or a village with a generous hand.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 善太夫, zen (good, virtuous) plus -dayu from 太夫, an old court rank title that became a name ending and, later, the title of troupe masters and chanters. Despite the nanori tag this is an everyday-name (tsusho) style used by samurai and commoners alike.

name: Zenkuro
explanation: Zenkuro - Composed of the elements "virtue" and "ninth son", this name symbolizes goodness in a child born late and low in the order. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of kindness and modesty.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo merchant registers. Kanji 善九郎, zen (good, virtuous) plus kuro (ninth son), a birth-order ending. A commoner everyday-name style.

name: Zoryu
explanation: Zoryu - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Growing Peak, in which a monk vowed to add one stone to a cairn each morning until it stood taller than his temple, and the mountain itself is said to have risen to meet him. It reflects qualities such as patience, accumulation, and quiet ambition.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period Buddhist bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 増隆, zo (increase) plus ryu (prosper, rise). A monk's name style in on-reading; read in kun the same kanji give the samurai nanori Masutaka.

name: Zean
explanation: Zean - Rooted in the ancient proverb "What is right is what is peaceful", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value calm judgment and the belief that justice brings ease.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Azuchi-Momoyama-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 是安, ze (this, right, correct) plus an (peace). An on-reading name of the kind taken by lay Buddhists, physicians, and retired warriors; despite the nanori tag it is not the usual kun-reading samurai formal-name style.

name: Bonshun
explanation: Bonshun - With origins in the legend of the priest Bonshun, who kept a daily record of every omen at the shrine for fifty years so that later diviners could read the will of the Heavens, this name evokes a sense of diligence and sacred memory. It appeals to those who admire those who serve by recording.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period Buddhist bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 梵舜, bon (Brahma, the sacred) plus shun (the sage-king Shun, hence wise). A monk's name style in on-reading. The historical Bonshun (1553-1632) was a Shinto-Buddhist priest of the Yoshida house whose diary is a major source for the period.

name: Wasuke
explanation: Wasuke - Stemming from the word "wa", which denotes harmony and peace, this name embodies the spirit of the helper who keeps a household in accord. It resonates with those who are conciliatory, patient, and quick to smooth a quarrel.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed on the attested Edo prefix-plus-suffix pattern of commoner names, here the prefix Wa- (和, harmony) with the suffix -suke (助, help). Kanji 和助. In honesty this combination is very likely attested: Wasuke is a stock Edo townsman name that appears in period fiction and records, though not in the registers we hold. A commoner everyday-name style.

name: Wakakichi
explanation: Wakakichi was a deity that was said to have brought the first green shoots up through a late frost after a village had given up its spring planting for lost.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed on the attested Edo prefix-plus-suffix pattern of commoner names (Wasuke 和助, Otokichi 乙吉), here the prefix Waka- (若, young) with the suffix -kichi (吉, good luck). Kanji 若吉. A commoner everyday-name style; a real Edo bearer may exist outside our registers. The deity in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Wakasuke
explanation: Wakasuke was a deity that was said to have taken the shape of a farm boy to carry water for an old couple through a drought after their own sons had gone to war.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed on the attested Edo prefix-plus-suffix pattern of commoner names (Wasuke 和助, Otokichi 乙吉), here the prefix Waka- (若, young) with the suffix -suke (助, help). Kanji 若助. A commoner everyday-name style; a real Edo bearer may exist outside our registers. The deity in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Rokubei
explanation: Rokubei - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the potter's wheel, this name represents the sixth guardian who tends the kiln fire through the night. It is often chosen by those who appreciate patient craft and have a deep respect for the artisans who serve the fire.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Sengoku-period bearer on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 六兵衛, roku (six) plus -bei from 兵衛, the old palace-guard office that became a stock name ending. Despite the nanori tag this is an everyday-name (tsusho) style shared by samurai and commoners. Kiyomizu Rokubei is a lineage of Kyoto potters continuing to the present day, hence the craft association.

name: Akinao
explanation: The name Akinao is associated with the famous Judgment of the Burned Ledgers, in which a provincial magistrate uncovered a ring of tax farmers who had cooked the rice tallies of a whole district, and read the true figures aloud before the daimyo from copies they had hidden in advance. Those who choose this name try to embody values of clear sight, incorruptibility and the courage to say plainly what the numbers show.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 詮直: 詮 ("to clarify, to examine, to explain") read with the nanori reading "aki", seen in the Ashikaga line (Yoshiakira 義詮), plus 直 (nao, "straight, honest, upright"). A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Akihide
explanation: The name Akihide is inspired by the Lantern Terraces of the Crane coast, known for their tiers of paper lamps lit each evening so that ships returning late can find the harbor. The name reflects the brightness of the place and is often chosen by those who value clarity of purpose, excellence in craft and a light kept burning for others.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 昭秀: 昭 (aki, "bright, shining") plus 秀 (hide, "excellent, to surpass"); both are standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Akimori
explanation: Akimori - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the Polished Mirror, a shrine observance held on the first clear night of autumn when every household sets out its brass mirror to catch the moonlight. People choose this name to reflect their values for self-examination, guarding what has been entrusted to them and a life that bears looking into.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: bearers of the Kamakura and Sengoku periods on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 鑑盛: 鑑 ("mirror, model, to examine") read with the nanori reading "aki", the reading the Otomo family of Kyushu used for it (as in Takahashi Akitane 鑑種), plus 盛 (mori, "to flourish, to prosper"). The "aki" reading of 鑑 is a stylized nanori reading, not an everyday one. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Akiyasu
explanation: Akiyasu - This name represents an evident and settled peace and is often chosen by those who are steady, plain-spoken heads of household or who are expected to keep a domain calm through plain and visible good order.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 顕泰: 顕 (aki, "evident, manifest, distinguished") plus 泰 (yasu, "peace, calm, great"); both standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Akitomi
explanation: Akitomi - This name means "present wealth". It represents the prosperity that is already in hand rather than the fortune that is hoped for, and the duty of a steward to keep what exists rather than gamble it on what might be.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 在富: 在 ("to exist, to be present") read with the nanori reading "aki", plus 富 (tomi, "wealth, abundance"). Note that 在 is more commonly read "ari" in names (Aritomi), so "Akitomi" is a stylized nanori reading; the Japanese Wikipedia record gives it this way. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Arimasa
explanation: Arimasa means "possessing elegance" or "refinement made real", which can suggest a courtier whose grace is more than manner or a man who carries the forms of the court into ordinary life. People with this name may be polished, exacting about etiquette and quietly proud of it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 有雅: 有 (ari, "to have, to exist") plus 雅 (masa, "elegance, refinement"); both are standard nanori readings, 有 as "ari" being the usual one for that character. A samurai formal-name style, and the 雅 element is characteristic of court-adjacent families. No notable modern association.

name: Arinori
explanation: Arinori means "possessing the rule" or "having a model", which can suggest a bushi who holds himself to the pattern of his ancestors or one who embodies the standard others measure themselves by. People with this name may be exacting, upright and hard to fault.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 有範: 有 (ari, "to have, to possess") plus 範 (nori, "model, rule, pattern"). Both are standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. Modern bearers include Mori Arinori (森有礼, 1847-1889), the Meiji statesman, though with a different second kanji.

name: Aritada
explanation: Aritada - This name signifies loyalty that a man actually possesses rather than merely professes, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values deeds over declarations and a fidelity that survives being tested.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 有忠: 有 (ari, "to have, to possess") plus 忠 (tada, "loyalty, devotion"); both standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Atsumori
explanation: Atsumori - A name that means "sincere and flourishing", evoking the young warrior who goes to his fate with a flute in his sash, whose earnestness outlives him in song.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, most famously Taira no Atsumori (1169-1184), the young Taira warrior slain at Ichi-no-tani. Written 敦盛: 敦 (atsu, "sincere, kind, cordial") plus 盛 (mori, "to flourish, to prosper"); both standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. The name is very strongly associated with the Noh play Atsumori and the kowakamai dance Oda Nobunaga is said to have performed before Okehazama ("Human life, fifty years").

name: Atsusada
explanation: Atsusada chose their name in honor of the famous Ikoma Atsusada, who held a mountain pass for three days with forty men so that the households of an entire valley could reach the safety of the castle town.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 篤貞: 篤 (atsu, "sincere, earnest, kind") plus 貞 (sada, "constancy, chastity, righteousness"); both standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Atsumichi
explanation: Atsumichi - A name derived from the fusion of "sincere" and "road", reflecting a balance between kindness of heart and the discipline of the way one walks. It is often embraced by those who strive for an honest path through the world and mastery of whatever road they are set on.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Azuchi-Momoyama period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 敦通: 敦 (atsu, "sincere, kind") plus 通 (michi, "to pass through, road, to be versed in"); both standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Arikage
explanation: Arikage - Derived from the phrase "there is a shadow where there is a light", this name embodies the idea of the quiet man who stands behind a lord and makes the lord look brilliant. It is often associated with those who serve as retainers, advisors and second sons.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 有景: 有 (ari, "to have, to exist") plus 景 (kage, "scene, light, shadow"); 景 as "kage" is a standard nanori reading and its meaning covers both light and the shadow it casts. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Fusaie
explanation: Fusaie - Composed of the elements "chamber" and "house", this name symbolizes the household itself, the private rooms and the lineage that inhabits them. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of domestic continuity and a family line that will not be broken.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 房家: 房 ("chamber, room, tassel") read with the nanori reading "fusa", plus 家 (ie, "house, family"); both are standard nanori readings, 房 as "fusa" being common in Sengoku names. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Fusanobu
explanation: Fusanobu - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Faithful Steward, in which a retainer keeps his lord and the household of the lord fed through a siege by trusting the word of a rice merchant every other samurai had scorned. It reflects qualities such as trust extended wisely, loyalty to the house and the good faith that binds a household together.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 房信: 房 (fusa, "chamber, room, tassel") plus 信 (nobu, "trust, faith"); both standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Fusatada
explanation: Fusatada - Rooted in the ancient proverb "Loyalty begins at the door of the inner room", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value fidelity to household and lord before any public show of it.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 房忠: 房 (fusa, "chamber, room, tassel") plus 忠 (tada, "loyalty, devotion"); both standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Fuyuhira
explanation: Fuyuhira - With origins in the legend of the Winter Magistrate, who kept a snowbound province at peace through a famine winter by rationing the granaries with a fairness no one could fault, this name evokes a sense of cold-weather steadiness and even-handed calm. It appeals to those who admire officials who are hardest to move when times are hardest.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 冬平: 冬 (fuyu, "winter") plus 平 (hira, "flat, level, peaceful"); both standard nanori readings, and 冬 is a hereditary name element of the Kamakura-era Nijo and Ichijo court families. A samurai formal-name style with a court flavor. No notable modern association.

name: Fuyunori
explanation: Fuyunori - This name is inspired by the natural element of winter, symbolizing the lean season in which teaching goes on when the fields are idle. It is often chosen for its connection to the long nights of study and its representation of patience, discipline and instruction that endures the cold.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 冬教: 冬 (fuyu, "winter") plus 教 ("teaching, doctrine") read with the nanori reading "nori"; both are standard nanori readings, and 冬 is a hereditary element of the Nijo and Ichijo court families. A samurai formal-name style with a court flavor. No notable modern association.

name: Fuyumune
explanation: Fuyumune - This name is inspired by the natural element of winter, symbolizing the season in which a house shows what it is truly made of. It is often chosen for its connection to the still, bare months and its representation of the principles a family holds to when there is nothing to distract from them.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Muromachi-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 冬宗: 冬 (fuyu, "winter") plus 宗 (mune, "principle, origin, main line, sect"); both standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Fujifusa
explanation: Fujifusa - A name derived from the fusion of "wisteria" and "chamber", reflecting a balance between outward grace and the inner rooms where a house keeps its counsel. It is often embraced by those who strive for courtly polish without losing the discretion of a private man.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Kamakura-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia, notably Madenokoji Fujifusa (万里小路藤房, 1296-1380), the courtier who served Emperor Go-Daigo and then took Buddhist vows. Written 藤房: 藤 (fuji, "wisteria", also the character of the Fujiwara) plus 房 (fusa, "chamber, tassel"); both standard readings. A court and samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association beyond the historical bearer.

name: Fujisada
explanation: Fujisada - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of wisteria training, in which a gardener guides a vine for decades so that its trailing blossoms fall in a single ordered curtain, this name represents constancy that shapes beauty over a lifetime. It is often chosen by those who appreciate patient discipline and have a deep respect for gardeners whose work will be finished by their grandchildren.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 藤定: 藤 (fuji, "wisteria") plus 定 (sada, "settled, fixed, constant"); both standard nanori readings. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Fuminaga
explanation: The name Fuminaga is associated with the famous Compilation of the Long Annals, in which a scribe of the Imperial archives spent forty years restoring the burned court records of three reigns from provincial copies, so that the history of the Empire would not have a gap in it. Those who choose this name try to embody values of scholarship, perseverance and a duty to the written record that outlasts the writer.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 文脩: 文 (fumi, "writing, letters, learning") plus 脩 ("to cultivate, to lengthen", a rarer variant of 修) read with the nanori reading "naga". The "naga" reading of 脩 is stylized and unusual; a modern reader would expect "shū" or "osamu", and the same name is sometimes read Fumiosa. A formal name of the Heian scholarly-official class rather than a warrior name. No notable modern association.

name: Fumiyuki
explanation: The name Fumiyuki is inspired by the Road of Scholars in the Phoenix lands, known for its wayside shrines where travelers leave a single written line for the Fortune of Wisdom. The name reflects the studious spirit of the place and is often chosen by those who value learning carried into action, a journey undertaken for the sake of knowledge and the pen kept as close as the sword.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Heian-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 文行: 文 (fumi, "writing, letters, learning") plus 行 (yuki, "to go, conduct"); both standard nanori readings. A formal name of the Heian official class, later a samurai-style nanori. No notable modern association.

name: Furuyasu
explanation: Furuyasu - This name pays tribute to the Festival of Old Peace, a village observance held on the anniversary of the day a domain laid down its arms after a generation of war, when the eldest villager reads the names of those who did not live to see it. People choose this name to reflect their values for the peace their grandparents bought, remembrance of the old wars and the settled quiet of a long-ordered land.
notes: Attested samurai nanori: Sengoku-period bearers on Japanese Wikipedia. Written 古康: 古 (furu, "old, ancient") plus 康 (yasu, "ease, peace, health"); both standard readings. 古 is an unusual first element for a nanori, likely inherited from a family name or lord, but the reading is straightforward. A samurai formal-name style. No notable modern association.

name: Fusataro
explanation: Fusataro - This name represents the eldest son of a house of many rooms and is often chosen by those who are firstborn heirs of a prosperous shop or who are expected to keep every branch of the family under one roof.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in late Edo merchant registers. Written 房太郎: 房 (fusa, "chamber, room, tassel") plus 太郎 (tarō, "eldest son", the standard commoner and everyday suffix for a firstborn). All readings are standard. A commoner and everyday (tsūshō) style, not a samurai formal name; -tarō names were used by townsmen and villagers of every station. No notable modern association.

name: Wakamaru
explanation: Wakamaru chose their name in honor of the famous Matsu Wakamaru, who as a boy not yet of age held his family's gate against raiders through a whole night until the household's bushi returned.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (the Edo commoner prefix + suffix pattern for men's everyday names); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 若 (waka, young) + 丸 (maru, circle) reads Wakamaru; -maru is the classic childhood-name suffix, so this reads as a boy's or everyday name rather than a formal one. Commoner everyday style, not a samurai formal name; a samurai boy might bear it before his coming of age. Wakamaru is also the name of a Mitsubishi household robot. The famous Matsu Wakamaru in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Waichi
explanation: Waichi - Rooted in the ancient proverb "harmony first, then the harvest", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value peace within the household, an eldest son who keeps his brothers in concord and the quiet work that must come before any reward.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (the Edo commoner prefix + suffix pattern for men's everyday names); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 和 (wa, harmony) + 一 (ichi, one) reads Waichi; -ichi is the standard eldest-son suffix in Edo commoner naming. Commoner everyday style, not a samurai formal name. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Wakamatsu
explanation: Wakamatsu - This name is inspired by the natural element of the young pine, symbolizing a hardy sapling that will stand for a hundred years. It is often chosen for its connection to the evergreen groves planted at a village edge and its representation of youthful vigor, long life and quiet endurance.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (the Edo commoner prefix + suffix pattern for men's everyday names); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 若 (waka, young) + 松 (matsu, pine) reads Wakamatsu. Commoner everyday style, not a samurai formal name; -matsu is a common auspicious suffix in Edo commoner names. Caution: Wakamatsu is far better known as a place name (Aizu-Wakamatsu) and a surname than as a given name.

name: Hidemasa
explanation: Hidemasa can be written with two different kanji. One means "excellent and correct", and the other means "excellent governance". The choice of kanji could reflect what a family hopes the boy will excel at, such as an upright personal conduct or a gift for administering a domain.
notes: Hidemasa is a real Japanese male given name, written 秀正 (excellent + correct) or 秀政 (excellent + governance). Several historical samurai bore this name.
